Their mother is travelling to Petra to visit her sister, whom she has not seen since the last flood. The younger girl wants good dates in every basket so her aunt's children can taste them too. Their mother is indoors sewing a waterskin. She comes out to test the seam, blows air into it, and asks why the girls have filled three baskets when she meant to carry two. The younger one admits she packed a third for the relatives. Mother smiles and asks them to make it small enough for the mule.

Another group in the yard is preparing for Bethlehem. Both groups draw from the same well, their buckets lined up beside it. A driver walks past with a bundle of blankets and nearly takes the wrong water jar. The younger sister calls him back, then looks at her unmarked baskets. "What if they take ours by mistake?" she asks you. The older one has a piece of charcoal but her hands are sticky from the dates. Their mother is still holding the waterskin open, waiting to know which basket to tie to the mule.
ev.cairo.caravan.choice.baskets: Help the sisters mark their baskets
ev.cairo.caravan.choice.bethlehem: Carry the baskets inside, then ask when the Bethlehem caravan leaves
ev.cairo.caravan.result.baskets:
You find a piece of charcoal. The younger sister draws a little star under each basket while the older writes their mother's name. Their mother comes out with the sewn waterskin and sees the marks at once. "Who taught you that?" The girl says she thought of it herself; even far from home, they will recognise their baskets.

The older sister puts the softest dates in her mother's small bag. They thank you, and the keeper of the yard remembers your help.
ev.cairo.caravan.result.bethlehem:
You carry the baskets to the door. Their mother is testing the waterskin seam and asks the girls to move the fruit into the shade. Outside, a driver bound for Bethlehem says his group leaves after dawn through the east gate and will wait for the rear wagons at the crossing.

The younger sister hears you asking directions and presses a date into your hand. "For the road. If you see a basket with a little star, that's ours."
ev.cairo.caravan.title: Date Baskets in the Caravan Yard
ev.calatu.a.body: On the wall above Calatu's harbour, a watchman has drawn the morning's ships with charcoal: two low boats, one high-sterned vessel and a grain carrier still outside the bend. His young assistant insists the high-sterned ship arrived first. “Then why is its gangplank still on deck?” the watchman asks. They look again and see that it has only turned to find deeper water. The assistant crosses out his mark and calls to a porter below to hold a space for the grain boat. You ask where the ships came from. The watchman points across the gulf toward Ormus, then along the coast toward Dufar. A merchant waiting on the steps says her pepper is on one of those vessels and wants to know when she can collect it. “When it ties up and the clerk reads your mark,” the assistant answers, pleased to say something certain. He invites you to walk the wall while he finishes the list.
ev.calatu.a.choice.buy_pepper: Buy a bag of pepper from the merchant
ev.calatu.a.choice.count_ships: Ask which ships are bound for Dufar
ev.calatu.a.choice.walk_walls: Spend a day walking the wall with the watchman
ev.calatu.a.title: The Watchman’s Harbour List
ev.calatu.b.body: At the storehouse, a guard is checking the grain reserved for the people on the wall. A younger porter has brought the wrong size of sack and wants to swap it quietly. “Put both weights on the board,” the guard tells him. “Then we can fix the count together.” The porter admits he was hurrying to meet his sister at the quay. You ask why the guard needs such a careful reserve. He points to the fortified harbour. “People from Ormus have used Calatu as a safer place when trouble came to the gulf. The walls are useful only while the town can feed the hands behind them.” A date seller nearby says her small boat brought food that morning and asks where to unload. The guard gives the porter a new tally and tells him to help her. Before they go, he offers to show you the coast road and the inland caravan names written on the storehouse map. The porter holds the corrected tally against his chest so he will not lose it on the way.
ev.calatu.b.choice.ask_inland: Ask about the roads to Camadi and Dufar
ev.calatu.b.choice.buy_dates: Buy a small serving of dates from the boat
ev.calatu.b.choice.hear_refuge: Ask how the town supplies people behind the walls
ev.calatu.b.title: The Storehouse by the Wall
ev.calatu.entry.body: A grain boat has just come into Calatu, and a woman is distributing its sacks between the town store and the market. Her son counts aloud, then pauses when a fisherman asks for the sack she promised his household. “I wrote his name on the other side,” she tells the boy. He turns the board over and finds it. You ask why a harbour town keeps such close track of grain. “The hills give us stone,” she says, “and the boats bring much of our food. My neighbours will ask before sunset whether their flour has arrived.” The fisherman offers to carry a sack for the older porter beside him. A guard at the wall calls down that he will leave the gate open until the last load is inside. His friend asks whether there will still be room for dates at the market. “If you stop eating them before they reach the stall,” the woman answers. She shows you the street through town and the mosque door near the wall.
ev.calatu.entry.choice.market: Spend a day among the harbour stalls
ev.calatu.entry.choice.pass: Ask the way through and continue
ev.calatu.entry.choice.shrine: Visit the mosque near the wall
ev.calatu.entry.title: The Grain Boat at Calatu
ev.calatu.shoemaker.body: A shoemaker near the wall has been asked to mend the sandals of a guard's daughter before she walks to her grandmother's house. The girl brings them in with one strap hanging loose. “You tied it again,” the shoemaker says. “I thought it would last until I got here,” she replies. Her father is at the harbour gate and cannot leave his post, so he has sent a little money with her. The shoemaker tests the leather and tells her the strap can be replaced. She asks whether he can use the old one; it belonged to her mother. He holds it against the light and finds a strong section near the buckle. “This part will do. Sit here and tell me how far you have to walk.” She names the lane and the grandmother's door. You can help the shoemaker cut and fit the strap, or accompany the girl through the lanes once it is ready.
ev.calatu.shoemaker.choice.mend: Help the shoemaker fit the old strap
ev.calatu.shoemaker.choice.walk: Walk with the girl to her grandmother’s door
ev.calatu.shoemaker.result.mend: You hold the sandal while the shoemaker cuts the sound piece of leather and sets it beneath the buckle. The girl tries both sandals on the shop floor and runs a few steps. Her father brings the promised payment; the shoemaker gives you a share for the work.
ev.calatu.shoemaker.result.walk: With her sandals mended, the girl leads you along the lane she described. Her grandmother opens the door before you knock and asks why she came with a stranger. “Because Father was at the gate,” the girl says, showing the repaired strap. The grandmother thanks you and sends a message back to him.
ev.calatu.shoemaker.title: Shoes for the Guard’s Daughter
ev.camadi.a.body:
Banu leads her grandson through a broken arch. ‘Your great-grandfather kept his dates over there,’ she says, pointing to a patch of wall. The boy asks why they moved. She tells him that the old quarter was damaged in fighting, and the family built again closer to the water.

There is still a path through the ruins toward the Kerman road. Banu will walk it with you, sell you a small bag of dates to eat on the journey, or introduce you to caravan people who know the way toward Cobinan.

The boy asks whether the old house had the same door as theirs now. Banu shows him two stone sockets where a wooden door once turned. ‘Your great-grandfather could hear a camel coming before he saw it,’ she says. You ask what he sold. ‘Mostly dates. If a neighbour had no fruit that week, he let her use the cool room to store hers.’ A caravan driver passing the arch calls Banu by name and asks whether the Kerman turn is still open. She offers to walk there with you and show you.
ev.camadi.a.choice.ask_raids: Ask the caravan people how they choose a safe road
ev.camadi.a.choice.buy_dates: Buy a small bag of dates for 1.2 silver
ev.camadi.a.choice.walk_ruins: Spend a day walking Banu’s old street
ev.camadi.a.title: Banu’s Old Street
ev.camadi.b.body:
A narrow channel feeds Banu’s date palms. Her neighbour covers a basket of fruit against the sun, while two travellers share water under the trees. Beside the fruit stall is a bale of cotton cloth packed for a merchant caravan. One traveller asks where the inland road reaches Hormuz, the port for ships toward Calatu.

Banu says she can name the road to Hormuz and its onward sea passage toward Calatu, as well as the road back to Kerman. You may rest with the travellers for the day or buy the full bale of cloth from the neighbour.

‘Do the boats leave every day?’ the traveller asks. Banu shakes her head. ‘Ask the sailors when you reach the port. I can tell you the road, not their departure.’ Her neighbour lifts the corner of the cotton bale and asks whether you want to see the weave before buying the whole lot. You ask if the cloth has travelled far already. ‘Only from the fields to my loom,’ she says. ‘Your caravan would take it farther than I have.’
ev.camadi.b.choice.ask_calatu: Ask Banu about Calatu and Kerman
ev.camadi.b.choice.buy_cotton: Buy the merchant bale of cotton cloth for 108 silver
ev.camadi.b.choice.rest_shade: Spend a day sharing the shade and water
ev.camadi.b.title: A Hot Afternoon by the Canal
ev.camadi.entry.body:
Camadi stands on a hot plain at the foot of the hills. Old walls stand beside lived-in houses, and date palms shade a row of stalls. A fruit seller named Banu sorts dates while her grandson searches the basket for a pistachio he dropped. Nearby, a merchant asks whether she has any of the fruit travellers call ‘apples of paradise.’

‘Leave that nut,’ Banu tells her grandson. ‘The birds will find it before you do.’ She gives him another, then shows the merchant what remains of the fruit. She tells you where to refill water before crossing the plain. She remembers when more families lived beyond the old walls, and she still knows the names of the lanes there.

A mule driver asks Banu whether her old lane still has a roofed place to rest. ‘The roof is gone,’ she says, ‘but my cousin’s house is beside it. Tell him I sent you.’ Her grandson asks why everyone comes to her for directions. Banu hands him a date and says, ‘Because I have sent them all to your cousin at least once.’ You ask how far the next dependable water is. She sets down the basket to point it out rather than guessing while she works.
ev.camadi.entry.choice.market: Spend a day at the fruit stalls
ev.camadi.entry.title: Camadi at the Edge of the Plain
ev.camadi.oldwell.body:
Behind a row of date palms, two siblings are clearing stones from a well mouth. Their mother remembers drawing water there as a child. The younger one has already hauled out three baskets of gravel and wants to stop; the elder thinks they can finish before the next caravan arrives.

Their mother asks what help you can give. You can spend the day clearing the last stones with them, or walk to the caravan yard and bring the water carriers back to help finish the work.

The younger sibling asks how much more stone they must move. His sister lowers a rope and lets him hear it touch water. ‘Only the top is blocked,’ she says. Their mother laughs at how seriously they have taken a well she once thought abandoned. You ask whether other people may use it when they finish. ‘Of course,’ she answers. ‘That is why the water carriers should know about it.’ The brother looks toward the caravan yard and wonders whether anyone there will lend them a stronger basket.
ev.camadi.oldwell.choice.clear: Spend a day clearing the well
ev.camadi.oldwell.choice.tell: Bring the water carriers to help finish the well
ev.camadi.oldwell.result.clear: You work with the family until the well can be used comfortably. Their mother draws the first bucket and shares the cool water with everyone. After a day’s labour and rest, you feel refreshed.
ev.camadi.oldwell.result.tell: At the caravan yard, the water carriers listen and follow you back to the palms. They help move the last heavy stones, and the family thanks you for bringing them. Word of your help spreads through Camadi.
ev.camadi.oldwell.title: The Well behind the Date Trees
ev.cambaet.entry.body: A dyer in Cambaet is hanging lengths of indigo cloth above the lane. Her apprentice holds one end too low, and a passing merchant nearly walks into it. “Lift it above his turban,” she says. The merchant ducks and asks whether his order has dried. “The dark bolts have. Your sister asked for the lighter shade, remember?” she replies. He admits that he has forgotten which of his family placed the order and pulls a creased note from his belt. She smooths it against a board and reads the mark she made beside the sister’s name. You ask why she uses two blue threads to mark the bundle. “One tells me how often it went into the vat. The other tells the porter whose doorstep to find.” The merchant laughs and helps the apprentice raise the line. Across the lane, cotton is being bundled for the next caravan. The dyer points you toward the through road, then offers to show you the stalls if you can spare a day.
ev.cambaet.entry.choice.look: Spend a day among the dyers and merchants
ev.cambaet.entry.choice.pass: Ask the way through town and continue
ev.cambaet.entry.title: The Blue Cloth Lane
ev.cambaet.site_gap.body: At the dye yard, an apprentice has laid two lengths of cloth side by side. One is a deep blue; the other has pale streaks near its folded edge. “The customer says they were meant to match,” he tells his aunt. She asks whether he unfolded the second length before dyeing it. He looks down at the fold and answers, “I thought the colour would reach through.” She does not scold him. Instead she fills a basin and asks him to rinse both edges so they can see how much dye remains. You ask how long the cloth must stay in the vat. “That depends on the cloth,” she says, lifting the wet end for you to see. “Watch the edge when it dries. If the colour sits only on the surface, another dip won't help until we wash it.” The apprentice fetches clean water. His aunt puts a marker by the road leading toward Semenat so the customer can find them when he returns.
ev.cambaet.site_gap.choice.interact: Help check the two cloth edges
ev.cambaet.site_gap.choice.route: Ask her about the Semenat road
ev.cambaet.site_gap.title: A Colour Returned to the Vat
ev.cambaet.tidemark.body: A boatman's daughter is standing beside a row of stakes at the muddy landing. One has come loose and rolled against a cargo basket. “Father will blame the tide,” she says, “but I tied this one yesterday.” Her father comes up carrying a coil of rope and studies the knot. “You used the short end. Look how it slipped.” She asks whether they can put it back before the next boat arrives. He says yes, then notices that the stake's painted mark has worn away. Without it, the carriers cannot tell where the shallower boats should stop. The girl offers to fetch a pot of pigment from her mother's stall. “Tell her I need the red one,” he says. She gives him a look: “She has only one pot for the landing. You used the rest on the door.” He grins and hands her his rope. You can hold the stake while they reset it, or listen as he explains which waterside road the carriers take toward Tana.
ev.cambaet.tidemark.choice.help: Help reset and mark the stake
ev.cambaet.tidemark.choice.route: Ask where the porters take the goods
ev.cambaet.tidemark.result.help: You hold the stake upright while the boatman drives it into firmer ground. His daughter paints a fresh mark and makes him test her knot. It holds when the next shallow boat touches the landing. The carriers thank you for giving them a place to unload without sinking into the mud.
ev.cambaet.tidemark.result.route: The boatman points along the waterside road used by carriers travelling toward Tana. His daughter corrects him at one fork: the old bank washed out last season, and people now use the higher path. You follow her correction on the ground before moving on, better prepared for the next leg.
ev.cambaet.tidemark.title: The Missing Harbour Mark
ev.cambaluc.a.body: The palace of Cambaluc is the largest roofed building in the world. The great hall, where the Kaan holds his feasts and receives ambassadors, can hold six thousand men seated at table. The roof is painted vermilion, blue, green, and gold — dragons coil around the beams, and phoenixes spread their wings across the ceiling. The floors are of polished marble so clear that a man can see his reflection. The walls are hung with silk embroidered with scenes of hunts on horseback, battles between elephants and tigers, and the celestial palace where the gods feast. The Kaan sits on a raised dais at the northern end of the hall, on a throne of carved jade, so that his gaze falls on every guest.
ev.cambaluc.a.choice.admire: Stand before the great hall and marvel at its size
ev.cambaluc.a.choice.audience: Present yourself at the Kaan's court with gifts
ev.cambaluc.a.choice.talk_guards: Talk to the Kaan's guards about the empire
ev.cambaluc.a.title: The Palace of the Great Khan
ev.cambaluc.b.body: Cambaluc has twelve gates, and beyond each lies a suburb larger than many cities of Christendom or Islam. Merchants from across the empire—Cathay, Manzi, Tangut, Tibet, the Golden Horde, Persia and India—keep warehouses and counting houses there. A thousand carts of silk enter the city each day; forty more carts of pepper, spices and rare goods are consumed. The Great Khan keeps public granaries where those who ask receive rice and millet. Beyond every gate an inn receives travellers who reach the city after curfew. An innkeeper hangs a lantern outside while the staff sing of a bed and grain for the weary traveller, silk from Cathay and scent from Persia, and trading again in the morning. “After the gates shut, we still take people in,” he says. “The granary distributes food by its rules. First let them rest; business can wait until dawn.”
ev.cambaluc.b.choice.count: Count the cart-loads of silk entering the city in a day
ev.cambaluc.b.choice.granary: Visit the public granaries — no one goes hungry here
ev.cambaluc.b.choice.silk: Buy silk at the Cambaluc price
ev.cambaluc.b.title: The Twelve Suburbs
ev.cambaluc.c.body: In the great park behind the palace, the Kaan has caused a mountain to be raised — a hill of green jade, of jasper, and of lapis lazuli, brought block by block from the quarries of Badakhshan and Cotan. It is covered with evergreens: cedars, pines, and cypresses, each one dug up by the roots in distant forests, wrapped in silk and wet earth, and carried here on the backs of elephants. The trees do not know they have been moved; they grow as green as in their native soil. A thousand gardeners water them daily by hand, climbing the artificial mountain with buckets hung from shoulder-poles. The Kaan comes here in the evenings, when the shadows are long, and walks alone among the transplanted trees. No one may disturb him.
ev.cambaluc.c.choice.evening: Climb the hill at sunset and see the whole city
ev.cambaluc.c.choice.gardener: Talk to the gardeners who water the trees by hand
ev.cambaluc.c.choice.walk: Walk among the transplanted trees on the green hill
ev.cambaluc.c.title: The Mountain of Green Jade
ev.cambaluc.entry.body: You must know that the city of Cambaluc hath such a multitude of houses, and such a vast population inside the walls and outside, that it seems quite past all possibility. There is a suburb outside each of the gates, which are twelve in number; and these suburbs are so great that they contain more people than the city itself [for the suburb of one gate spreads in width till it meets the suburb of the next, whilst they extend in length some three or four miles]. In those suburbs lodge the foreign merchants and travellers, of whom there are always great numbers who have come to bring presents to the Emperor, or to sell articles at Court, or because the city affords so good a mart to attract traders. [There are in each of the suburbs, to a distance of a mile from the city, numerous fine hostelries for the lodgment of merchants from different parts of the world, and a special hostelry is assigned to each description of people, as if we should say there is one for the Lombards, another for the Germans, and a third for the Frenchmen.] And thus there are as many good houses outside of the city as inside, without counting those that belong to the great lords and barons, which are very numerous. You must know that it is forbidden to bury any dead body inside the city. If the body be that of an Idolater it is carried out beyond the city and suburbs to a remote place assigned for the purpose, to be burnt. And if it be of one belonging to a religion the custom of which is to bury, such as the Christian, the Saracen, or what not, it is also carried out beyond the suburbs to a distant place assigned for the purpose. And thus the city is preserved in a better and more healthy state. Moreover, no public woman resides inside the city, but all such abide outside in the suburbs. And ’tis wonderful what a vast number of these there are for the foreigners; it is a certain fact that there are more than 20,000 of them living by prostitution.
ev.cambaluc.entry.choice.customs: Declare your goods at the shìbó sī (市舶司)
ev.cambaluc.entry.choice.lore: Ask what men say of this city
ev.cambaluc.entry.title: Concerning the City of Cambaluc, and Its Great Traffic and Population
ev.cambaluc.mentor_iching.body: A chronologer of the Astronomical Bureau will sit with you fourteen days and teach the casting of hexagrams for the road. He does not ask after fortune. He asks after time and position — which season a road is open, and where a man stands when he chooses it.
ev.cambaluc.mentor_iching.choice.ask: Hear how hexagrams speak of roads
ev.cambaluc.mentor_iching.choice.learn: Pay the fee and learn I Ching
ev.cambaluc.mentor_iching.title: I Ching at Khanbaliq
ev.campichu.a.body: You stand in the capital of the whole province of Tangut, where the governor's clerks weigh out salt certificates and tally the tribute of the western marches. Caravans from the sandy desert to the north unload camels in the outer wards, and the market runs from dawn until the third watch without ceasing.
ev.campichu.a.choice.caravan: Bargain with desert caravans for tea
ev.campichu.a.choice.clerks: Watch the governor's clerks at their tally
ev.campichu.a.choice.pass: Pass through the government quarter without delay
ev.campichu.a.title: The Seat of Tangut
ev.campichu.b.body: In Campichu you find three very fine Christian churches standing near many idol abbeys after the local fashion. Within the latter lie enormous gilded figures, some ten paces in length, with lesser images adoring before them. Saracens also keep their mosques here, so that four faiths share one street without quarrel.
ev.campichu.b.choice.abbey: Walk the idol abbeys and note their gilded figures
ev.campichu.b.choice.churches: Enter one of the three Christian churches
ev.campichu.b.choice.offering: Leave a small offering at an abbey gate
ev.campichu.b.title: Churches and Abbeys
ev.campichu.entry.body: Campichu is also a city of Tangut, and a very great and noble one. Indeed it is the capital and place of government of the whole province of Tangut. The people are Idolaters, Saracens, and Christians, and the latter have three very fine churches in the city, whilst the Idolaters have many minsters and abbeys after their fashion. In these they have an enormous number of idols, both small and great, certain of the latter being a good ten paces in stature; some of them being of wood, others of clay, and others yet of stone. They are all highly polished, and then covered with gold. The great idols of which I speak lie at length. And round about them there are other figures of considerable size, as if adoring and paying homage before them. Now, as I have not yet given you particulars about the customs of these Idolaters, I will proceed to tell you about them. You must know that there are among them certain religious recluses who lead a more virtuous life than the rest.
ev.campichu.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the gate without delay
ev.campichu.entry.title: Of the City of Campichu
ev.camul.a.body:
At the melon market, the seller Nuri is tying a reed tag to a basket. Her brother has been tending the water gate and says the next family has asked to open it early. Their melon vines are wilting. Nuri checks the wooden turn board: her own garden still has an hour of water left. ‘If they take it now, the end of our row stays dry,’ she says.

A child from the neighbouring garden arrives carrying a cut melon. She asks whether Nuri will trade the hour for this one. Nuri smiles but tells her the board belongs to everyone, so the adults must agree. You ask how they keep track. Her brother shows you the marks for each garden and the small channels leading from the well.

The child sits beside the baskets to wait for her mother. Nuri cuts a slice and holds it up for you to see while they talk. You can spend the day walking the beds and learn their watering routine, buy a small piece for 0.6 silver and eat it, or ask the drivers which roads lead to Lop and Suzhou.
ev.camul.a.choice.ask-traders: Ask the drivers about Lop and Suzhou
ev.camul.a.choice.buy-melons: Buy a small piece of melon for 0.6 silver
ev.camul.a.choice.walk: Spend the day among the melon beds
ev.camul.a.title: The Melon Seller’s Water Turn
ev.camul.b.body:
An older keeper is sweeping sand from the courtyard of a local shrine. His nephew has laid out mats for travellers, but one has a torn edge and catches on everyone’s shoes. The keeper asks him to take it back inside. ‘The visitors can use the good ones while I mend this,’ he says.

A woman arrives with her father, who needs shade after the road. She asks whether they may sit for a moment. The keeper pours tea and tells his nephew to bring the low stool. The boy asks about an old local tale of how their families once welcomed passing strangers. ‘I heard it from my uncle,’ the keeper answers. ‘First find this gentleman somewhere comfortable to sit. We can tell the story while he rests.’

You help move the stool and ask whether the old man would like more water. He says he would rather hear where the next well lies. You can stay a day to hear the keeper’s account, quietly observe the courtyard gathering, or ask him about the eastern road toward Etzina.
ev.camul.b.choice.ask-east: Wait a day for a returning driver and ask about Etzina
ev.camul.b.choice.listen: Stay a day and hear the keeper’s story
ev.camul.b.title: The Courtyard Keeper’s Guest
ev.camul.entry.body:
At the Hami oasis, a cart driver is counting the water skins beside a melon stall. His daughter has marked each one with a strip of cloth so the family will not confuse drinking water with water for washing the animals. She finds two with the same colour and asks him which he filled at the well. ‘The heavy one,’ he says, then lifts both and admits he cannot tell.

The melon seller calls them over. She calls the morning water carrier over. He recognises the patched strap on the skin he filled at the sweet well, and the seller gives the girl a fresh strip of cloth. You ask where a traveller can sleep. The seller points to a lodging yard; the driver says its owner keeps the animals under shade, though the courtyard fills quickly when caravans arrive.

The girl ties the new strip and asks whether you have room for a melon. Her father laughs: ‘First make sure your own water is marked.’ You can mark Hami and go on, spend a day among the market stalls, or visit the local place of worship and meet the people who care for it.
ev.camul.entry.choice.market: Spend a day among the market stalls
ev.camul.entry.choice.shrine: Visit the local place of worship
ev.camul.entry.title: At the Hami Oasis
ev.camul.waterboard.body:
At a narrow channel beyond the market, two children are looking for the board that shows whose garden receives water next. Their grandfather set it beside the sluice, but the wind has carried it into the reeds. One child wants to guess from yesterday’s order; the other says their neighbours swapped turns this morning.

You ask the grandfather whether the board can be replaced. ‘We can make another,’ he says, ‘but the old marks will tell us what everyone agreed.’ A woman from the next garden arrives with a jar of drinking water and asks if they have found it. The younger child spots a corner of wood by the bank. All three lean down, and the grandfather warns them to hold the gate before anyone pulls the board free.

You can spend a day helping them recover and repaint the turn marks with the neighbours, or listen as the grandfather explains each mark and write down how the oasis shares the channel.
ev.camul.waterboard.choice.learn: Ask how the turn marks work
ev.camul.waterboard.choice.restore: Spend a day restoring the water board
ev.camul.waterboard.result.learn: The grandfather explains the marks while the children put the board back. You write down the watering order and the way they record changes, then leave them to open the gate for the next garden.
ev.camul.waterboard.result.restore: You help repaint the marks and wait while each neighbour checks their agreed turn. At dusk the children hang the board under shelter. Their grandfather thanks you, and the families along the channel know your name.
ev.camul.waterboard.title: The Missing Water Board
ev.caracoron.entry.body:
At the wagon yard outside Caracoron, a carpenter is fitting a new wheel spoke while his sister holds the rim steady. A boy beside them wants to take the wagon to his grandmother before sunset. ‘It will travel faster once the wheel stays round,’ the carpenter tells him. The boy crouches to watch the last peg go in.

You ask whether the yard has been here long. The sister says families have used this ground through many changes of rulers and routes. Her mother still calls one lane by an older name, and travellers who ask for the market sometimes end up at the wrong gate. The carpenter laughs that his mother gives better directions once she knows which family the visitor wants. A neighbour arrives with tea and asks whether the boy has checked the other wheel too. He has not.

The sister invites you to stay a day and hear how the roads meet here. The boy takes the tea to his grandmother first, then comes back to hold the wagon while his uncle tests it.
ev.caracoron.entry.choice.look: Stay a day and hear the family’s road names
ev.caracoron.entry.choice.pass: Ask which road leaves the yard and continue
ev.caracoron.entry.title: The Wagon Yard at Caracoron
ev.caracoron.site_gap.body:
Outside a camp tent, groom Altan is twisting washed horsehair into a thin cord. His daughter holds the loose end around a wooden peg. A young horse reaches toward her sleeve, and she pulls back just before it catches the cord in its teeth. ‘He likes anything that moves,’ she says. Altan asks her to keep the peg beyond the horse’s reach.

You ask what the cord is for. Altan says his brother’s saddlebag has torn, and the family will need it when they leave. His daughter asks whether a knot tied tight in dry weather will still hold after rain. He wets a short length so she can feel it draw in, then leaves a little slack in the practice knot. His brother brings the bag and thanks her for remembering the question.

Altan has travelled toward Camul with pack trains and can tell you the road. He also has spare strands ready if you want to try twisting while his daughter finishes the repair.
ev.caracoron.site_gap.choice.route: Ask Altan about the road to Camul
ev.caracoron.site_gap.title: The Groom’s Horsehair Cord
ev.caracoron.teapot.body:
At a yard where several families have stopped, Bayan is heating tea in a dented kettle. Her father repaired the handle last winter, and she now wants to take it to an aunt whose wagon broke at the far gate. Her youngest son asks why they cannot wait until the aunt comes over. Bayan says the older woman has spent the morning under the wagon and deserves tea before she gets back up.

You ask whether the handle will hold. Bayan lifts the kettle by a cloth and shows you the loose pin. Her brother, a metalworker, arrives with a replacement pin but no one to steady the handle while he fits it. The child offers both hands; his uncle asks him to keep them away from the hot side. Bayan sets the kettle down and lets it cool.

A pin costs 1 silver at the market, or you can spend the following day helping the family mend the wagon and carry tea to the aunt. The son has already found a clean cup for her.
ev.caracoron.teapot.choice.pin: Pay 1 silver for the replacement pin
ev.caracoron.teapot.choice.wagon: Spend another day helping repair the wagon
ev.caracoron.teapot.result.pin: You bring back the pin. Bayan’s brother fits it while you steady the cool handle, and the boy carries the first cup to his aunt. The families at the yard thank you for helping them finish the repair.
ev.caracoron.teapot.result.wagon: You spend the next day beside the aunt’s wagon, handing tools and holding the wheel steady. Bayan brings tea at midday; her aunt finally sits down to drink it. You remember how the family shared the work.
ev.caracoron.teapot.title: The Kettle Sent Across the Yard
ev.cascar.a.body:
In an orchard outside the market, grower Rima is checking a narrow channel with her daughter. Their neighbour’s branch takes water first today, but a loose stone has let some spill into the path. ‘Should I block it?’ the girl asks. Rima shakes her head. ‘Call him over. It is his turn, and he should see what we mend.’ The neighbour comes with a small spade and thanks them for waiting.

You ask whether the fruit has suffered. Rima points to one vine whose leaves are still cool, then to a younger row that needs the afternoon flow. The neighbour offers to lift the stone while you hold the channel gate. Her daughter has picked a melon for sale at 0.5 silver and packed a parcel of dried grapes for 1 silver. She asks which will travel better, and Rima lets her answer after she has carried both across the yard.

The water begins to run where it should. Rima invites you to stay a day and see the orchard after its turn; her daughter keeps the two parcels in the shade until you decide.
ev.cascar.a.choice.orchard: Stay a day to see the orchard water turn
ev.cascar.a.title: The Orchard Water Turn
ev.cascar.b.body:
At a weaving bench, Saliha is finishing a carpet while her aunt stirs a dye vat outside. Her younger brother has copied the border pattern onto scrap cloth, but he has left out the small turn at one corner. ‘It will still lie flat,’ he says. Saliha shows him the finished edge. ‘Yes, but your grandmother will know which hand made it.’ He tries again, this time watching her fingers.

You ask whether the pattern belongs to their family. The aunt says they learned it from her mother and have changed it for different buyers. She sets out a packet of dye samples for 1.5 silver; Saliha has one finished trading carpet priced at 116 silver. Her brother asks whether buyers care about the small turn. One waiting customer says he did not notice until Saliha pointed it out, but now he wants to see the whole border.

Saliha invites you to sit for a day if you wish to learn the work. The aunt checks the vat, and the customer bends down to follow the pattern around the corner.
ev.cascar.b.choice.carpet: Buy the finished carpet for 116 silver
ev.cascar.b.choice.dyes: Buy the dye samples for 1.5 silver
ev.cascar.b.choice.learn_weave: Stay a day and learn the border pattern
ev.cascar.b.title: The Weaver’s Narrow Border
ev.cascar.c.body:
At a cave outside Kashgar, keeper Mariam is sweeping the space where visitors sit. An older Muslim neighbour brings a lamp; a Christian traveller arrives with a small candle. Both ask where they may set them. Mariam points to separate shelves, then asks them to leave the walking path clear. Her son carries away a basket of spent wicks and asks whether the two visitors tell the same story about the sleepers.

‘We remember it in our prayers,’ the neighbour says. The traveller adds, ‘I learned different names from my father.’ Mariam tells her son to listen to each guest before repeating either version. You ask whether the cave itself has always been called by that story. ‘The people who come here know it by that name,’ she says. ‘My family looks after the place they actually use.’ The child checks the shelves and makes room for one more light.

The visitors invite you to sit with them. Mariam can give you a sheltered place for the night if you want to stay and help tidy the cave in the morning.
ev.cascar.c.choice.both: Stay the night and hear both visitors
ev.cascar.c.choice.christian: Hear the Christian traveller’s family version
ev.cascar.c.choice.muslim: Hear the neighbour’s version of the sleepers
ev.cascar.c.title: Two Visitors at the Cave
ev.cascar.entry.body:
At a relay yard in Kashgar, a weaver’s son named Tariq is repairing a cord that records the handover of pack animals. His father has sent him a roll of cloth, but one knot has slipped beneath the seal. ‘If I count it as an animal, they will charge us for a horse we never had,’ Tariq says. The yard clerk makes him loosen the cord and show the older mark.

You ask where to find water before the next stage. Tariq points to a channel running by the market, then asks the clerk whether it is flowing today. ‘It is,’ she says, ‘but the far orchard gets its turn after noon.’ A fruit seller behind her has a sealed lot of jade for 135 silver, though he is more interested in whether his melons have reached the stall without bruising. Tariq asks him to move the crate out of the animal path.

The clerk invites you to stay two days and learn the relay’s records. Tariq can introduce you to his family’s garden tomorrow. The merchant pulls a sample from the jade pack while the repaired cord dries on the fence.
ev.cascar.entry.choice.customs: Stay two days to learn the relay records
ev.cascar.entry.choice.lore: Spend a day with Tariq’s family in the gardens
ev.cascar.entry.choice.market: Buy the sealed jade lot for 135 silver
ev.cascar.entry.title: The Relay Cord at Kashgar
ev.cascar.mentor_closure.body:
Guide Habib is mending a harness at the relay bench when a young carrier asks how much water to take over the next pass. Habib does not answer until the carrier shows him the weight of his load. ‘Your uncle travelled light last week,’ he says. ‘You have two more bundles.’ The carrier looks at his pack and admits he copied his uncle’s plan without checking.

You ask how Habib learns when a path changes. He keeps notes from returning drivers and walks the first stage when he can. Tariq comes through the yard with his repaired cord and adds that one trough has been fixed since yesterday. Habib asks him to show the carrier the new mark. The carrier says he can wait while they check the next station’s water.

Habib invites you to listen at his bench if you have a day. He has a map cloth and several old accounts, and he wants to know what you noticed on your own way into Kashgar.
ev.cascar.mentor_closure.choice_1: Ask Habib about the next pass
ev.cascar.mentor_closure.choice_1_result: Habib asks about your load, then has Tariq show you the repaired trough on the cord. The young carrier copies the same mark. You leave knowing the guide and the first question he asks every traveller.
ev.cascar.mentor_closure.choice_2: Stay a day with Habib and check the route accounts
ev.cascar.mentor_closure.choice_2_result: You stay a day at Habib’s bench. He compares the cloth map with accounts from three drivers, and the young carrier writes his own load beside the water stops. Habib asks you to come back if you want to see how he checks the remaining stage.
ev.cascar.mentor_closure.choice_3_result: You thank Habib and continue. He is still adjusting the harness for the young carrier, who has finally added a second water skin. Tariq calls out the next station’s name as you leave the yard.
ev.cascar.mentor_closure.title: The Relay Guide’s Bench
ev.cascar.redthread.body:
Near the weaving quarter, a girl named Nura is trying to match a short red thread to a much older one sewn into her grandmother’s shawl. Her mother has asked her to repair the loose edge before Grandmother’s visit. The new thread looks right in the sun, but indoors it turns brighter than the old dye. ‘She will see it at once,’ Nura says. Her younger brother answers that Grandmother mostly notices whether they come to sit with her.

You ask where the old thread came from. Nura’s mother says her own mother dyed it many years ago and has mended the shawl several times since. She does not mind a visible seam; she would rather the cloth hold through the next cold season. Nura tests a stitch on the inner edge, then asks whether the thread should run all the way around or only across the worn part.

Their mother can teach you the repair as she works. If you stay for the day, Nura will also tell her grandmother who helped finish it. The younger brother has already pulled up an extra stool.
ev.cascar.redthread.choice.learn: Ask the mother to show the stitch
ev.cascar.redthread.choice.sew: Stay a day and finish the shawl edge
ev.cascar.redthread.result.learn: Nura’s mother shows you how to catch the old edge without pulling it tight. You try a stitch on a scrap, and Nura compares it with her own. She keeps working on the shawl after you go; you record the small repair in your travel notes.
ev.cascar.redthread.result.sew: You spend the day sewing the worn edge with Nura and her mother. Grandmother arrives in the evening, feels the strong new seam, and asks Nura who sat with her through the work. The family thanks you, and the repaired shawl is ready for cold weather.
ev.cascar.redthread.title: The Red Thread for Grandmother
ev.chamba.a.body: A clerk at the harbour has two lists in front of him. One names bundles of grass for an elephant waiting in the store yard; the other names timber and sandalwood for ships. His young assistant has put a feed bundle on the cargo list. ‘The men will load it if I leave it there,’ she says, embarrassed. The clerk asks her to follow the porter who brought it and find out where the elephant is kept. You go with her. At the yard, the keeper says the animal has eaten poorly since arriving, and asks that the green grass be brought before the heat rises. The assistant returns, crosses out the wrong line, and asks the clerk why an old ledger mentions elephants sent overseas. ‘That ledger tells you what people shipped years ago,’ he says. ‘Today we have one hungry animal in our care.’ A pilot sorting mooring ropes nearby offers to show you which ships sail north and which continue toward Pentam. The assistant stays to finish the new list and asks you to tell her if the keeper needs another bundle.
ev.chamba.a.choice.buy_sandalwood: Buy a packed load of sandalwood
ev.chamba.a.choice.hear_tribute: Ask the clerk about the older elephant records
ev.chamba.a.choice.watch_harbour: Stay a day to help check harbour loads
ev.chamba.a.title: A Clerk and the Elephant Feed
ev.chamba.b.body: A pepper merchant is sealing bags under the harbour roof. His niece holds the wax, but keeps turning each bag to hide a small stain near the seam. ‘That one rode through rain yesterday,’ she tells him. The merchant asks her to cut it open rather than send damp pepper aboard. A broker carrying papers from the town office arrives for the shipment list. He notices the opened bag and waits while they count it again. You ask whether the northbound ships are already taking cargo. ‘The one for Zayton has room if the wind holds,’ the broker says. ‘The crew going on to Fuju will ask about the sacks before they name a day.’ The niece wants to know why a ship cannot simply leave whenever the buyer is ready. The broker brings her to the quay and points to two crews mending sails while they wait for a steady wind. Her uncle offers you a dry bag to smell and asks whether you want goods, the sailors’ directions, or time to meet the people who approve each load.
ev.chamba.b.choice.ask_sea_road: Ask the crews about Zayton and Fuju
ev.chamba.b.choice.buy_pepper: Buy a sealed load of pepper
ev.chamba.b.choice.visit_court: Spend two days with the town clerks and brokers
ev.chamba.b.title: The Pepper Merchant’s Sealed Bags
ev.chamba.entry.body: A boy at the harbour is trying to keep a bundle of elephant grass out of the wet sand. Each time he lifts one end, the other slides toward the water. His aunt, who keeps a stall by the quay, calls you over to hold the bundle while she finds a length of rope. ‘Whose elephant eats all this?’ you ask. ‘The one waiting in the yard behind the storehouse. He has refused the dry stalks since morning.’ The boy says the elephant accepted a pear from his hand but pushed the old grass aside. His aunt laughs. ‘Then bring him the fresh bundle before he starts pulling at the gate.’ A sailor waiting for his cargo asks where to buy a meal while he is in town. The aunt points across the market and tells him which cook serves rice before noon. Farther up the street, people are gathering at the mosque. She asks the boy to carry a smaller bundle to the yard, then tells you how to reach the market and the prayer house from the quay.
ev.chamba.entry.choice.market: Spend a day among the harbour stalls
ev.chamba.entry.choice.shrine: Visit the mosque above the quay
ev.chamba.entry.title: The Elephant Grass at the Wharf
ev.chamba.net.body: A fisher and her daughter are spreading a net across a dry patch beside the harbour. One edge keeps lifting in the breeze. ‘There should be a stone weight here,’ the mother says, holding up a loose loop. Her daughter searches the basket and finds only a broken cord. ‘I tied it after the last catch.’ The mother asks her to show where she made the knot. It came loose against a sharp shell, and the stone must have fallen on the way home. You ask whether they can use another. ‘Yes, if we find one smooth enough not to cut the net again.’ The daughter runs to the beach and returns with two stones. One is heavy but rough; the smaller one fits the loop. A neighbour arrives to ask when they will set out. The mother looks at the tide line on the quay wall and says they have time to mend one more tear. The daughter offers you the spare cord, then asks her mother why the boat always leaves when the water reaches that mark. She wants to watch the tide rise herself before their next trip.
ev.chamba.net.choice.listen: Stay a day and watch the tide with them
ev.chamba.net.choice.mend: Help mend the net before they sail
ev.chamba.net.result.listen: You spend the next day beside the daughter at the quay wall. The water reaches the mark later than she expected. Her mother explains how she checks the wind as well as the tide before putting out. The daughter chooses the moment to call the neighbour, and you leave knowing how the harbour fishers time a departure.
ev.chamba.net.result.mend: You hold the edge taut while the daughter ties the smooth stone into place. Her mother tests the weight by dragging the net across the sand. It stays flat. The neighbour helps carry it to the boat, and the family thanks you before they push off.
ev.chamba.net.title: The Net with a Missing Weight
ev.chandu.a.body:
At a builder’s yard, carpenter Batar is setting a light reed wall into a wooden frame. His daughter holds the lashing while her grandfather asks whether the joint can be untied without breaking it. Batar loosens one loop and shows him. The family has built shelters for travelling households for years; an older drawing on the wall shows a much grander hall that people here still tell stories about.

You ask whether the wall will stand in rain. Batar shows the coating on the reeds and points to a covered test frame outside. His daughter says she spent the morning painting a blue border on the new panel, then hid it because she thought it looked crooked. Grandfather finds it and says the line follows the curve of the reed. She takes another look before choosing to repaint it.

Batar charges 5 silver to take visitors through the working yard and explain the frame closely. The family also welcomes you to look from the meadow or spend a day sketching their joinery. The daughter is tying the next loop as you decide.
ev.chandu.a.choice.admire: Look at the reed hall from the meadow
ev.chandu.a.choice.enter: Pay 5 silver for Batar’s working-yard tour
ev.chandu.a.choice.sketch: Spend a day sketching the reed frame
ev.chandu.a.title: The Reed Builder’s Yard
ev.chandu.b.body:
At the meadow edge, a herder named Hulan is bringing a small group of white mares toward water. Her son counts them, then counts again because one foal keeps walking behind its mother’s tail. A falconer on the next path asks Hulan to keep the mares clear of the place where he is training a bird. She points to the stream and says she will cross after the bird has settled.

You ask whether visitors may watch the training. The falconer says his fee is 8 silver for a lesson with the bird and lure. Hulan says you can walk the outer path freely and meet the herd where it stops. Her son asks what a falcon eats. The falconer answers, then asks him what the young foal needs after a long walk. ‘Water, and a quiet place,’ the boy says.

The two families have used these grounds in different seasons. Hulan moves her mares slowly toward the stream, and the falconer checks his bird’s hood before letting anyone nearer.
ev.chandu.b.choice.falcon: Pay 8 silver for a lesson with the falconer
ev.chandu.b.choice.horses: Watch Hulan’s white mares at the stream
ev.chandu.b.choice.walk: Spend a day walking the meadow edge
ev.chandu.b.title: Along the Meadow Path
ev.chandu.c.body:
At morning milking, Hulan’s aunt is setting out wooden bowls while her granddaughter brings the white mares one by one. The girl asks why her aunt keeps a small bowl apart from the rest. ‘That one is for our family’s thanks before we drink,’ the older woman says. She tells the girl where to place it, then asks her to wash her hands.

You ask what the family gives thanks for. The aunt names good grass, healthy animals and relatives who returned safely from the road. A neighbour who shares the pasture says her own family uses different words for the same morning. The two women talk as they work, and the granddaughter asks whether she may hear both versions. The aunt lets the neighbour speak first.

The aunt asks you to pass the small bowl to her granddaughter, then asks the neighbour what words her mother once used. They talk while the milk warms in their hands. The granddaughter returns and listens, waiting for a chance to ask another question.
ev.chandu.c.choice.listen: Ask the aunt who taught her the practice
ev.chandu.c.choice.offering: Give 1 silver toward the family gathering
ev.chandu.c.choice.watch_mares: Watch the family milk the white mares
ev.chandu.c.title: The White Mares at Morning
ev.chandu.entry.body:
At a stable yard on the grassland, a woman named Orina is sorting saddle straps while her son holds a foal that keeps trying to nose the bundles. He asks whether the animal can carry a small pack yet. ‘When it can stand quietly for the fitting,’ she says. She gives him a brush instead of a load, and the foal settles under his hand.

You ask where to declare your goods. Orina points toward the clerk’s desk and says a full check takes two days. Her sister, a cloth trader, has a full camlet trading bale for 146 silver. She also knows families who have lived beside these meadows through changes of camps and roads; each keeps a different account of the old buildings. The son asks which one his aunt tells best. ‘The one about Grandfather losing his sandals,’ she says.

A rider arrives asking for a repaired strap. Orina checks the stitches, then tells her son to walk the foal while she finishes the work. The clerk calls the next traveller to the desk.
ev.chandu.entry.choice.customs: Spend two days checking your goods with the clerk
ev.chandu.entry.choice.lore: Spend a day listening to the meadow families
ev.chandu.entry.choice.market: Buy the full camlet bale for 146 silver
ev.chandu.entry.title: The Horse Yard on the Meadow
ev.chandu.mareblanket.body:
Behind the horse yard, an older woman named Saran has laid out a worn felt blanket. Her grandson wants to sew a new border around it, but his mother has set out fresh felt for a different blanket. ‘This one belonged to my first mare,’ Saran says. The boy asks whether the mare was white like Hulan’s. ‘Brown, and quicker to steal a drink than any of them.’ His mother smiles; she has heard the story many times, but the boy asks for the part about the stream again.

You ask why they do not mend the old blanket together. The mother turns over a corner to show you thin patches that would tear under a saddle. She wants the new felt for the working horses and the old piece kept at home. Saran agrees to the new blanket, yet wants the boy to remember which horse taught her to ride. The boy fetches a scrap of blue wool. ‘Could her name go on this corner?’ he asks. Saran cannot write it, but she remembers the shape of the mark she once stitched. You hold the blanket as she searches for the right thread.
ev.chandu.mareblanket.choice.felt: Stay a day and make the working blanket
ev.chandu.mareblanket.choice.mark: Help Saran find the old stitched mark
ev.chandu.mareblanket.result.felt: You stay a day cutting fresh felt and binding its edges. The boy makes a small practice patch before touching the working blanket. At evening Saran lays her old piece beside the new one and says the horses will have warm backs this winter.
ev.chandu.mareblanket.result.mark: You lift the faded edge into the light. Saran finds three blue stitches under an old repair and shows her grandson how to copy them on the new corner. The mother folds the old blanket carefully; Saran tells the stream story once more while the boy sews.
ev.chandu.mareblanket.title: The Mare’s Old Blanket
ev.chandu.mentor_closure.body:
Orina’s horse keeper is brushing a quiet mare while a young helper tries to read a worn hoof print in the mud. ‘This one belongs to the grey horse,’ the helper says. The keeper asks him to look at the chipped edge and try again. He finds the right animal and grins.

You ask how she decides which horse should carry a traveller. She looks at your pack, then at the roads you have marked. ‘How much weight? How many days between water?’ she asks. Her helper fetches two saddles so you can feel their different balance. When you say one sits better, she asks why. You explain what you noticed, and she adds the point you missed. She is willing to talk now, spend a whole day showing you her work, or let you return when your route is settled.

The helper asks if he may try the saddle test too. She nods and lets him explain what he sees first.
ev.chandu.mentor_closure.choice_1: Ask how she judges a horse for the road
ev.chandu.mentor_closure.choice_1_result: She shows you where the saddle has rubbed the mare and how a short walk reveals it. Her helper takes the animal round the yard while you watch. You thank her for the first lesson and remember her name.
ev.chandu.mentor_closure.choice_2: Stay a day and learn at the horse yard
ev.chandu.mentor_closure.choice_2_result: You stay the day. By evening you can tell why the grey horse needs a lighter load and why the quiet mare should rest before a long march. The keeper asks you to come back for a final demonstration.
ev.chandu.mentor_closure.choice_3: Thank her and return to your journey
ev.chandu.mentor_closure.choice_3_result: You thank the keeper and leave the yard. The helper is still comparing hoof prints as you go; she lets him arrive at the answer himself.
ev.chandu.mentor_closure.title: Orina’s Horse Keeper
ev.charchan.entry.body:
By a stream outside Charchan, a boy is washing sand from a handful of river stones. His aunt, who buys stones for a trader, asks him to put the cracked pieces back. He holds one up to the light. ‘This one looks sound.’ She turns it in her fingers and shows him a thin line along the edge.

You ask whether every stream here has good drinking water. ‘No,’ the aunt says, and points to two water carriers walking in from different directions. One fills at a sweet well; the other brings water for washing from a bitter source. The boy asks how you can tell the difference. ‘You ask the person who filled the skin,’ she replies. The carrier agrees, then tells him to stop setting the clean stones in the wet sand.

The boy spreads his sleeve and starts again. His aunt says merchants take sound jasper and chalcedony east, though finding a piece worth keeping takes patience. You can mark Charchan and continue, or spend a day asking which wells travellers use and learning how she sorts the stones.
ev.charchan.entry.choice.look: Stay a day by the stream and ask about the wells
ev.charchan.entry.title: A River Stone at Charchan
ev.charchan.site_gap.body:
At the oasis well, a water carrier named Aysa is changing a worn rope. Her younger brother has tied the replacement to the bucket, but the knot catches on the stone rim each time he lowers it. Aysa asks him to pull it up and try again. He worries the people waiting with their jars will complain.

‘They have seen us fix worse,’ she says. A woman in the queue sets down her jar and asks whether Aysa can still fill it before the cooking fire goes out. Aysa tells her yes and asks you to hold the loose end of the rope. You do, while her brother unwinds the knot and tries a flatter one.

You ask which road reaches Pein. Aysa says she can show you after the bucket comes up smoothly; she knows the drinking wells on that road. Her brother gives the rope a cautious pull. This time the knot clears the rim, and the waiting woman leans forward to see whether the bucket has stayed upright. You can ask Aysa to trace the road, or stay at the well and learn the knot yourself.
ev.charchan.site_gap.choice.interact: Learn to tie the new rope
ev.charchan.site_gap.choice.route: Ask Aysa to trace the road to Pein
ev.charchan.site_gap.title: The Rope at the Oasis Well
ev.charchan.stonebag.body:
A girl at the river crossing is searching the sand for a small cloth pouch. She had gathered three stones for her grandfather, who teaches her to polish them, but one strap broke while she helped a traveller lift his basket. Her grandfather sits nearby with his polishing wheel and calls her back for a drink. She shakes her head: she remembers leaving the pouch above the wet bank.

You ask what the stones look like. ‘One dark, two pale,’ she says. ‘The dark one has a white line.’ A boatman points out that the water has already fallen since morning; anything dropped near the bank may still be between the reeds. Her grandfather calls again, asking whether she wants him to come. She finally tells him what happened. ‘We can look together,’ he says, leaving the wheel covered against the dust.

You can spend the day searching the reeds with them, or help the boatman finish sorting his cargo and earn a little money before the next crossing. The girl says she will keep looking either way, and her grandfather brings her water first.
ev.charchan.stonebag.choice.search: Search the reeds for a day
ev.charchan.stonebag.result.cargo: You sort the sacks by crossing and the boatman pays you 0.8 silver. As you finish, the grandfather and girl find the pouch at the edge of the reeds. She holds it up for you to see before they go home.
ev.charchan.stonebag.result.search: You find the torn strap caught beneath a reed root. The three stones are still in the pouch. The girl shows her grandfather the one with the white line; he says she may polish it tomorrow. You spend the day there, and the family thanks you.
ev.charchan.stonebag.title: The Missing Stone Pouch
ev.chinangli.a.body: A great and wide river runs through Chinangli, and upon it you see silk goods, spices, and other costly merchandize passing up and down without pause. The quays are stacked with bales, and boatmen shout the names of towns far south and north while they warp their vessels to the bank.
ev.chinangli.a.choice.quay: Walk the quay and count the upstream boats
ev.chinangli.a.choice.silk: Buy a bolt of river-traded silk
ev.chinangli.a.choice.spice: Ask which spices the downstream boats carry
ev.chinangli.a.title: The Great River Traffic
ev.chinangli.b.body: The people of Chinangli are idolaters subject to the Great Kaan, and they trade with stamped paper-money in every shop and stall. You watch clerks exchange worn notes for fresh ones, and merchants weigh out goods against the Khan's seal without once touching silver.
ev.chinangli.b.choice.clerks: Ask the exchange clerks how the notes are renewed
ev.chinangli.b.choice.exchange: Watch the paper-money exchange at a stall
ev.chinangli.b.choice.porcelain: Buy a small porcelain bowl with paper-money
ev.chinangli.b.title: Paper-Money of Cathay
ev.chinangli.entry.body: Chinangli is a city of Cathay as you go south, and it belongs to the Great Kaan; the people are Idolaters, and have paper-money. There runs through the city a great and wide river, on which a large traffic in silk goods and spices and other costly merchandize passes up and down. When you travel south from Chinangli for five days, you meet everywhere with fine towns and villages, the people of which are all Idolaters, and burn their dead, and are subject to the Great Kaan, and have paper-money, and live by trade and handicrafts, and have all the necessaries of life in great abundance. But there is nothing particular to mention on the way till you come, at the end of those five days, to TADINFU. This, you must know, is a very great city, and in old times was the seat of a great kingdom; but the Great Kaan conquered it by force of arms. Nevertheless it is still the noblest city in all those provinces. There are very great merchants here, who trade on a great scale, and the abundance of silk is something marvellous.
ev.chinangli.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the gate without delay
ev.chinangli.entry.title: Arriving at CHINANGLI
ev.chinghianfu.binder.body: A bookbinder has promised to mend a small picture book for a neighbour’s child. The child has arrived early and is counting the loose leaves on the table. ‘There were eight pictures,’ she says. The binder finds seven. His husband remembers seeing a leaf beneath the drying rack, where it was placed after a drink spilled. You retrieve it, but the ink has run near the corner. The child can still recognize the goat in the picture. ‘That is the one my grandfather likes,’ she says. The binder asks whether she wants him to cut off the stained edge. She shakes her head; the goat would lose its ear. His husband suggests sewing the page in as it is and putting a plain sheet behind it so the stain will not touch the next one. The child helps count the order again and asks you to hold the leaves while they stitch, or return tomorrow to read the finished book with her grandfather.
ev.chinghianfu.binder.choice.listen: Return a day later for the finished book
ev.chinghianfu.binder.choice.sort: Hold the leaves while they stitch
ev.chinghianfu.binder.result.listen: You return the next day. The repaired book is dry, and the child reads the goat’s page aloud while her grandfather fills in a word she misses. The binder’s husband serves tea. You stay long enough to hear why that worn page matters to the family.
ev.chinghianfu.binder.result.sort: You hold the leaves in order as the binder threads them together. The child counts all eight pictures and shows the goat to her grandfather when he comes to collect her. The family thanks you, and the binder remembers your help when you pass his shop again.
ev.chinghianfu.binder.title: A Book for the Neighbour’s Child
ev.chinghianfu.entry.body: A reader from a small Christian congregation has come to the bookbinder with a loose page. It slipped from a volume used at their gathering, and the children have handled it so often that the corner is soft. The binder’s daughter holds it beside the book. ‘This page belongs after the story about the traveller,’ she says. The reader checks the first words of the next leaf and agrees. ‘Can it be stitched in before the meeting?’ you ask. ‘It has to dry flat first,’ the binder says. The reader looks at the damp corner. ‘Then we will read another passage today,’ he replies. Someone had tried to paste it with too much glue. The reader offers to leave it overnight and asks his daughter to tell the other children they will use a different passage today. At the doorway, a boatman wants directions to the landing toward Chinginju. The binder points him down the street and asks his daughter to guide him past the crowded market. She invites you to follow now, or return tomorrow when the repaired book is ready and she can show you more of the town.
ev.chinghianfu.entry.choice.look: Stay a day with the reader and binder
ev.chinghianfu.entry.title: The Reader’s Missing Page
ev.chinginju.entry.body: Leaving the city of Chinghianfu and travelling three days south-east through a constant succession of busy and thriving towns and villages, you arrive at the great and noble city of CHINGINJU. The people are Idolaters, use paper-money, and are subject to the Great Kaan. They live by trade and handicrafts, and they have plenty of silk. They have also abundance of game, and of all manner of victuals, for it is a most productive territory. Now I must tell you of an evil deed that was done, once upon a time, by the people of this city, and how dearly they paid for it.
ev.chinginju.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.chinginju.entry.title: Of the City of Chinginju and the Slaughter of Certain Alans There
ev.cobinan.entry.body:
At a Cobinan metalworker’s shop, an apprentice holds a polished steel mirror so her father can inspect the surface. His reflection wavers where she has not finished working, and he sends her back to the bench with a smile.

Across the lane, another workshop tends a furnace for mineral work. The workers keep the pale deposit caught above the furnace separate from the residue below; traders call the first tutiya and the second spodium. The apprentice points you toward a place to rest and asks whether you have seen a polished steel mirror before.

The apprentice asks her father whether she should start again on the uneven patch. ‘Just that patch,’ he says. ‘Turn it toward the doorway and look at the line of light.’ She does, and the uneven patch is easier to see in the shifting light. You ask what the workers across the lane sell from their furnace. The father names the two materials they keep apart and adds that traders come looking for them as well as for mirrors. His daughter asks you to come back when she has finished polishing; she wants another pair of eyes on her work.
ev.cobinan.entry.choice.look: Spend a day visiting the workshops
ev.cobinan.entry.title: At the Mirror Workshop
ev.cobinan.mirrorcase.body:
At the metalworker’s shop, the apprentice’s father has finished a small mirror for his sister. She is opening a stall and wants it to hang beside the door. He has made a wooden case to protect it on the journey across town, but he cannot leave the forge before dusk.

He offers to pay you for taking it over and helping her hang it, a job that will take the day. If you are short of time, he can instead show you how the mirror’s face was finished while the case is still open.

His apprentice asks whether the case needs more padding. ‘Enough to keep the mirror from knocking against the lid,’ he says, pressing the cloth down around it. You ask why his sister wants a mirror beside a market door. ‘She sells ribbons,’ he replies. ‘People like to see how they look before buying.’ The apprentice suggests carrying it herself, but her father reminds her of the unfinished work at the bench. She asks you to tell her aunt who polished the mirror if you take it over.
ev.cobinan.mirrorcase.choice.deliver: Spend a day delivering and hanging the mirror
ev.cobinan.mirrorcase.choice.learn: Ask how he finished the mirror’s face
ev.cobinan.mirrorcase.result.deliver: You carry the case to his sister’s new stall and help hang the mirror. She checks its angle, then sends a note of thanks to her brother. When you return, he pays you 0.5 silver for the day.
ev.cobinan.mirrorcase.result.learn: He tilts the mirror in the light and shows you the faint marks left before the final polish. You write down what he tells you about Cobinan’s metalwork and leave him to his forge.
ev.cobinan.mirrorcase.title: The Mirror for His Sister
ev.codex_legend_seed.body: Among a scholar's papers you find wonder-tales and Chinese road chronicles — Prester John beside Wang Dayuan, paradise beside Zhenla. Will you copy them into your own book?
ev.codex_legend_seed.choice_1_result: You copy Prester John, the Earthly Paradise, and the Chinese road leaves into your codex.
ev.codex_legend_seed.choice_2_result: You leave the stack undisturbed. The wonder can wait.
ev.codex_legend_seed.title: Leaves of Wonder and Chronicle
ev.coigangiu.entry.body: Huaiyin — a boat-town on the Grand Canal. Every family keeps a sampan; the children learn to row before they learn to walk. The grain fleet passes through here in autumn on its way to Cambaluc; the inns are full of boatmen, and the smell of river-fish frying drifts across the water from dawn till midnight.
ev.coigangiu.entry.choice.rest: Rest half a day by the road
ev.coigangiu.entry.title: Arriving at Coigangiu
ev.coiganju.entry.body: Coiganju is, as I have told you already, a very large city standing at the entrance to Manzi. The people are Idolaters and burn their dead, and are subject to the Great Kaan. They have a vast amount of shipping, as I mentioned before in speaking of the River Caramoran. And an immense quantity of merchandize comes hither, for the city is the seat of government for this part of the country. Owing to its being on the river, many cities send their produce thither to be again thence distributed in every direction.
ev.coiganju.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.coiganju.entry.title: Concerning the City of Coiganju
ev.coilum.baker.body: A baker near the harbour has kept a tray of bread warm for porters coming off a late ship. Her grandson counts the loaves and frowns. “There are six men on that boat and only five left.” She opens the oven and finds a small loaf she set aside for herself. “That makes six,” she says, “but what will you eat?” He offers to split his supper with her. The first porter arrives carrying a wet rope over his shoulder and asks if the others have come. “They are helping a boat make fast,” the boy tells him. The baker passes the man water and asks him to wait until everyone is there. When the rest arrive, one says the youngest porter has gone to bring an older neighbour home through the dark lanes. The baker puts the tray back by the oven so his bread stays warm too. You can help the boy find the neighbour and bring him here, or spend the evening at their table while the porters tell you which coast road they use when ships cannot sail.
ev.coilum.baker.choice.fetch: Go with the boy to bring the neighbour in
ev.coilum.baker.choice.table: Stay for supper and hear the porters’ roads
ev.coilum.baker.result.fetch: You and the boy meet the young porter and his older neighbour at the lane's bend. You carry the neighbour's bag while the boy lights the path. At the bakery the last loaf is still warm. The porters thank you, and the baker makes room so the neighbour can sit beside her.
ev.coilum.baker.result.table: You stay until the bread is shared. One porter draws the land road toward Maabar in spilled flour, then brushes it away when the baker brings another plate. She gives you supper, and the company leaves you feeling welcome in the town. You depart with a clearer sense of the coastal road.
ev.coilum.baker.title: Bread for the Late Porters
ev.coilum.entry.body: In Coilum, a porter sets down a basket of pepper beneath the warehouse eaves and argues with a young ship's cook over a torn label. “It says whose basket this is,” he tells her. “The rain took half the ink,” she replies. An older woman sorting galangal recognizes the knot in the basket handle. “My sister ties hers that way. She will be here before the tide turns.” The porter does not open the basket; he moves it to a dry bench and asks the cook to write a new label when the owner arrives. You ask how many ships are waiting outside. “Enough to make every porter claim he has worked all night,” the cook says. “Most of them have,” the older woman answers, passing him a cup of water. Merchants of several communities keep houses near the harbour, and the lanes between them are busy with carts of pepper, galangal and cloth. The porter points out the road through town. If you stay for the day, he says, you can meet the owner and see how the harbour sorts its cargo.
ev.coilum.entry.choice.look: Spend a day getting to know the harbour
ev.coilum.entry.choice.pass: Ask for the road through town and continue
ev.coilum.entry.title: The Basket Under the Eaves
ev.coilum.site_gap.body: A woman who weighs pepper has two sacks open in front of her. One smells sharp and dry; the other has a damp patch along its seam. Her son wants to hurry the weighing because a buyer is waiting. “If I put them both on the same account, he will come back with the wet one,” she says. She makes him lift each sack from the floor so he can feel the difference. You ask how she can tell whether the weight comes from pepper or moisture. She shows you the empty sack first, then rubs a few grains between her fingers. The boy notices that they clump together. “Set this one on boards and spread it,” she tells him. “We'll weigh it again when it dries.” Outside, a carrier asks which road goes toward Maabar. The woman points along the coast, away from the boat landing, and the boy repeats the turn so he will remember it himself. Before you leave, the son offers you a dry grain to compare with the clumped ones.
ev.coilum.site_gap.choice.interact: Help her weigh the pepper again
ev.coilum.site_gap.choice.route: Ask about the land road to Maabar
ev.coilum.site_gap.title: Pepper at the Weighing Shed
ev.constantinopolis.entry.body:
At the Golden Horn, a water carrier named Anna finds that one of her jars is empty. Her brother has taken the full jar to a household above the harbour and left her the empty one by mistake. She laughs, then counts her customers aloud so she can decide whom to visit first.

A channel brings water into the city, and covered cisterns hold supplies for its many households. Anna has spent years carrying water up these streets. She points out the dome of Hagia Sophia between the roofs, then asks whether you have a place to stay; she can show you the quay or the lodging lane once she gets her jar back.

A baker by the quay asks, ‘Have you forgotten my water again?’ Anna lifts the empty jar for him to see. ‘My brother has yours. I’ll bring it as soon as he comes down.’ He offers her a piece of bread while she waits. You ask whether the cistern is far. ‘The small covered one is around that corner,’ she says. ‘If you go up the hill, take the lane with the stone steps. My brother always chooses the flatter way and arrives late.’
ev.constantinopolis.entry.choice.look: Spend a day following Anna’s directions
ev.constantinopolis.entry.title: Water at the Golden Horn
ev.constantinopolis.waterjar.body:
Anna’s brother returns carrying the empty jar and an apology. The household on the hill has asked for more water for a neighbour who is ill. Anna still has two regular deliveries to make before dark.

‘Come with me up the hill and I’ll manage the rest,’ she says. Her brother offers to carry your pack if you would rather pay for a filled cup and rest by the cistern. He is determined to deliver the next jar correctly.

Her brother says the sick neighbour is the baker’s mother. ‘I told her I’d come back,’ he says, taking the heavy end of the pole. Anna asks why he left an empty jar at the quay. ‘I thought you would want one ready to fill.’ She taps his shoulder with her free hand. You ask whether there is time for the hill before dark. Anna looks at the light on the roofs: ‘If we leave now, yes. Otherwise I can still sell you a cup from the cistern.’
ev.constantinopolis.waterjar.choice.drin: Buy a cup of water for 0.4 silver
ev.constantinopolis.waterjar.result.carr: You walk uphill with Anna and leave the jar at the neighbour’s door. She thanks you, and the people on her route learn your name before you return to the harbour.
ev.constantinopolis.waterjar.result.drin: You pay 0.4 silver for water and rest beside the covered cistern. Anna’s brother sets down your pack, fills the cup once more, and returns to his deliveries. You feel ready to walk on.
ev.constantinopolis.waterjar.title: Anna’s Brother and the Empty Jar
ev.cotan.a.body:
At a shallow bend near Khotan, river washer Yusuf tips a tray of pebbles into the sun. His daughter Amina is sorting them by the marks she can see, but she has put a cracked stone with the smooth ones. ‘Turn it once more,’ he says. She finds the fine line only when water runs across it. A merchant waiting by the bank asks whether they have another full jade lot to sell; Yusuf says one sealed package is ready at 135 silver.

You ask how they decide where to search. Yusuf points to the changing current, then asks Amina where she found today’s stones. She remembers the gravel bar but not the exact place. He takes her to the bank to look at the water from above before either of them steps in. An older washer calls that he can show you what his hands learned here if you stay until the light changes.

Amina returns with a small dry cloth. Her father waits while the merchant checks the seal, and the older washer sets an empty tray beside you.
ev.cotan.a.choice.jade: Buy Yusuf’s sealed jade lot for 135 silver
ev.cotan.a.choice.wade: Spend a day learning the shallow river bend
ev.cotan.a.choice.watch: Listen to the older washer from the bank
ev.cotan.a.title: The River Washer’s Tray
ev.cotan.b.body:
In a Khotan weaving room, sisters Farah and Zuleika are finishing a length of silk for market. Farah reaches for a blue thread that should mark the edge and finds an empty bobbin. Zuleika says she wound another one after breakfast; their aunt has moved it to the shaded shelf so the colour would not fade. ‘I told you,’ the aunt says. Farah answers that she had heard, then forgot while counting the warp.

You ask how much cloth is ready to sell. The aunt points to a complete trading bolt priced at 100 silver, separate from the piece the sisters are still making. She also has a small packet of dye samples for 1.2 silver: indigo, madder, safflower and walnut, all labelled so travellers will not mix them. Zuleika asks whether the samples need extra wrapping. Her aunt says to keep them dry first, then worry about the sun.
