The family watches them work through it instead of rushing to load the animals.

Arslan charges 2 silver to guide a party; a shared place with a later caravan costs 1.2 silver and means waiting eight days. The innkeeper also keeps a prepared provisions bundle for 0.8 silver. The daughter stays beside the repaired skin until she sees that it holds water.
ev.lop.caravanserai.choice.hire_guide: Hire Arslan to guide you for 2 silver
ev.lop.caravanserai.choice.provision: Buy the prepared provisions for 0.8 silver
ev.lop.caravanserai.choice.wait_caravan: Wait eight days and reserve a caravan place for 1.2 silver
ev.lop.caravanserai.title: The Guide at the Caravan Inn
ev.lop.entry.body:
At the inn in Lop, Aysen is checking the seams of a water skin while her nephew counts the sacks for a departing caravan. He counts a sack twice and cannot understand why the list has one too many. Aysen sets the skin down and asks him to start with the loads already tied. You help him separate the empty bags from the full ones.

You ask how long they prepare for the crossing. Aysen says some families stay several days to rest their animals and learn which wells are usable; every party makes its own plan from the water it can actually carry. A well keeper comes in with a new report about a bitter well. The nephew asks whether that means their caravan must wait. ‘It means we talk to the guide before we choose,’ Aysen tells him.

She offers you a place to sleep for the day. The well keeper is staying until evening and will answer questions once he has eaten. The nephew finally gets the sacks to match the list and calls his aunt over to check them.
ev.lop.entry.choice.ask: Ask the well keeper about the crossing
ev.lop.entry.choice.rest: Rest a day at Aysen’s inn
ev.lop.entry.title: A Night at the Lop Inn
ev.lop.mentor_closure.body:
At the edge of Lop, an older guide named Mergen is tightening the cords on a small wind screen. His niece holds one end and complains that he always asks her to watch the sand rather than the sky. He asks where the last gust came from. She points to the marks it left against the screen and gives him the right answer.

You ask how he taught her. Mergen says they walk the same ground on different mornings and compare what has changed. His niece adds that he also makes her ask the caravan cook about water before she names a route. ‘I did that because you were right once,’ he says. She reminds him it was more than once, and he lets her finish the knot.

Mergen has time for a short answer now or a full day of practice. He folds the screen and asks his niece to show you the dust that has gathered along its lower edge.
ev.lop.mentor_closure.choice_1: Ask Mergen how he reads the wind
ev.lop.mentor_closure.choice_1_result: Mergen lets his niece explain the sand marks first, then shows you which gust made them. You repeat the method with another patch of ground. He says you can come back with more questions.
ev.lop.mentor_closure.choice_2: Spend a day practising with Mergen and his niece
ev.lop.mentor_closure.choice_2_result: You spend a day walking with the two of them, comparing the ground in morning and afternoon light. His niece insists you ask the cook about water as well. At the end Mergen invites you back for one more account.
ev.lop.mentor_closure.choice_3: Thank them and return to your caravan
ev.lop.mentor_closure.choice_3_result: You thank Mergen and his niece. She waves with the loose end of the cord before her uncle tells her to tie it down. You go back to your caravan with their demonstration in mind.
ev.lop.mentor_closure.title: The Wind Reader at Lop
ev.lop.shrine.body:
In a shallow cave outside Lop, an elderly keeper named Tuma trims the wick of a small lamp. Her grandson sweeps sand from the threshold, stopping every time the wind blows it back. ‘Sweep the corner first,’ she tells him. ‘Then the door.’ He asks why the travellers have left so many names on the wall. Tuma says some wanted their families to know they reached this place; others simply wanted someone to read them.

You ask which marks Tuma can still read. She points to an old prayer, then to a more recent note about a well. A passing merchant says that well changed after last year’s flood. Tuma asks him to add the new account beside the older one, with the date, so the next travellers understand both. He finds a piece of charcoal and kneels near the wall.

Tuma accepts half a silver for lamp oil from those who wish to give. Her grandson finally clears the doorway and sits down to listen as the merchant tells her what happened at the well.
ev.lop.shrine.choice.watch: Stay and hear the travellers’ accounts
ev.lop.shrine.title: The Keeper of the Cave Lamps
ev.lop.stopper.body:
At the inn’s outer bench, a leatherworker named Saran is testing a water-skin stopper for her brother’s next caravan. He pours in a cup of water, turns the skin and waits. A drop appears along the seam. Her brother says the leather looked sound yesterday. ‘It did when it was dry,’ Saran answers, and loosens the stitching to see where it pulls.

You ask whether she has time to mend it before the caravan leaves. Saran says her brother can take another skin, but she wants this one returned to its owner without a leak. A girl from the next table says the owner is her mother, who needs it for the small orchard behind the inn. She has come every morning to ask if it is ready. Saran promises to bring it herself when it holds water.

Her brother offers to pay a helper 0.8 silver to carry the repaired skin across town today. Saran can also show you how she tests the seam if you stay until the following day. She fills the skin again and watches the stopper closely.
ev.lop.stopper.choice.deliver: Deliver the repaired skin to the orchard
ev.lop.stopper.choice.learn: Stay until tomorrow and learn Saran’s leak test
ev.lop.stopper.result.deliver: You carry the repaired skin to the girl’s mother. She fills it at the orchard well and finds the seam dry. Saran’s brother pays you 0.8 silver as promised, and the girl runs back to tell her the good news.
ev.lop.stopper.result.learn: You stay another day while Saran wets and tests several seams. She lets you find the weak stitch on an old practice skin. Her brother leaves with another water skin, and you carry the method into your next crossing.
ev.lop.stopper.title: The Stopper That Would Not Hold
ev.maabar.courtyard.body: In a courtyard off the market, an old man is trying to move a wooden crate away from a young fig tree. His granddaughter has put it there to hold the shade cloth, but its corner is pressing against the trunk. “I was making a place for you to sit,” she says. He thanks her and asks if the cloth can be tied to the wall instead. She finds an old ring in the masonry; it comes loose when she pulls it. A neighbour who works with wood offers a sound hook from his box and asks someone to hold the cloth while he fits it. The old man promises to pay for the new hook and the work. The girl wants to help but her grandfather sends her first to bring water for the neighbour. “You can hold the other end when you come back.” The tree's leaves are already bending in the heat. You can help the neighbour fit the hook, or help the girl move the crate and make a safe seat for her grandfather.
ev.maabar.courtyard.choice.seat: Help the girl make her grandfather a seat
ev.maabar.courtyard.result.hook: You hold the shade cloth while the neighbour sets his new hook in the wall. The granddaughter returns with water and ties her end. The old man sits beside the fig tree without the crate against its trunk and asks the neighbour to pay you a share of the repair fee.
ev.maabar.courtyard.result.seat: You and the granddaughter move the crate clear of the tree and turn it into a steady seat. Her grandfather tries it and asks her to bring the cloth a little lower. The neighbour fixes the hook, and the household thanks you for making the courtyard comfortable again.
ev.maabar.courtyard.title: A Crate for the Fig Tree
ev.maabar.entry.body: At the Maabar market, a mother and son are moving their fish baskets into the shade before the sun reaches them. He has put his largest basket in front, blocking the cloth seller next door. “She needs to open her stall too,” his mother says. The boy drags it aside and asks the neighbour whether the space is enough. She spreads a bolt of cotton and thanks him. A horse groom passes through with an animal recently brought by sea; the boy moves the last basket so its hooves have room. You ask which road continues along the coast. The cloth seller points beyond the market well and says carriers use it toward Coilum. The mother offers you water, then asks her son to bring the groom a cup as well. “He can pay for fish later,” she says. The boy runs after him, pleased to have a reason to see the horse up close. If you stay, the two sellers will show you where the day's goods go after the market closes.
ev.maabar.entry.choice.look: Spend a day getting to know the market
ev.maabar.entry.choice.pass: Ask the road through town and continue
ev.maabar.entry.title: The Fish Baskets at Maabar
ev.maabar.site_gap.body: At a weaving shed in Maabar, a woman has stopped her loom because a thread in the warp has snapped. Her apprentice reaches for a thick strand to replace it. “Try that against the others first,” she says. He pulls it between his fingers and sees that the weave would stand out. You ask how they can join a thread without leaving a hard knot in the finished cloth. She overlaps the ends, rolls them gently and tucks the join toward the edge. The apprentice tries the next one and asks whether dampening it helps. “A little,” she answers, handing him a wet cloth. A carrier comes to collect cloth for the coast road toward Coilum. She asks him to wait until the loom is moving again, and he sits near the door watching the boy work. He points out the road he will take when you ask, then waits for the woman to check the repaired line. The carrier puts his hands behind his back rather than touching the unfinished cloth.
ev.maabar.site_gap.choice.interact: Help the apprentice join the thread
ev.maabar.site_gap.choice.route: Ask the carrier about the Coilum road
ev.maabar.site_gap.title: The Weaver’s Broken Thread
ev.maldive.battuta_a.body: In an island courtyard, a village clerk has papers spread beside two fishing families. They have shared a net for years, but its repair costs were never written down. “My brother paid for the last rope,” one woman says. The other replies, “And my daughter spent two mornings sewing it.” The clerk asks both to speak slowly while his niece records their names. She is also preparing for a family wedding in two days and worries that the work will keep her from helping with the meal. Her uncle says the families can take their time; he will pay an assistant to copy the account over the next three days. A pilot waiting at the gate is bound for Melibar after the celebration. “If you need the sea road, come down to the landing tomorrow,” he tells you. The niece asks whether you would rather stay with the clerk, help her household at the wedding, or meet the pilot once the tide is right.
ev.maldive.battuta_a.choice.flight: Spend a day with the pilot before departure
ev.maldive.battuta_a.choice.judge: Help the clerk record the families’ accounts
ev.maldive.battuta_a.choice.marry: Contribute to the wedding meal and stay
ev.maldive.battuta_a.title: Three Plans in the Island Courtyard
ev.maldive.entry.body: At an island landing, a woman is trying to lift a coil of coconut-fibre rope out of her brother's boat before the tide reaches it. Her daughter takes the lighter end and asks why he left it so close to the water. “I thought I would be back before the boat moved,” the brother says, climbing ashore. You help make space beside a stall where cowrie shells are being counted for small purchases. The stallkeeper asks where your vessel has come from and offers to show you the path through the village. The daughter wants to know whether people at your last port use shells as money. You tell her what you saw there; she holds out two clean shells and asks how much a piece of fruit might cost. Her mother laughs and says to ask the stallkeeper before spending them. A few households gather to meet the arriving boat, and the brother carries the dry rope up the path at last.
ev.maldive.entry.choice.arrive: Step ashore and greet the island households
ev.maldive.entry.title: A Landing among the Coconut Palms
ev.maldive.mat.body: In a courtyard near the island landing, two sisters are weaving a new sleeping mat. Their cousin is due to visit with his wife and child, and the older mat is too short for the three of them. The younger sister wants to finish before the boat arrives. She pulls a coconut leaf through the weave too hard and tears it. ‘We have another,’ the older one says, handing her a fresh strip. You ask whether the child is old enough to sleep on the mat. ‘Only when someone can convince him to leave his own grandmother’s arms,’ she replies. The sisters’ mother comes out carrying a folded cloth and reminds them the guesthouse has a dry room ready for their relatives. The younger sister asks whether you can hold the mat steady while she weaves the last edge. Her older sister says someone will also have to carry it to the guesthouse before their cousin sees it half finished. The boat’s sail is already visible beyond the palms. Their mother gives the cloth to her daughter and goes to the shore to greet the visiting family.
ev.maldive.mat.choice.carry: Carry the mat to the guesthouse
ev.maldive.mat.choice.weave: Help finish the mat’s last edge
ev.maldive.mat.result.carry: You and the older sister take the finished mat into the dry guest room. Their cousin arrives with his wife and child and recognizes the sisters’ familiar pattern. He thanks you in front of his aunt, who makes room for the child’s things beside the mat.
ev.maldive.mat.result.weave: You hold the mat steady while the younger sister works coconut leaves through the final edge. Their mother tests the firm border and pays you for the help. When their cousin arrives with his family, he spreads it in the guesthouse and laughs: his son has already fallen asleep in the child’s grandmother’s arms.
ev.maldive.mat.title: A Mat for the Returning Family
ev.mecha.cloak.body: At the roadside shelter, a seamstress has an old coat spread across her knees. She promised to mend it for a traveller who left before dawn, but two different names have been stitched inside the collar. Her son guesses the coat was passed from one brother to another. “It was,” she says, “but I need to know which one is coming back for it.” A woman filling a water skin recognizes the older brother's neat letters and says the younger one now wears the coat. The seamstress asks her son to add a fresh patch beneath the collar, leaving the old names in place. “He will want to remember who carried it first.” The boy asks you to hold the cloth while he makes the first stitch. He wants to catch the traveller before the northbound group leaves; his mother says they can wait at the shelter's gate and ask each person by name. The boy asks whether the younger brother will know his new stitches; his mother says the uneven first one will give him away.
ev.mecha.cloak.choice.find: Help find the coat’s current owner
ev.mecha.cloak.choice.stitch: Stay a day and help mend the collar
ev.mecha.cloak.result.find: You wait with the boy at the gate and ask the northbound travellers by name. The younger brother recognizes the coat and shows you an old patch on its sleeve. He thanks you for bringing it back, and the people at the shelter remember your help.
ev.mecha.cloak.result.stitch: You stay for a day while the boy practises his stitches and his mother repairs the collar. The younger brother comes back for the coat before the group leaves. He reads both names and tells the boy who wore it first; you have time to talk over a shared meal before moving on.
ev.mecha.cloak.title: A Coat with Two Names
ev.mecha.entry.body: Near Mecha, a family at a roadside shelter is sorting water skins for people arriving from different directions. A woman writes each owner's name on a wooden tag. Her brother points to two skins with the same mark and asks which belongs to an older traveller waiting in the shade. She asks him to feel the seams. “He patched his own with red thread yesterday,” she says. The brother finds the thread and carries the skin over. You ask which way travellers go if they continue north toward Medina. The woman says her cousin made that journey recently and will return to the shelter by evening. A group of pilgrims pauses nearby to adjust their clothing before entering the city; the woman gives them space and lets them take water in turn. Her brother brings you a cup and asks whether you are leaving today. If you can stay, he says, his cousin will show you the road on a board after supper.
ev.mecha.entry.choice.look: Stay a day and ask about the northern road
ev.mecha.entry.choice.pass: Ask the way through and continue
ev.mecha.entry.title: Names on the Water Skins
ev.mecha.site_gap.body: A potter beside the water shelter has set two clay jars in the shade. One is thick and heavy, the other light enough for his daughter to lift alone. She wants to send the lighter one with a traveller going north. “He has a cart,” she says. Her father taps the rim and asks her how she will keep it from knocking against his other goods. She fetches a rolled cloth. You ask whether the thick jar would be safer. “Perhaps,” he says, “but he'll have to lift it at every water stop.” The daughter fits the cloth around the lighter jar and shows you that its mouth is wide enough to clean. A traveller arrives to collect it, asking which road to take toward Medina. She points to the same northern route used by people at the shelter and asks him to bring back word of how the jar travels. He promises to do so if it reaches the next stop intact. The potter reminds his daughter to keep the spare cloth for the return journey.
ev.mecha.site_gap.choice.route: Ask about the road to Medina
ev.mecha.site_gap.title: The Potter’s Water Jars
ev.medina.entry.body: At a Medina guesthouse, a traveller from the north is trying to remember where she left her bundle of dates. The keeper's young son finds it beside the water jar. “I moved it out of the sun,” he says. She thanks him and asks if there is room to sit while she sorts the food for her return journey. The keeper brings out a mat and asks where she is headed. She names the road toward Petra, then admits that she needs to ask about the next water stop before leaving. You have the same question. “Let us ask together after the morning crowd has had water,” the keeper says. Outside, people travelling to visit the city's sacred places pass along the street. The woman tells the boy to keep one date for finding her bundle; he says he would rather hear how far she has come. She begins with the first town she can remember clearly and the keeper sets another cup down for you.
ev.medina.entry.choice.pass: Ask for the onward road and continue
ev.medina.entry.choice.rest: Rest at the guesthouse for a day
ev.medina.entry.title: The Bundle beside the Water Jar
ev.medina.lantern.body: A lantern maker has brought a repaired lamp to the guesthouse gate. The keeper's mother ordered it after two travellers missed the turn in the dark. Her granddaughter takes the lamp and asks why its glass has a faint crack. “It is the old pane, cleaned and set into a new frame,” the maker says. “We tested it at home.” The grandmother lights it and notices the flame sits too low to show the painted arrow above the gate. The maker brings a small hook from his bag, but the granddaughter knows a better place on the post. She holds the lamp there while the grandmother stands across the lane to check what a traveller will see. “There,” the older woman calls. “I can read the arrow.” The granddaughter asks you to help carry the maker's tools back, or stay until evening to see whether the lamp really guides the first arrivals.
ev.medina.lantern.choice.evening: Stay until evening to test the lantern
ev.medina.lantern.choice.tools: Help the maker return his tools
ev.medina.lantern.result.evening: You stay for the day and watch the lantern as the sky darkens. The first travellers see the arrow and turn into the guesthouse without calling for directions. The grandmother serves you supper and makes up a place to sleep; you leave rested the next morning.
ev.medina.lantern.result.tools: You carry the maker's tools as he walks back through the lane. The granddaughter stays to light the lantern at the gate. When the keeper's mother sees you return, she thanks you for helping them finish before dusk; nearby households remember the new light.
ev.medina.lantern.title: The Lantern at the Guesthouse Gate
ev.medina.site_gap.body: At the guesthouse door, the keeper has set a shared water jar in the shade. His daughter is turning the ladle upside down on a clean cloth after each visitor. A man leading an animal asks whether he may water it from the jar. “Use the trough beyond the wall,” she says, “then come back for your own drink.” He thanks her and leads the animal around. You ask why she keeps the ladle off the jar's rim. She shows you the dust on the wall where the wind meets it and says the cloth is easier to wash. A traveller setting out toward Petra asks about the north road. The keeper comes out with a full bucket and points from the gate. The daughter asks him to wait before pouring: a leaf has blown into the jar. She lifts it out, and he lets her make the next round of cups herself. She asks the keeper to leave the clean cloth beside the jar for the evening visitors.
ev.medina.site_gap.choice.route: Ask about the road to Petra
ev.medina.site_gap.title: The Guesthouse Water Jar
ev.melibar.a.body: A harbour watchman has taken a pepper sack off the wet stones and set it on boards beneath the shed. A young loader asks why he moved it when a boat is about to take cargo. “Because it will spend much longer on the boat than it spent here,” he says. The pepper seller arrives and checks the seam. You ask which vessels she sends toward Cail. She points out one loading beyond the fishers' boats, then asks the watchman whether the harbour entrance is clear. He says a larger ship is still turning and asks everyone to leave room at the quay. The loader lifts another sack without blocking the path. The seller asks you to watch the loading for a day if you want to understand how the dry sacks reach the ships. A pilot nearby offers to name the southern coast roads when he finishes bringing a boat in. The seller asks the loader to read the mark on the sack before it joins the others. He gets it right this time.
ev.melibar.a.choice.ask-south: Ask the pilot about Coilum and Maabar
ev.melibar.a.choice.buy-pepper: Buy a full trade sack of pepper
ev.melibar.a.choice.watch: Spend a day watching the pepper loading
ev.melibar.a.title: The Pepper Shed by the Harbour
ev.melibar.b.body: On the steps near a harbour shrine, a pearl seller waits for her brother to bring a small lamp. She has a parcel of pearls to show a buyer, but the last light is too dim to judge them. “He went for the lamp before you came,” she tells you. A priest tending the shrine asks her to keep the steps clear for visitors, so she moves her basket aside. An older sailor sitting nearby points toward the water. “When the sky opens, you can find the northern star low over that mast.” You ask how he uses it. He shows you where the mast meets the horizon and says that he compares the star with a fixed point rather than guessing its height. Her brother returns with the lamp, carefully shielding the flame. The pearl seller opens the parcel and invites you to examine it while the sailor continues showing the younger boatmen how to sight along the mast. Her brother asks whether the pearls will look different by lamplight; she says the buyer can compare them again in the morning.
ev.melibar.b.choice.buy-pearls: Buy the seller’s parcel of pearls
ev.melibar.b.choice.measure-star: Help the sailors compare the star and mast
ev.melibar.b.choice.observe: Spend a day near the shrine and harbour
ev.melibar.b.title: A Pearl Seller after Sunset
ev.melibar.battuta_a.body: At a lodging house near Melibar's harbour, a woman is setting out cups for sailors who will come ashore when their boat finishes unloading. Her nephew says the people from the large vessel will fill the whole yard. “Then fetch the second bench,” she tells him. He asks whether to put it by the prayer room. “Leave that path open. Some guests will go there before they eat.” A pilot waiting for water tells you the boat has called at Coilum and will need a day in harbour for its cargo to be checked. You ask how people find the coastal passage. He shows you the turns on a worn board, then puts it away before the cups can spill over it. A pepper trader comes to the door with a full sack for sale. The woman makes room for him under the awning and asks her nephew to set out the dry mat. The first sailors arrive, hungry and grateful for a place to sit.
ev.melibar.battuta_a.choice.junks: Spend a day learning the Coilum passage from the pilot
ev.melibar.battuta_a.choice.prayer: Stay a day helping guests at the lodging house
ev.melibar.battuta_a.choice.trade: Buy the trader’s full sack of pepper
ev.melibar.battuta_a.title: A Day at the Harbour Lodging House
ev.melibar.entry.body: At Melibar, a pepper grower has brought a small sample to the market and left the rest of her sacks under a dry awning. Her son wants to open the largest one so buyers can smell it. “Let them smell this bowl first,” she says, pushing it toward him. A ship's cook tries a few grains and asks whether the next load will be ready before his boat leaves. The grower asks which boat he means; he points across the harbour. “Then ask your captain to wait until I have weighed it,” she answers. You ask where the road through town runs. The son points past the water stall and the shrine, then offers to introduce you to the pepper buyers if you stay. His mother tells him to cover the sample before he goes: a shower is gathering beyond the houses. The cook promises to return with his captain after the market has had time to hear the price. The grower asks the boy to keep the bowl inside until the captain comes back. He covers it with a clean cloth.
ev.melibar.entry.choice.battuta: Meet the harbour lodging house family
ev.melibar.entry.choice.market: Spend a day in the pepper market
ev.melibar.entry.choice.pass: Ask the road through town and continue
ev.melibar.entry.title: The Pepper Sample at Melibar
ev.melibar.seedlings.body: Behind Melibar's market, a grower is tying young pepper vines to supports. Her nephew has pushed one support too close to an older root. “That vine has been here longer than you,” she tells him. He pulls the stake back and asks how to know where the older roots end. She loosens the soil with her fingers and shows him a fine pale root near the surface. You ask why the young vines are being moved today. “A neighbour gave us cuttings,” she says. “I promised her I'd look after them until they take.” The nephew carries a small pot of water between the rows, careful not to spill it on the market path. A woman from next door arrives to see where her cuttings went. She laughs when she sees the boy taking such care and asks whether they need another pair of hands. The grower offers you a place beside her nephew, or a seat to watch how they tend the vines through the day. The neighbour asks the boy which support he moved, and he proudly shows her the spot that no longer presses on the old root.
ev.melibar.seedlings.choice.plant: Help set the young vine supports
ev.melibar.seedlings.choice.stay: Stay a day with the grower’s family
ev.melibar.seedlings.result.plant: You hold each support away from the older roots while the nephew presses it into place. The neighbour sees that her cuttings have room to grow and thanks you for helping the family keep its promise. The grower gives the boy the last stake to set on his own.
ev.melibar.seedlings.result.stay: You stay through the day while the family waters and ties the young vines. At noon the neighbour brings rice and you eat together in the shade. The nephew returns the borrowed pot before evening. You leave rested, knowing the hands behind the pepper sold at the market.
ev.melibar.seedlings.title: The Pepper Vines behind the Market
ev.merva.entry.body:
A shallow pool lies where one of Merv’s old canals has filled with silt. Ducks walk over the low bank. At the roadside lodging, Hamid is replacing the thatch above a room his sister uses for travellers. She calls up to him that the soup is getting cold. ‘The roof can have its turn after lunch,’ she says. He lowers the bundle of reeds but stays on the ladder to show you where last night’s rain came through.

You ask whether the canal still serves anyone. Hamid’s sister points to a narrower channel behind the lodging. ‘We use that one. This old bed holds water only after a hard rain.’ Their neighbour arrives with a shovel and says his mulberry trees have had too little water this week. Hamid promises to help clear the small channel once the roof is safe. The neighbour looks at the soup and asks whether there is room for him at the table.

Hamid’s sister brings out another bowl. She has a mat ready if you stay the day; the neighbour is leaving soon and can show you the road past the working wells.
ev.merva.entry.choice.pass: Go on after asking about the working wells
ev.merva.entry.choice.rest: Rest a day and share their meal
ev.merva.entry.title: The Roof Beside the Canal
ev.merva.site_gap.body:
Nuri, a copyist, is drying fresh sheets beneath a mulberry tree. Her young cousin holds the corners with thin strips of wood. He lifts one strip too soon and a page curls toward the dirt. ‘That is the letter for my father,’ he says, trying to catch it. Nuri catches the clean edge and lays it flat again.

You ask why the letter needs such care. Nuri says her uncle works on the road toward Sapurgan and reads every line his son sends, even the accounts of their donkey. The boy has written that the animal stole half a melon. ‘It only took the rind,’ he protests when Nuri reads it back. She smiles and tells him to correct the page once it is dry.

Nuri tests the corner with the back of her hand. She has spare paper for you to try a line, and the boy knows which stopping places his father uses when he travels east. He watches the page and waits for the wind to settle.
ev.merva.site_gap.choice.interact: Try writing on Nuri’s spare sheet
ev.merva.site_gap.choice.route: Ask the boy about his father’s road to Sapurgan
ev.merva.site_gap.title: The Copyist’s Drying Pages
ev.merva.waterturn.body:
At a small working canal, Zahra has placed two pebbles beside the sluice to remember whose turn comes next. Her brother insists the pebble nearest the water is his. She asks him to read the names she scratched on the board above it. He leans close, then laughs: he had been looking at the board upside down.

Their neighbour brings a cracked wooden shutter to replace the one in the channel. You ask why Zahra is waiting. ‘If we put it in before the afternoon turn, his vegetables lose their water,’ she says, nodding toward her brother. He says he can help fit the board after his field has its share. Zahra promises to bring supper if they finish before dark.

The new shutter is ready, but its lower edge needs to be held steady while the brother fastens it. Their mother, coming from the fields, asks whether everyone has eaten. Zahra lifts the empty water jug so she can see the answer for herself.
ev.merva.waterturn.choice.board: Pay 1 silver for the replacement board
ev.merva.waterturn.choice.wait: Stay until tomorrow’s water turn and learn the schedule
ev.merva.waterturn.result.board: You put 1 silver toward the board. Zahra writes down the payment before her brother fixes the shutter, then brings supper as promised. The neighbours thank you when the water reaches both fields in turn.
ev.merva.waterturn.result.wait: You stay until the next day’s water turn and help Zahra read the worn names on the board. Her brother shows you how far the water runs before he closes the gate. By evening you understand the timing well enough to plan another canal crossing.
ev.merva.waterturn.title: The Water Turn
ev.mien.entry.body: And when you have travelled those 15 days through such a difficult country as I have described, in which travellers have to carry provisions for the road because there are no inhabitants, then you arrive at the capital city of this Province of Mien, and it also is called AMIEN, and is a very great and noble city. The people are Idolaters and have a peculiar language, and are subject to the Great Kaan. And in this city there is a thing so rich and rare that I must tell you about it.
ev.mien.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.mien.entry.title: Arriving at MIEN
ev.moscovia.birchletter.body:
Before the northern traveller departs, Darya’s son returns with the note he took out of the packet. He has copied it twice in larger letters because he worries the first will be hard for his grandmother to read. Both say that he has learned to mend a net and wants his grandmother to visit when the river opens. The traveller is mending the last strap on his wagon outside.

Darya suggests giving him the clearer copy and keeping the other. Her son asks you to read it aloud first. You can sit with him over the words, or take the note to the traveller yourself and earn a small fee for the errand.

The boy points to a crooked letter and asks whether his grandmother will think it says ‘boat’ instead of ‘net.’ Darya leans over the bark: ‘Read the whole sentence to me.’ He does, slowly. The traveller knocks at the doorway and says his wagon is nearly ready. ‘One more moment,’ Darya calls. You can help the boy choose the clearer copy, or carry it down to the wagon while Darya finishes tying the cloth.
ev.moscovia.birchletter.choice.deliver: Take the note to the traveller
ev.moscovia.birchletter.choice.read: Read the note with the boy
ev.moscovia.birchletter.result.deliver: You place the note in the traveller’s packet and return to tell the boy it is safely tucked away. Darya pays you 0.4 silver for the errand. He keeps the other copy and reads it once more to her.
ev.moscovia.birchletter.result.read: You read each line and let the boy correct his own spelling. He takes the clearer copy to the traveller himself. Darya thanks you; the family will remember your patience.
ev.moscovia.birchletter.title: A Note for Grandmother
ev.moscovia.entry.body:
At the Moscow landing, a woman named Darya is wrapping a packet of cloth for a northern traveller. Her little son presses a birchbark note into the knot. ‘For Grandmother,’ he says. Darya unties the packet, puts the note inside where it will stay dry, and makes him tie it again.

Houses and workshops spread from the river toward the town’s churches and walls. Timber, wax, and furs pass through the landing. Darya tells you where the caravans stop, then calls her son back before he can ask the traveller for a second promise.

The traveller asks the boy, ‘What did you write?’ The boy grips the packet and says it is a surprise. Darya replies, ‘Your grandmother can barely see small letters. Did you make them large enough?’ He takes the note back for a moment, frowns, and promises to check. You ask when the northern party leaves. Darya says it is waiting for a wagon axle to be repaired; there is time to find a bed by the landing before they set out.
ev.moscovia.entry.choice.rest: Rest for a day by the river
ev.moscovia.entry.title: A Letter beside the River
ev.nanghin.entry.body: Nanghin is a very noble Province towards the west. The people are Idolaters (and so forth) and live by trade and manufactures. They have silk in great abundance, and they weave many fine tissues of silk and gold. They have all sorts of corn and victuals very cheap, for the province is a most productive one. Game also is abundant, and lions too are found there. The merchants are great and opulent, and the Emperor draws a large revenue from them, in the shape of duties on the goods which they buy and sell.
ev.nanghin.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.nanghin.entry.title: Concerning the City of Nanghin
ev.nicaea.entry.body:
Nicaea sits beside a lake, its old walls visible from the road. Eleni is washing a blanket at the shore. Her grandson Leon sits on a stone, holding the wooden pegs she uses to dry it. Each time she asks for one, he gives her two.

“One for the blanket, one for the next blanket,” he explains. Eleni tells you that when he was smaller he tried to dry a fish with a peg. The fish escaped into the lake, taking the peg with it. Leon says he no longer does that. He is watching the water carefully now.

Eleni asks whether you have come from the east or the west. She shows you the lane that meets the road beyond the walls and offers a place to rest. Leon points out the easiest place to walk down to the water, then checks whether his grandmother has enough pegs left for the blanket.

You ask Leon how he knew the fish would take the clip with it. ‘I did not,’ he says. ‘I only found out when Grandmother counted the clips and one was gone.’ Eleni says a neighbour returned it a week later, caught in a reed beside his boat. Leon asks if she still has it. She points to the slightly bent one in his hand. He tries it on the thick edge of the blanket; it holds, though he has to press harder than with the others. Eleni asks him to leave that one for the last corner.
ev.nicaea.entry.choice.pass: Thank Eleni and continue beside the lake
ev.nicaea.entry.choice.rest: Stay a day at Eleni's house
ev.nicaea.entry.title: By the Lake at Nicaea
ev.nicaea.figpath.body:
Along the lane above the lake, Irem is packing figs into a shallow basket. Her mother has written a message for Aunt Zoe, who lives across the hills on the road toward Smyrna. Irem folds it three times and tucks it beneath the fruit, then takes it out again because juice has begun to leak through the cloth.

Aunt Zoe taught Irem to graft the tree when she was young. This is the first year it has borne enough fruit to send any away. Irem has learned the southward road from her aunt's letters, including the way toward Smyrna. Her mother is walking with her as far as the caravan stop tomorrow and invites you along. They also have lunch ready if you would rather sit with them and hear why Irem kept the tree alive through its first dry summer.

You ask whether the fruit will last until tomorrow. Irem’s mother presses one gently and says the ripest should stay at home; her sister can wait for the firmer ones. ‘Will Aunt Zoe mind if I choose them?’ Irem asks. ‘She will be pleased you grew them,’ her mother replies. Irem moves the damp letter into a dry cloth and asks you to check that the address is still legible. You can read it, though a corner has curled. She straightens it beneath the basket handle and tells you her aunt always writes back with news of the road and the family’s old garden.
ev.nicaea.figpath.choice.meal: Stay for lunch and hear about the fig tree
ev.nicaea.figpath.choice.walk: Walk with Irem to the caravan stop tomorrow
ev.nicaea.figpath.result.meal: At lunch, Irem tells you how she carried water to the young tree during its first dry summer. Her mother remembers that Irem forgot her own sandals twice but never forgot the tree. They cut open one ripe fig to share, then pack the rest with fresh cloth. You eat with them and set out feeling stronger.
ev.nicaea.figpath.result.walk: You spend the day walking with Irem and her mother. At each turn Irem recalls something Aunt Zoe wrote about the southward road. At the caravan stop they find a traveller bound toward Smyrna and give him the basket, the letter now wrapped in dry cloth. You mark Nicaea, Smyrna, and the route between them on your map. Irem asks the traveller to bring back word when her aunt tastes the fruit.
ev.nicaea.figpath.title: The Figs for Aunt Zoe
ev.ninive.entry.body:
Mosul’s houses stand beside the Tigris, with the old mounds of Nineveh across the water. At the ferry, a father tries to persuade his daughter to let go of a sack of grain long enough to get into the boat.

‘It’s for Aunt Laila,’ she tells you. ‘Last month she sent us a bowl and told us to fill it when the harvest came.’ Her father takes one handle and lets her keep the other. Around them, travellers are finding space for their bundles and deciding which bank they need.

The ferryman calls for people bound across to wait until the animals are aboard. Mariam asks her father whether Aunt Laila will see them from the bank. ‘She always comes early when she knows we are bringing grain,’ he says. You ask if there is room for one more traveller. He glances at the boatman, who holds up two fingers for the places left. Mariam tries to shift the sack without dropping it. Her father tells her to set it on the dry plank first and keep her hand on the tied end. She does, then checks twice that the knot is secure.
ev.ninive.entry.choice.rest: Spend a day resting by the river
ev.ninive.entry.title: Across from Nineveh
ev.ninive.ferrybowl.body:
When the ferry returns, Mariam is carrying Laila’s bowl. It is full of roasted grain. ‘She said I brought enough for her neighbours too,’ Mariam says. ‘Then she filled this so we’d have something for the way home.’

Her father offers to show you the quieter path toward Tabriz after he puts the boat in order. Mariam is happy to share the roasted grain now if you would rather sit with her on the bank.

You ask whether Laila kept the bowl full while they visited. Mariam says her aunt emptied it into smaller cups for the neighbours, then refilled it from the pan before they left. ‘She never lets a dish go home empty,’ her father says. Mariam asks him if he told Laila about the torn sack. He nods; Laila sent back a stronger needle and told him to keep it with the ferry gear. The boatman calls for the next crossing, and her father rises to help move a bundle. Mariam rests the warm bowl on her knees and waits until he has the boat settled.
ev.ninive.ferrybowl.choice.eat: Sit with Mariam and share the grain
ev.ninive.ferrybowl.choice.path: Walk with her father to the Tabriz road
ev.ninive.ferrybowl.result.eat: Mariam pours grain into your palm and tells you how Laila roasts it in a shallow pan. You eat slowly while the ferry crosses again. The rest leaves you with more strength for the road.
ev.ninive.ferrybowl.result.path: You walk to the turning with her father. He names the next places to stop and waits until you have marked the route toward Tabriz and the city beyond it on your map. Then he turns back toward the boat.
ev.ninive.ferrybowl.title: The Bowl Comes Back
ev.novogardia.barknote.body:
A boatman finds a birchbark note tucked into Anfisa’s wax bundle. It is a reminder from her sister: bring a little wax home for candles and stop working after the evening bell. Anfisa laughs at the second part but folds the note carefully.

Her daughter offers to carry a small parcel to her aunt. You can walk with her and see the town beyond the market, or stay to help Anfisa finish weighing the last bundles before dusk. Anfisa will pay for the work.

‘Did she really write that I should stop at the bell?’ Anfisa asks her daughter. ‘Twice,’ the girl says, showing her the second line. Anfisa tucks a little wax into the parcel and asks you whether it will survive the walk without breaking. Her daughter suggests wrapping it in old cloth. Her father calls that the last bundles are ready for the scales. Anfisa hands the parcel to the girl and says she may go as soon as someone helps finish the weighing.
ev.novogardia.barknote.choice.walk: Walk with her daughter to her aunt’s house
ev.novogardia.barknote.choice.weigh: Stay and weigh the wax bundles
ev.novogardia.barknote.result.walk: You accompany her through the lanes. Her aunt takes the wax and asks after Anfisa. On the way back, the girl shows you a quiet place to sit, and you recover some strength before leaving.
ev.novogardia.barknote.result.weigh: You help Anfisa weigh the last bundles, then spend the night nearby. At dawn she pays you 0.5 silver for the day’s work. Her daughter returns with a candle her aunt made from last year’s wax.
ev.novogardia.barknote.title: The Note in the Wax Bundle
ev.novogardia.entry.body:
At Novgorod’s river market, a woman named Anfisa counts bundles of wax while her father argues with a boatman over space. Her daughter carries a birchbark note from one stall to another: a neighbour has borrowed their scales again.

‘Tell him to bring them back before noon,’ Anfisa calls. Then she turns to you and explains where travellers gather for the road south. The city’s churches and trading yards stand close to the water; the river makes it easy for news to arrive with the cargo.

Her father asks whether they can use another trader’s scales. Anfisa shakes her head: ‘I promised the buyer I would weigh it on ours, so he can check the mark himself.’ The girl returns without the scales and says the neighbour has found one pan bent and is coming to apologize. Anfisa asks her to help lay out the bundles in order. You ask where to find a bed after the market closes; she points to a house behind the landing, then reminds her daughter that the small bundles go first.
ev.novogardia.entry.choice.rest: Rest for a day near the river
ev.novogardia.entry.title: The River Market
ev.ormus.a.body:
At the harbour customs table, a clerk is weighing a sealed bundle while a pearl sorter waits with a shallow basket. Her son has written the shell count on a scrap, but the ink ran when he set it beside the water jar. ‘The shells have not changed,’ he says. His mother asks him to count them again anyway.

You ask whether the basket came from the near shore. She points across the water and names Calatu, where she knows people who handle boats and divers. The clerk says this basket of pearl shells needs a separate 3 silver yard entry. The pearl sorter asks whether you have paid for this basket before she lets you through the working yard; the boy rolls his eyes but carries the basket back into the shade.

A watchman on the wall calls down the names of the boats coming in. The clerk checks the next bundle, while the boy makes fresh marks for the shells. His mother hands him a dry board to write on this time.
ev.ormus.a.choice.pearl_diver: Ask the pearl sorter about Calatu
ev.ormus.a.choice.toll: Pay 3 silver to register the pearl basket
ev.ormus.a.choice.watch_ships: Spend a day watching the boats from the wall
ev.ormus.a.title: The Customs Scale and Pearl Basket
ev.ormus.astrodice_tide.body:
At the landing, a captain has set his cargo by the boat but has not given the order to load. The pilot checks the tide mark on the wall, and his niece counts the water jars. One of the crew asks whether you will cast the three dice you learned or simply ask the captain when he is ready.

You ask what has delayed them. The captain holds up a wet rope. It slipped during loading, and he wants a new knot before anyone carries another bundle aboard. The pilot says the water is still favourable, then kneels to help the sailor tie it. His niece writes the time beside the tide mark.

A porter arrives with the last cargo bundle. He asks whether to put it down or wait. The captain points to dry stones until the rope is secure. The pilot’s niece moves the leather dice cup away from the splash and leaves it beside you while the knot is tested.
ev.ormus.astrodice_tide.choice.cast: Cast the three dice for this departure
ev.ormus.astrodice_tide.choice.sail: Ask the captain and prepare to sail
ev.ormus.astrodice_tide.title: Before the Tide Turns
ev.ormus.b.body:
In a spice warehouse, an Indian trader is trying to read the labels his son tied on the sacks. The boy has written the ship’s name where the buyer’s name should go. ‘Both names matter,’ his father says, and makes room on a clean tag. An older porter brings the sack back from the doorway before it can be loaded onto the wrong caravan.

The trader offers a full pepper lot for 150 silver. At a nearby stall, his wife has a small dish of dried ginger for 3 silver; she warms a piece over the brazier and lets you smell it. You ask how the goods move onward. The porter explains which boats cross toward Calatu and which inland caravans take goods toward Cobinan.

The son copies the two names in the right places. His mother calls from the stall, asking whether the ginger is ready for the traveller. He glances at you, then at his father, waiting to see which tag needs the next knot.
ev.ormus.b.choice.ginger: Buy and eat a small ginger portion for 3 silver
ev.ormus.b.choice.pepper: Buy the full pepper lot for 150 silver
ev.ormus.b.choice.trade_routes: Ask about Calatu and Cobinan trade routes
ev.ormus.b.title: The Spice Warehouse Tags
ev.ormus.c.body:
A hot wind reaches the port lane while a dates seller is tying down his awning. His sister is bringing water jars inside; her little son insists he can carry one alone. She gives him the smallest and asks you to help with the heavy pair. The seller looks up at the dust rising beyond the roofs and calls to a guide who knows when the gusts usually ease.

‘Will it pass before supper?’ the boy asks. The guide says he will watch the sky for a while before promising anything. You ask where the family keeps cool when the shutters are closed. The sister shows you a lower room where the jars stand out of the heat. A neighbour is already there, sewing a torn shade cloth.

The guide offers two days of help reading the weather for 1.5 silver. The family can also give you space to wait out several windy days. The seller pulls the last knot tight and asks his sister whether all the jars are safely inside.
ev.ormus.c.choice.guide: Pay the guide 1.5 silver for two days
ev.ormus.c.choice.observe: Watch how the neighbours prepare for the wind
ev.ormus.c.choice.wait: Wait out the wind for three days
ev.ormus.c.title: When the Hot Wind Reaches the Lane
ev.ormus.entry.body:
At the Hormuz landing, a trader’s daughter is checking the cords on a steel shipment before it goes from a boat to a pack animal. Her father has written the count on a wooden tag, but she finds one bundle with no tag at all. ‘If it goes inland unnamed, someone will count it twice,’ she says. He asks the porter to put it back on dry ground.

A pilot nearby is explaining the tide to a young sailor who wants to leave before his mother arrives with food. ‘She knows this landing better than you,’ the pilot says. The mother appears with a covered bowl and asks whether the boat has water for the crossing. You help the porter keep the steel bundle away from the spray while the trader and his daughter agree on its mark.

The trader offers the full Damascus steel lot for 146 silver. The customs desk will need two days to clear other cargo, and the pilot has time later to talk about the port. His daughter ties the tag firmly, then checks it once more before letting the porter lift the bundle.
ev.ormus.entry.choice.customs: Spend two days clearing cargo at the customs desk
ev.ormus.entry.choice.lore: Spend a day talking with the pilot
ev.ormus.entry.choice.market: Buy the Damascus steel lot for 146 silver
ev.ormus.entry.title: At the Hormuz Landing
ev.ormus.mentor_astrodice.body:
A pilot at the Hormuz landing has three marked dice in a leather cup. His niece is making a tide list for the crews while her father answers a sailor who wants to know whether to cast before departure. ‘First tell me whether the water jars are aboard,’ the pilot says. The sailor admits one is still at the well and goes to fetch it.

The niece shows you the marks on the dice and asks what you would want to know before crossing. You mention wind. She writes it beside the tide, then asks her father whether she has forgotten anything. ‘The boat itself,’ he says, pointing to a frayed rope laid across the table. You ask whether the dice can settle that. He smiles and gives you the rope to inspect.

He teaches the dice over seven days for 70 silver, beginning with the names of their faces. If you only want an explanation now, he will read one example while his niece finishes the tide list. The sailor returns with the last water jar, breathing hard but pleased to have remembered it.
ev.ormus.mentor_astrodice.choice.ask: Ask the pilot to explain one cast
ev.ormus.mentor_astrodice.choice.learn: Pay 70 silver for seven days of star-dice lessons
ev.ormus.mentor_astrodice.title: The Pilot’s Three Dice
ev.ormus.netweight.body:
At a fishing boat, a woman is repairing a net while her brother searches a basket for one missing weight. Their father made the weights from small pieces of fired clay; the last one broke when the net caught on a stone. The brother says they can sail with a gap. She shakes the net and shows him how one corner lifts without the weight.

You ask whether the boat must leave today. ‘When the tide is right,’ she says, ‘after this corner stays down.’ A boy from the neighbouring boat offers a spare weight, but it is too heavy. The brother chooses a smaller clay weight from the basket and asks you to hold the mesh while he ties it on. The woman tests the net in shallow water and calls him back to shorten the cord.

She can pay you 0.5 silver if you stay and help them finish the net, or show you how she sets the weights if you have little time. Her brother passes you the loose corner and waits for your hand.
ev.ormus.netweight.choice.finish: Stay a day and finish the net
ev.ormus.netweight.choice.learn: Ask how the weights are set
ev.ormus.netweight.result.finish: You spend the day helping fit the weights. In shallow water the net settles evenly, and the siblings take it aboard before the tide changes. The woman pays you 0.5 silver; their father will find his work in use again.
ev.ormus.netweight.result.learn: She shows you why the corner rose and how she spaces each weight. You write it down while her brother adjusts the last cord; the boy from the next boat retrieves his heavy spare.
ev.ormus.netweight.title: A Weight for the Fishing Net
ev.paukin.entry.body: When you leave Coiganju you ride south-east for a day along a causeway laid with fine stone, which you find at this entrance to Manzi. On either hand there is a great expanse of water, so that you cannot enter the province except along this causeway. At the end of the day’s journey you reach the fine city of PAUKIN. The people are Idolaters, burn their dead, are subject to the Great Kaan, and use paper-money. They live by trade and manufactures and have great abundance of silk, whereof they weave a great variety of fine stuffs of silk and gold. Of all the necessaries of life there is great store.
ev.paukin.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.paukin.entry.title: Of the Cities of Paukin and Cayu
ev.pein.entry.body:
On the riverbank at Pein, an elderly stone picker is washing two pale pebbles in a shallow bowl. Her grandson calls both of them jade. She makes him dry them before deciding what to write on their tags. ‘Your uncle will ask where each one came from,’ she says. ‘If you mix them up, he has to walk back to the river.’

You ask the boy whether his uncle trades the stones. He says the uncle cuts some for local buyers and sends the rest with caravans. The old woman points to a cotton stall across the path. Her daughter works there and keeps the family’s accounts while the boy goes out with the pickers. ‘She knows what I brought in yesterday better than I do,’ the woman says. The daughter hears her and calls back that yesterday’s count was three stones, not four. The boy finds the fourth pebble in the water bowl.

A caravan is preparing to leave the bank. The woman wraps the two stones separately and asks whether you have already settled where you will find water next.
ev.pein.entry.choice.look: Stay a day and hear how the family works
ev.pein.entry.title: At the Riverbank in Pein
ev.pein.jarnames.body:
At the potter’s yard, a young woman named Amina is tracing two names onto a fired water jar. Her father hands her a brush and asks which name belongs nearest the handle. ‘Both should be easy to see,’ she says. The jar is for her sister and the sister’s new household. They have agreed to share water from one well while the younger family builds its own storage.

You ask why she has written the names herself. Amina says her sister cannot come to the yard today: she is repairing the roof before the next rain. Their aunt, who promised to collect the jar, arrives without a cart and laughs at how large it is. Amina says they can carry it together, but the brushwork must dry first. Her father offers a small wage if someone takes it across town after the writing sets.

The aunt sits in the shade and tells Amina to finish the second name slowly. She wants the sister to see that the whole family was thinking of her when the jar arrived.
ev.pein.jarnames.choice.deliver: Deliver the jar after the writing dries
ev.pein.jarnames.choice.stay: Stay a day to help Amina finish the household marks
ev.pein.jarnames.result.deliver: You wait for the lettering to dry, then carry the jar with the aunt across town. Amina’s sister sees both names and calls for her family to bring water. Her father pays you 0.8 silver for the delivery.
ev.pein.jarnames.result.stay: You spend the day helping Amina mark smaller cups for both households. Her aunt takes the large jar home, and Amina sets a cup aside for her sister’s first meal beneath the repaired roof. You remember their care for one another.
ev.pein.jarnames.title: Two Names on a Water Jar
ev.pein.site_gap.body:
A salt seller named Rustam has set two pinches on a clay dish, one grey and one bright. His daughter reaches for the bright pile. He stops her gently: ‘That one belongs to the family who brought it here. We have to finish testing before they take it home.’ She says their camel has been waiting since morning. Rustam looks at the animal chewing dry grass and admits she is right.

You ask what the test is for. He mixes a pinch of each salt with clean water and lets the grit settle. His wife, who keeps the measures, checks the grey pile and says it will do well for the neighbour’s cooking. The daughter asks if the pale one is better. ‘For this buyer, perhaps,’ her mother says. ‘But first let us tell him what is in his own sack.’

The buyer comes back with a water jug. Rustam puts the dish where all of them can see it, and his daughter holds the camel’s lead while they talk.
ev.pein.site_gap.choice.interact: Help the family compare the two salts
ev.pein.site_gap.choice.route: Ask Rustam how caravans reach Yarcan
ev.pein.site_gap.title: The Salt Seller’s Dish
ev.pentam.entry.body: At Pentam’s landing, a girl is chalking the names of boats onto freshwater jars. Her grandfather carries the filled jars down from the well, and she tells him which boat has already paid. A sailor from a larger vessel points to one marked for another crew. ‘We ordered two,’ he says. She checks the cord on his receipt and finds that his mate wrote down tomorrow’s delivery. The grandfather sets his load beneath the shade while they sort it out. ‘If we give you that jar now, whose boat waits thirsty?’ he asks. The sailor goes to bring his mate and returns with an empty jar of his own. The girl promises to fill it after the next walk to the well. You ask how the larger ship will leave through the shallow water. Her grandfather points to a pilot’s little boat moored beyond the jars. ‘Ask him when the tide turns,’ he says. The girl gives the sailor his corrected receipt and asks whether you are going on through the town or staying to watch the harbour for a day.
ev.pentam.entry.choice.look: Stay a day to learn the harbour
ev.pentam.entry.title: The Freshwater Jars at Pentam
ev.pentam.well.body: On a lane above the landing, the well keeper has found a crack in the jar reserved for an older neighbour. Her son wants to fill another jar at once, but all the spare ones have been promised to boats coming in that afternoon. ‘We can carry the water in two smaller pots,’ he says. His mother reminds him that the neighbour cannot lift them from the ground. The neighbour comes to the gate while they are still arguing and explains that her granddaughter will be home before dusk. ‘Put it on my low shelf,’ she says, ‘and she can pour it when she returns.’ The keeper asks whether the granddaughter knows the jar is cracked. The neighbour says she will leave a note beside it. You find a clean basket large enough to hold the two pots without tipping them. The son tests its handles and decides he can carry it alone, though his mother asks him to take the path without the broken stones. They invite you to walk with him now, or stay the next day to learn how the well supplies both the lane and the visiting crews.
ev.pentam.well.choice.carry: Help carry water to the neighbour
ev.pentam.well.choice.rest: Stay a day and learn the well’s work
ev.pentam.well.result.carry: You steady the basket on the rough part of the lane while the son holds both handles. At the neighbour’s house, he sets the pots on the low shelf as she requested. She asks his mother to keep the cracked jar for seedlings, and the family thanks you on your way back.
ev.pentam.well.result.rest: You spend another day beside the keeper as her son fills jars for the lane and the arriving boats. The neighbour’s granddaughter comes to return the two small pots and helps mark which boats still need water. The keeper tells you where the next well can be found, and her son asks you to read the marks back to him.
ev.pentam.well.title: The Well Keeper’s Spare Jar
ev.petra.entry.body:
You follow a narrow gorge into Petra. Old water channels are still visible along the rock. Near the opening, Rashida has stretched a cloth shelter and moved the waterskins into its shade. Her grandson Sami counts with pebbles. Each time someone has a bowl of water, he moves one pebble to the other side.

“Why haven't we touched that skin?” Sami asks.

“It's for your father,” Rashida says. “He went to look for the goats beyond the slope. Last time he came back late, everyone had drunk the water. He ate dry bread first and waited.”

Sami says his father had forgotten to take a waterskin with him. Rashida laughs. “This time I'm remembering for him.” She sees you standing nearby and sets out an empty bowl. Sami quickly moves a pebble back. He says a guest should drink before he counts it.
ev.petra.entry.choice.pass: Thank Rashida and continue through the gorge
ev.petra.entry.choice.rest: Spend a day beneath Rashida's shelter
ev.petra.entry.title: Petra
ev.petra.goatbell.body:
Beside a rock face with a carved doorway, Inan is looking for a grey goat. His daughter Maya hears a bell and takes a few steps into the gorge. Then the sound seems to come from the other side, and she stops.

“Which way did it go?” she asks.

Inan looks at the hoofprints. “It went around that big rock and into the shade. The sound moves between the walls. We'll follow the prints.” Maya says this was the first goat she had been trusted to watch alone. She hurried away to help carry water that morning and did not tie its rope tightly enough.

Inan lets her take a moment. He lays the grass he brought beside the stone steps. “It might come out when it smells this. Will you follow the prints with her, or wait here with us?”

You ask Maya what she calls the goat. ‘Cloud,’ she says, because its grey back looks pale in the morning. Inan asks whether Cloud knows the sound of her grain pouch. Maya shakes it gently; the goat bleats from behind the stone. ‘There you are,’ she says, but her father asks her to walk slowly so it will not bolt farther into the shade. She looks back at the loose rope in her hand and asks him to show her the knot once more when they reach it.
ev.petra.goatbell.choice.wait: Wait by the stone steps and rest overnight
ev.petra.goatbell.result.tracks:
You and Maya walk around the large rock and find the grey goat beside a narrow crevice. It is eating a low patch of grass, the bell still around its neck. Maya holds out the cut grass and waits until it approaches before taking the rope. This time she ties the knot twice and asks her father to pull it tight.

Inan pats the goat and thanks you. Back at the resting place he tells the nearby families what happened. When you pass them again, they call you over for water.
ev.petra.goatbell.result.wait:
You wait beside the steps with Inan and Maya until dark. Maya starts towards the gorge several times, but Inan asks her to listen. The bell is drawing closer. The grey goat looks out from behind the rock wall. Maya lures it over with grass and reties the loosened rope.

Inan's family asks you to stay and shares warm bread and soup. You sleep against the rock that night and leave the next morning with your strength restored.
ev.petra.goatbell.title: A Bell in the Gorge
ev.road.00.body: Two camps share a well on the steppe. Rain has cut a fresh rut across the path, and a cart from the southern camp sits with one wheel sunk to the hub. The courier who moved the route stone after the storm kneels beside it. “I thought I was keeping people off the soft ground,” he tells the herder. “The stone sent us straight into it,” she answers, though she helps him lift the wheel. His daughter brings out a sketch she made before the rain. Her pony slipped at the old bend, so she marked the firmer track by the scrub. “Take this to the keeper at the far well,” the herder says. “He knows where both camps come in.” Going there to settle the marker adds two days to your journey. A guide whose family keeps other wells offers a longer circuit for a fee; it adds four days. The daughter holds the paper flat against the wind while the adults study it.
ev.road.00.choice.choice_0: Take the disputed track with the courier's sketch
ev.road.00.choice.choice_1: Pay a fee for the guide's four-day circuit
ev.road.00.title: The Marker Between Two Camps
ev.road.01.body: At a river landing on the road, a ferry keeper has taken up the planks used by heavy wagons. A young clerk arrives with a bag of letters and stops at the gap. “The seals are dry now. How do I get them across?” The keeper points upstream to his mother’s small boat. She is carrying a load of reeds to the bank and calls back, “I can take people and light bags, a few at a time. Wrap the letters before you step in.” The clerk pulls an oilcloth from his sleeve. “Would this do?” She makes him tuck the loose corner under the bag. Her boat charges a fare. The keeper will repair the heavy landing so carts and animals can follow; waiting for both crossings adds two days. The keeper can also arrange guarded landings for a larger travelling party; that route charges a higher fee and adds three days. The clerk holds out the wrapped bag for the woman to inspect.
ev.road.01.choice.choice_0: Pay the boat fare and carry your baggage upstream
ev.road.01.choice.choice_1: Pay a fee for the guarded landings
ev.road.01.title: The Ferry Keeper's Second Landing
ev.road.02.body: Beside an orchard on the road, a cart has pushed through the wrong opening and left an irrigation gate swinging. The owner catches the water running down the wheel track. “My sister comes to pick apricots in the morning,” he tells the driver. “The lower trees need this water tonight.” His nephew wedges the gate shut and points to the public road beside an old boundary wall. “I’ll put a sign there before the next cart arrives.” A traveller remembers an old tale about a ruler who fooled young men with a garden. The nephew gives him an apricot. “My uncle grew these. Help me keep the ditch open.” Walking the proper turn with the nephew and fixing the sign adds two days to your journey. An escort offers the longer public road for a fee; it adds four days but keeps the carts away from the orchard. The owner checks the gate once more while the nephew looks for a board to paint.
ev.road.02.choice.choice_0: Follow the nephew and help mark the orchard turn
ev.road.02.choice.choice_1: Pay a fee for the longer escorted road
ev.road.02.title: The Orchard by the Old Wall
ev.road.03.body: At an island jetty, a boatbuilder is repairing the steering oar of the vessel you have joined. The cook turns a water jar and finds a thin stream running from its base. “That one was for the rowers,” she says. “If we do not refill soon, they will have to share the little one.” A pilot draws two channels in wet sand. The short passage passes a shoal shifted by the last storm; sounding it will add two days to the journey. “Can the oar bear a scrape?” the cook asks. The boatbuilder fits a spare and makes her test the lashings herself. “It can, if you do not force it against the bottom.” The pilot knows a chain of sheltered harbours as well. His fare covers that longer passage, which adds four days. The cook puts the leaking jar where everyone can see it and asks the crew to fill the sound ones first.
ev.road.03.choice.choice_0: Take the short channel and sound the shoals
ev.road.03.choice.choice_1: Pay a fee for the sheltered harbours
ev.road.03.title: The Boat at the Island Jetty
ev.road.04.body: Two groups of riders meet at a steppe waystation, each asking after a horse with a white mark on its foreleg. One rider holds a loose bridle and says the horse carried her younger sister’s bedding. The keeper’s grandson has been tracking prints in the dry streambed. “It went east with a mixed herd,” he says. The second rider frowns. “Our animals went west.” The boy presses his thumb beside a fresh hoofprint. “This one crossed behind the others. Let me follow it before more carts blur the marks.” The streambed is also the way your party meant to travel. Waiting for the search and helping clear the soft bank will add two days. A hired guide offers a loop through watched grazing ground instead; his fee and the circuit add four days. The first rider gives the boy a strip torn from the horse’s blanket so he can recognize it.
ev.road.04.choice.choice_0: Wait for the searchers, then take the streambed
ev.road.04.choice.choice_1: Pay a fee for the grazing-ground loop
ev.road.04.title: The Horse Line at the Waystation
ev.road.05.body: At a steep section of road, a pilgrim and her father are replacing a loose iron handhold beside the steps. A water carrier has stopped at the foot of the climb with two full jars; she cannot use that step until they finish. The pilgrim shows you a drawing of a distant mountain shrine she hopes to visit, where long chains help people climb. “I drew the chains first,” she says, “then I saw how little room the carriers had to put a jar down.” Her father pulls the new fastening. “It holds my weight. Try it with a pack before anyone carries water past it.” Testing the steps and helping people up will add two days to your journey. Porters offer to take baggage by a gentler road for a fee; that trip adds five days. The water carrier sets one jar on a flat stone and waits for the pilgrim to call her forward.
ev.road.05.choice.choice_0: Test the handhold and take the hill steps
ev.road.05.choice.choice_1: Pay a fee for the porters' gentler road
ev.road.05.title: The Chain on the Hill Path
ev.road.06.body: At a road station, a courier is saddling two horses while his sister sorts the mail. She pulls out a sealed bag for an office beside a river. “The clerk wrote twice asking for it,” she says. Her brother puts the bag inside his own satchel. “I have the first horse. The other is for a paying traveller, if they can keep pace at the bends.” She checks the second girth and makes him tighten it again. At the gate a potter is waiting with bowls wrapped in straw. “The cook down the ordinary road asked for these,” he tells you. “She taps every bowl before she pays. Take her receipt, and keep the agreed share from the sale.” The hired relay horse takes a one-day detour beyond your planned route; carrying the bowls to the cook and returning to your route adds two days. The sister holds up the sealed mailbag once more so her brother can check the knot.
ev.road.06.choice.choice_0: Pay a fee and ride with the courier
ev.road.06.choice.choice_1: Carry the potter's bowls for an agreed share
ev.road.06.title: The Courier's Empty Saddle
ev.road.07.body: Beside a road, a sailor from Abash is repairing the tack of two horses brought by ship. One shies when a cart wheel bumps a stone. “They stood on a rolling deck for weeks,” he tells the mounted caravan leader. “Let them find their feet before you ask them to run.” The leader rubs the horse’s neck and offers you a paid place with his party; going with them adds two days to your journey. The sailor has another problem: a stable farther along the ordinary road ordered spare straps, but he must stay until the buyer comes for the horses. He ties a knot the stable keeper will recognize. “She pays the normal price there,” he says. “Keep your agreed share from that money and send the rest back.” Making the delivery adds three days. He shows you where the leather must sit so the keeper can test it on a horse.
ev.road.07.choice.choice_0: Pay a fee for the two-day mounted caravan
ev.road.07.choice.choice_1: Sell the spare tack and keep a commission
ev.road.07.title: The Abash Sailor's Tack
ev.road.08.body: On a road, a cart carrying pottery from Taianfu drops a wheel into a rut. The potter listens to the cups rattle inside their crate. “I packed the corners myself,” she says, “but the last turn was hard.” Her father opens the lid and finds that one handful of straw has slipped. “Hold the box while I push it back,” he asks you. The potter lifts a cup and turns it toward the light to check its rim. A passing caravan can give you and your baggage a paid place; its change of animals will add one day to your planned journey. The potter also has a crate ordered by a tea seller along the ordinary road. “She counts every cup,” she says. “Bring me her marked receipt; take your share from what she pays.” Carrying that crate and returning to your route adds two days. Her father closes the lid only after the cups stop moving.
ev.road.08.choice.choice_0: Pay a fee for the one-day caravan
ev.road.08.choice.choice_1: Deliver the cups and keep a commission
ev.road.08.title: The Potter from Taianfu
ev.road.09.body: At a market, a dyer spreads white cloth for a family gathering. His daughter measures the second bolt and notices it ends a handspan early. The buyer holds the first piece against her arm. “Both must cover the same tables,” she says. “Give me a moment,” the daughter answers. “I can trim the long one and stitch the cut edge neatly.” Her father asks her to save the offcut for patching a canopy, then turns to the cloth still stacked behind him. Another household beyond the next market ordered part of it. A hired merchant train will carry you past the exchange point for a fee, adding two days to your planned journey. Delivering and selling the cloth to that household adds three days; the dyer offers you an agreed share of what the buyer pays. His daughter writes the buyer’s name on a slip and asks you to make sure it travels with the right bolt.
ev.road.09.choice.choice_0: Pay a fee for the two-day merchant train
ev.road.09.choice.choice_1: Sell the dyer's cloth for an agreed share
ev.road.09.title: The White Cloth Order
ev.road.10.body: Beside a road, a pearl seller who trades at coastal markets has overturned a small box by his weighing table. His apprentice kneels in the dust and counts each pearl as he returns it. “Forty-nine,” he says, looking at the empty lid. The seller wets a cloth and wipes under the table legs. “Wait before you blame the road. One may be caught in the mat.” A guarded caravan is leaving for a nearby market; a paid place with it adds one day to your journey. The seller cannot leave his table until the count is right. He hands you a different packet, sealed and already checked: shell beads ordered by a workshop along your road. “Ask the maker to mark my receipt,” he says. “Keep the share we agreed from her payment.” Taking the packet there adds two days. The apprentice lifts the edge of the mat while you choose your road.
ev.road.10.choice.choice_0: Pay a fee for the one-day guarded caravan
ev.road.10.choice.choice_1: Deliver the shell beads for a commission
ev.road.10.title: The Pearl Seller's Count
ev.road.11.body: At a steppe station, a storyteller has gathered listeners around an old account of Chinggis Khan and the ruler it calls Prester John. A boy interrupts when the reader mentions riders bearing a letter. “Would one letter really bring all of them?” His mother, the station keeper, sets today’s sealed packets beside him. “This one goes only to the next station,” she says. “Another rider takes it farther.” The boy turns the packet over, looking for the knot. A harness trader at the same table is tying a label to a bundle for the next camp. “Show him mine,” he tells the keeper. “If the knot comes loose, the buyer will not know whose straps these are.” The keeper offers you a paid place with her relay riders; taking that route adds two days. Selling the trader’s bundle along the ordinary road adds three, and he promises you an agreed share of the sale. The boy holds the loose end of the label while the trader finishes the knot.
ev.road.11.choice.choice_0: Pay a fee for the two-day horse relay
ev.road.11.choice.choice_1: Sell the harness bundle for a commission
ev.road.11.title: The Old Letter and the New Horse
ev.road.12.body: At a roadside district office, a clerk discovers that his copy of a land register has one page twice and another page missing. The assistant spreads the original sheets across the table. “The missing names are here,” she says, putting a weight on the corner before the wind takes it. The clerk points to a line that runs into the margin. “Copy that one fully. The receiving office must be able to find the household.” An official courier waits by the door for the corrected pages. He has a paid place in his party; taking it adds one day to your journey. The assistant also has paper ordered by a school along the ordinary road. “One class has been sharing the same sheet for maps,” she says. “Their teacher asked for another bundle.” Taking it to the school adds two days, and the assistant promises you an agreed share of the sale. She dips her pen and asks the clerk to read the missing name again.
ev.road.12.choice.choice_0: Pay a fee for the one-day courier caravan
ev.road.12.choice.choice_1: Deliver the school paper for a commission
ev.road.12.title: The Clerk's Second Copy
ev.road.13.body: At a coastal landing, a fisherwoman and her son are turning fish on bamboo racks before the afternoon rain. A sailor waiting for the tide points to two islands on his chart and repeats an old tale that men and women lived apart on them. The son asks, “How did they carry water between the islands?” The sailor studies the chart. “The person who told me never said. I saw only one landing when I passed.” His mother moves a rack out of the spray. “Then help me with the fish you can see,” she tells the boy. He asks whether you can hold the mat while he ties the dried bundles for a buyer. The sailor has room on his boat and knows a channel that adds one day to your journey for a fare. Staying to dry and load the catch adds two days. The son presses a corner of the mat under a stone as the first drops fall.
ev.road.13.choice.choice_0: Pay the boat fare and sail with the tidewise crew
