The calligrapher asks if she has already decided what to write. She says she will tell her sister about the new apprentice who keeps leaving his sandals in the drying yard; the boy hears her and moves them at once.

Yusuf sells a full paper trading bale for 100 silver. The calligrapher has a bound decorated manuscript for 10 silver. Mariam asks whether you would like to watch the paper work before they set the letter down.
ev.samarcanda.b.choice.learn: Spend a day watching Yusuf make paper
ev.samarcanda.b.choice.manuscript: Buy the decorated manuscript for 10 silver
ev.samarcanda.b.choice.paper: Buy the full paper bale for 100 silver
ev.samarcanda.b.title: At the Paper Maker’s Yard
ev.samarcanda.bluetile.body:
At a tile yard, Safiya is fitting a few blue pieces onto a bench her father built for the family courtyard. One piece is missing from the stack. Her cousin thinks a buyer took it by mistake. Safiya asks him which buyer came today; he names only the paper seller, who never entered the yard. Her father suggests checking the shaded drying shelf before accusing anyone.

You ask why this bench needs a particular pattern. Safiya says her grandmother chose it: a little blue line to show where each child once sat while waiting for bread. The grandmother comes out carrying lunch and laughs when she sees them searching. She had moved the tile under the shelf to keep rain from staining the unfired back. Her grandson fetches it and admits he should have checked there first.

Safiya has the piece again, but the bench still needs a day’s careful setting. The grandmother asks you to sit and hear why she chose the blue line before anyone starts work with wet mortar.
ev.samarcanda.bluetile.choice.listen: Share lunch and hear the grandmother’s bench story
ev.samarcanda.bluetile.choice.set: Spend a day setting the tiles with Safiya
ev.samarcanda.bluetile.result.listen: You eat with the grandmother while she names the places her children used to sit. Safiya listens and changes the order of two tiles to match the memory. You leave with their family story in your notes.
ev.samarcanda.bluetile.result.set: You spend the day setting the blue line with Safiya and her cousin. Her father checks the last joint, and the grandmother is first to sit on the finished bench. The family thanks you when neighbours come to admire the work.
ev.samarcanda.bluetile.title: The Tile That Went Missing
ev.samarcanda.c.body:
In a mosque courtyard, caretaker Rashid is wiping rain from a dark stone beside the wall. His daughter wants to leave one drop so her grandmother can see it. ‘She has seen plenty of rain,’ he says. The girl replies that grandmother will still ask whether this stone caught any. Rashid lets her keep the small wet patch until the older woman arrives.

You ask why people watch the stone. Rashid says neighbours have told stories about it for years; some say the dampness came before troubled seasons, others bring family news when they visit. His mother arrives with a folded cloth and asks the girl to show her the drop. She touches the stone, then asks Rashid whether he has mended the leak in the roof above. ‘That is the part I can answer,’ he says, pointing to new mortar.

The family is staying for the evening prayer. Rashid has an old notebook of dated weather and repairs; his mother says she remembers one of those wet seasons differently. They make space for you at the bench.
ev.samarcanda.c.choice.touch: Touch the cool stone and hear the family’s story
ev.samarcanda.c.choice.watch_pilgrims: Ask Rashid’s mother about the dated notes
ev.samarcanda.c.title: The Stone After Rain
ev.samarcanda.entry.body:
At the gate of Samarcand, a clerk named Shirin is sorting travel permits while her younger brother carries a roll of paper to their father’s shop. He asks whether he may keep one clean sheet for a letter. Shirin says their father has already set one aside, if the boy remembers to take the parcel to the right house. He points to the blue-tiled roof beyond the lane, sure he knows the way.

You ask Shirin where to declare your goods. She shows you the desk and says the count will take two days if you join the line. Her brother says he knows a family in the market who can explain the city’s different communities and the stories their elders tell. ‘Ask them yourself,’ Shirin says. ‘He leaves out the parts where he got lost.’ The boy protests that he only took the wrong bridge once.

A merchant opens a full jade trading parcel nearby, asking 135 silver. Shirin notes the seller’s name before turning back to you; her brother has finally picked up the paper roll and is waiting for someone to show him the bridge on the map.
ev.samarcanda.entry.choice.customs: Spend two days declaring your goods with Shirin
ev.samarcanda.entry.choice.lore: Spend a day hearing the neighbours’ city stories
ev.samarcanda.entry.choice.market: Buy the full jade parcel for 135 silver
ev.samarcanda.entry.title: The Clerk at the Samarcand Gate
ev.samarcanda.mentor_closure.body:
Nadir’s older fellow student, Bashir, is drawing a street map for a young mason whose family has moved across the canal. He marks the bridges, then asks the mason to trace the route back with his finger. The young man misses a turn. Bashir erases that line and redraws it wider. ‘A map is for the person who has to walk it,’ he says.

You ask how he learned to draw so clearly. Bashir says he spent years carrying books between teachers and asking the people on each street what they called it. His sister, a paper seller, comes by and points out that one bridge has been repaired since his last drawing. He asks her for the date and adds it beside the line. The mason now finds his new home on the page.

Bashir offers to show you his method in a short conversation, spend a full day walking the route, or let you carry on. His sister leaves a clean scrap of paper for the next map.
ev.samarcanda.mentor_closure.choice_1: Ask Bashir how he checks a route
ev.samarcanda.mentor_closure.choice_1_re: Bashir lets you draw the mason’s route, then asks his sister to name the bridge she used that morning. You revise one line and learn how he checks a map against a person’s walk.
ev.samarcanda.mentor_closure.choice_2: Walk the route with Bashir for a day
ev.samarcanda.mentor_closure.choice_2_re: You spend a day walking streets and bridges with Bashir. His sister joins you at the repaired crossing and asks you to draw it from memory. Bashir invites you back to compare the page with his own.
ev.samarcanda.mentor_closure.choice_3: Thank Bashir and continue through the city
ev.samarcanda.mentor_closure.choice_3_re: You thank Bashir and his sister. The mason folds his new map and sets off toward home. You go your own way, remembering how carefully they asked him to read it.
ev.samarcanda.mentor_closure.title: The Older Student’s Map
ev.sapurgan.cupseal.body:
Beside a public well, a woman named Maryam is carving a small mark into the handle of a wooden cup. Her mother had kept the cup for travellers to use, but its old mark wore away and two neighbours each thought it belonged to their own well. Maryam has asked them both to come and watch her cut a new sign. One arrives with a water jar; the other brings a piece of cloth to dry the cup.

You ask why the mark matters if everyone shares the water. Maryam says the cup must be cleaned and returned to the right shelf each evening. Her mother used to do it; now Maryam’s young son has that job and needs a mark he can recognise. The boy asks whether he may carve it himself. Maryam lets him try on a scrap of wood, then guides his hand on the handle.

The neighbours agree on the sign. Maryam needs someone to fetch a fresh leather cord from the market for 1 silver, or to stay until tomorrow and teach the boy how to keep the well shelf clean. The child holds the new cup up to the light.
ev.sapurgan.cupseal.choice.cord: Buy a new leather cord for the cup for 1 silver
ev.sapurgan.cupseal.choice.stay: Stay another day and show the boy how to tend the shelf
ev.sapurgan.cupseal.result.cord: You bring back the cord, and Maryam ties the cup to the agreed shelf. Both neighbours see the new mark and thank you. Her son can now find the cup when he cleans the well at dusk.
ev.sapurgan.cupseal.result.stay: You spend the next day with Maryam’s son, washing the cup and keeping the shelf clear. His mother checks it at dusk, and the neighbours see that the shared cup is where they expect it. You leave with their well routine in mind.
ev.sapurgan.cupseal.title: The Cup with a New Seal
ev.sapurgan.entry.body:
At a melon stall in Sapurgan, an older seller is stacking the fruit his daughter brought from the fields. Her little boy asks to keep the smallest one for his father, who is out with the pack animals. The seller says he may choose it after they count the load. The boy counts aloud, then discovers one melon still hiding beneath the cloth.

You ask where travellers fill their water skins. The daughter points to a working well beyond the stalls and says the carters use it before they leave. Her father adds that some stretches beyond the cultivated ground are dry, so each party checks the water it can carry. The boy asks whether a melon counts as water. His mother hands him a cup and says, ‘Drink this first. Then you can have a slice.’

The carters return with dust on their sleeves. The boy runs to show his father the small melon he saved. The seller offers you shade beside the stall for the day and has time to tell you which road the carters use.
ev.sapurgan.entry.choice.look: Stay a day and hear the carters’ accounts
ev.sapurgan.entry.choice.pass: Fill your water skin and continue
ev.sapurgan.entry.title: Melons at the Sapurgan Roadside
ev.sapurgan.site_gap.body:
At the market scale, coppersmith Amina has set out two weights. Her brother says the old one still bears the right mark; she puts it beside the standard and shows how its rounded edge changes the balance. A neighbour carrying a sack of dried fruit asks which one they used when he sold his last load. Amina checks the date in her small book before answering.

You ask whether the neighbour lost money. He says the difference was slight but wants the next sale weighed fairly. Amina offers to calibrate the scale in front of him. Her brother wipes the green tarnish from the old weight and asks her not to throw it away. She says it can stay on the shelf as long as everyone knows which one now sets the measure.

The neighbour will soon join a caravan for Taykan and can name its stops. Amina has left the empty scale ready if you want to help her check the beam while the buyer watches.
ev.sapurgan.site_gap.choice.route: Ask the neighbour about the road to Taykan
ev.sapurgan.site_gap.title: Two Copper Weights
ev.semenat.entry.body: At Semenat’s market, a flower seller is helping her father move baskets away from the path used by the crews bringing goods from the landing. He points to the smallest basket. ‘That one belongs at the shrine. Your aunt will wonder where it has gone.’ She replies, ‘Auntie borrowed it yesterday to carry supper home.’ The father asks whether you have seen a woman with a basket of yellow flowers. You have not, but a basket maker beside them has. He says she passed toward the temple lane and promised to bring it back when she had emptied it. The daughter laughs: ‘Then the flowers are probably gone and the supper stayed in the basket.’ A sailor comes to ask which boat next sails toward Tana. The basket maker knows a captain at the landing who has room for passengers. The father asks his daughter to keep the stall open while he checks on his sister, and she offers to show you the market if you can spend the day here. She ties the stall cloth back so the crews can pass without stepping over the baskets.
ev.semenat.entry.choice.look: Spend a day among the market stalls
ev.semenat.entry.choice.pass: Ask the road through town and continue
ev.semenat.entry.title: The Borrowed Flower Basket
ev.semenat.lamps.body: A keeper at a small shrine is checking the lamps before visitors arrive. His niece has cleaned them and set them in a row, but one has a wick much shorter than the others. “You took a bit from it to mend the kitchen lamp,” he says. She nods and shows the strip she saved. He asks her to put the spare strip in the shrine lamp, then notices that the shelf beneath it tilts toward the doorway. A carpenter from the neighbouring stall offers to adjust the shelf after he finishes a customer's box. The niece wants to do it sooner: visitors will come before dusk. “Then ask him what tools you may borrow,” her uncle says. She walks over, returns with a wooden wedge and asks you to steady the shelf while she places it. The keeper watches the lamps from the doorway, making sure people can pass without brushing the flames. The niece tests the wedge with the empty shelf first. Her uncle hands her a lamp only after the wood has stopped shifting.
ev.semenat.lamps.result.shelf: You hold the shelf while the niece taps the wedge beneath it. The carpenter comes over to check her work, and the keeper lights each wick. Visitors can pass without touching the lamps. He thanks you in front of them for helping make the entrance safe.
ev.semenat.lamps.result.stay: You stay through the day. The niece learns to set the wicks at equal height, and her uncle asks her to light the first lamp at dusk. After visitors leave, they invite you to eat with them. You rest before returning to the market the next morning.
ev.semenat.lamps.title: The Shrine Keeper’s Oil Lamp
ev.semenat.site_gap.body: Under a market awning, a basket maker is showing his daughter how to fold a fresh palm leaf back through the rim. She has made the base sound but keeps pulling one side tighter than the other. ‘It looks like a boat,’ she says. ‘A boat that drops the fruit when you lift it,’ he answers, smiling. You ask how long the leaves must dry before the basket can carry a load. He lifts an older one from a beam and lets you feel its firm edge. The girl tries again, turning the basket as she works rather than tugging at one place. A deckhand waiting for fruit baskets asks whether they will finish before his boat sails toward Tana. ‘Tell her where you stop along the coast,’ the father says. The deckhand names a sheltered landing where they take on water. The girl insists he repeat it after she has tightened the last leaf. He sets down his rope coil to watch her test the basket with both hands.
ev.semenat.site_gap.choice.interact: Help the girl finish the basket rim
ev.semenat.site_gap.choice.route: Ask the carrier about the Tana road
ev.semenat.site_gap.title: A Basket Made from Leaves
ev.siju.a.body: When you leave Piju and travel two days south through districts abounding in game, you reach Siju, a great and rich city flourishing with trade and manufactures. The southern road brings in grain and harness, and the workshops here finish what the northern towns begin.
ev.siju.a.choice.grain: Walk the grain market on the fertile plain
ev.siju.a.choice.sugar: Buy sugar from a refiner's stall
ev.siju.a.choice.workshops: Tour the manufactures brought down from Piju
ev.siju.a.title: Manufactures from Piju
ev.siju.b.body: The people of Siju are idolaters who burn their dead and use paper-money, and you see funeral parties pass toward the cremation grounds outside the walls. They lay out paper offerings beside the pyre, and the smoke rises all day above the southern road.
ev.siju.b.choice.ask: Ask an elder why they burn rather than bury
ev.siju.b.choice.observe: Stand at a respectful distance and watch a funeral rite
ev.siju.b.choice.paper-money: Buy paper-money at a stall near the cremation ground
ev.siju.b.title: Burning the Dead
ev.siju.entry.body: When you leave Piju you travel towards the south for two days, through beautiful districts abounding in everything, and in which you find quantities of all kinds of game. At the end of those two days you reach the city of SIJU, a great, rich, and noble city, flourishing with trade and manufactures. The people are Idolaters, burn their dead, use paper-money, and are subjects of the Great Kaan. They possess extensive and fertile plains producing abundance of wheat and other grain. But there is nothing else to mention, so let us proceed and tell you of the countries further on. On leaving Siju you ride south for three days, constantly falling in with fine towns and villages and hamlets and farms, with their cultivated lands. There is plenty of wheat and other corn, and of game also; and the people are all Idolaters and subjects of the Great Kaan. At the end of those three days you reach the great river CARAMORAN, which flows hither from Prester John’s country.
ev.siju.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the gate without delay
ev.siju.entry.title: Concerning the City of Siju, and the Great River Caramoran
ev.sindafu.entry.body: When you have travelled those 20 days westward through the mountains, as I have told you, then you arrive at a plain belonging to a province called Sindafu, which still is on the confines of Manzi, and the capital city of which is (also) called SINDAFU. This city was in former days a rich and noble one, and the Kings who reigned there were very great and wealthy. It is a good twenty miles in compass, but it is divided in the way that I shall tell you.
ev.sindafu.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.sindafu.entry.title: Concerning the Province and City of Sindafu
ev.sinju.a.body: Sinju stands on the greatest river in the world, which men call Kian. Though the city is of no great size, the waters before it are black with vessels, and boatmen swear that more wealth passes here than on all the rivers and seas of Christendom together.
ev.sinju.a.choice.count: Stand at the bank and count the moored vessels
ev.sinju.a.choice.tea: Buy tea from a river bargeman
ev.sinju.a.choice.toll: Ask the toll clerks how many vessels pass in a year
ev.sinju.a.title: The Greatest River
ev.sinju.b.body: The people are idolaters subject to the Great Kaan, and they use paper-money in every transaction on the quay. For all its modest walls, Sinju sees a very great amount of shipping and trade, and the revenue the Khan draws here is something marvellous.
ev.sinju.b.choice.harbour: Walk the harbour and note how small the city is for such traffic
ev.sinju.b.choice.porcelain: Buy porcelain from a river trader
ev.sinju.b.choice.quay: Watch merchants pay tolls in paper-money
ev.sinju.b.title: Paper-Money Port
ev.sinju.entry.body: You must know that when you leave the city of Yanju, after going 15 miles south-east, you come to a city called SINJU, of no great size, but possessing a very great amount of shipping and trade. The people are Idolaters and subject to the Great Kaan, and use paper-money. And you must know that this city stands on the greatest river in the world, the name of which is KIAN. It is in some places ten miles wide, in others eight, in others six, and it is more than 100 days’ journey in length from one end to the other. This it is that brings so much trade to the city we are speaking of; for on the waters of that river merchandize is perpetually coming and going, from and to the various parts of the world, enriching the city, and bringing a great revenue to the Great Kaan.
ev.sinju.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the gate without delay
ev.sinju.entry.title: Concerning the City of Sinju and the Great River Kian
ev.sinjumatu.entry.body: On leaving Tadinfu you travel three days towards the south, always finding numbers of noble and populous towns and villages flourishing with trade and manufactures. There is also abundance of game in the country, and everything in profusion. When you have travelled those three days you come to the noble city of SINJUMATU, a rich and fine place, with great trade and manufactures. The people are Idolaters and subjects of the Great Kaan, and have paper-money, and they have a river which I can assure you brings them great gain, and I will tell you about it. You see the river in question flows from the South to this city of Sinjumatu.
ev.sinjumatu.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.sinjumatu.entry.title: Concerning the Noble City of Sinjumatu
ev.smyrna.entry.body:
The road reaches Smyrna beside a wide bay. Aysel is rinsing a basket at the water's edge while her daughter Mina keeps a smaller one out of reach of the waves. They brought figs down from the hillside this morning; Mina insists the small basket was full too, though only three figs remain.

“I gave two to the boatman,” she says. Aysel asks about the other three. Mina admits she ate them on the way. The boatman calls from his boat that he received only one. Mina looks at her mother and begins counting again.

Aysel offers you a fig and points out the lane toward the houses above the water. She asks which way you are travelling. Mina adds that the boats know the bay better than anyone, but her mother knows which footpath is shortest. Both wait to see which one you ask.
ev.smyrna.entry.choice.pass: Thank Aysel and continue along the bay
ev.smyrna.entry.choice.rest: Stay a day at Aysel's house
ev.smyrna.entry.title: At the Bay of Smyrna
ev.smyrna.grapes.body:
On a terrace above the bay, sisters Esma and Lale are turning grapes that have lain on woven mats for several days. Their older brother sails with a small boat and asked for dried grapes he can keep in a bag. Esma wants to send him the largest bunches. Lale says the small ones are nearly ready, and he leaves in two days.

Their mother comes out with bread and asks why one mat has not been turned. The sisters explain at once, each talking over the other. Their mother takes a grape from each pile, tastes them, and says they can send both. Esma turns the large bunches; Lale shows her how to leave space for air between them.

The family sells some of its dried fruit to travellers. They will sell you a small packet today, or welcome another pair of hands to turn the grapes for the rest of the day and tomorrow morning.

You ask whether their brother knows they have saved him the first dried batch. Esma says she told him to bring a clean bag; Lale says he will forget it and use his cap. Their mother hears both and brings out a cloth pouch she has already sewn. ‘He can keep the cap on his head,’ she says. Lale asks whether the pouch should be tied tight before they finish drying. ‘Not while the fruit is warm,’ their mother answers. Esma holds up a handful for you to feel; it is still soft in the middle. The sisters spread it back on the mat and make room for the breeze.
ev.smyrna.grapes.choice.stay: Stay until tomorrow and help turn the grapes
ev.smyrna.grapes.result.buy: You pay for a packet. Lale checks that the grapes inside are dry and ties the cloth closed. Esma says their brother will get a larger bag, with both sorts mixed together. You eat a few on the road and regain strength. The sisters go back to their mats, now both full.
ev.smyrna.grapes.result.stay: You spend the day helping Esma and Lale turn the grapes. Their mother feeds you supper and gives you a place to sleep. At dawn Lale tests a small bunch and decides it is ready; Esma fills the bag for their brother. He comes by on his way to the boat, tastes one grape, and says he hopes the voyage lasts long enough to eat them all. You leave after breakfast. The family remembers your help when you pass this terrace again.
ev.smyrna.grapes.title: Grapes for the Brother at Sea
ev.suju.a.body: Suju is a very great and noble city with a circuit of some sixty miles, and the people possess silk in great quantities from which they make gold brocade and other stuffs. You walk a weaving quarter where the shuttles never rest, and the master tells you the city's name means Earth in our tongue.
ev.suju.a.choice.brocade: Watch the gold brocade looms at work
ev.suju.a.choice.circuit: Ride part of the city's sixty-mile circuit
ev.suju.a.choice.silk: Buy a length of gold brocade
ev.suju.a.title: Gold Brocade and Sixty Miles
ev.suju.b.body: The city hath merchants of great wealth and an incalculable number of people, though they are accomplished traders and not soldiers at all. Between the canals you find gardens where wealthy men keep fishponds and plant ginger and rhubarb in the shaded plots.
ev.suju.b.choice.bridges: Stand on a stone bridge and watch the canal traffic
ev.suju.b.choice.gardens: Walk the canal gardens with a merchant's clerk
ev.suju.b.choice.rhubarb: Buy rhubarb from a garden stall
ev.suju.b.title: Merchants and Canal Gardens
ev.suju.entry.body: Suju is a very great and noble city. The people are Idolaters, subjects of the Great Kaan, and have paper-money. They possess silk in great quantities, from which they make gold brocade and other stuffs, and they live by their manufactures and trade. The city is passing great, and has a circuit of some 60 miles; it hath merchants of great wealth and an incalculable number of people. Indeed, if the men of this city and of the rest of Manzi had but the spirit of soldiers they would conquer the world; but they are no soldiers at all, only accomplished traders and most skilful craftsmen. There are also in this city many philosophers and leeches, diligent students of nature. And you must know that in this city there are 6,000 bridges, all of stone, and so lofty that a galley, or even two galleys at once, could pass underneath one of them. In the mountains belonging to this city, rhubarb and ginger grow in great abundance; insomuch that you may get some 40 pounds of excellent fresh ginger for a Venice groat.
ev.suju.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the gate without delay
ev.suju.entry.title: Of the Noble City of Suju
ev.taican.a.body:
At the corn market, grain master Hamza has written two tallies for the same cart. His apprentice says one belongs to the miller and one to a caravan bound toward Badashan. The marks on the sacks are faint, so Hamza asks the carter to name each family before he weighs the load. ‘My sister will be here soon,’ the carter says. ‘She tied them. She will know.’

You ask why he cannot simply untie the sacks. Hamza says he can, but the families agreed to keep them sealed until the grain is weighed. The sister arrives with a strip of blue thread and puts it beside the cart’s rear wheel. The caravan sacks were tied with blue; the miller’s were not. The apprentice checks each knot and writes the names in the right columns.

Hamza’s wife has a full bale of cotton cloth for 108 silver. Hamza invites you to watch the weighing for a day, or to ask the caravan masters about Balc and Badashan once they have collected their grain.
ev.taican.a.choice.ask_balc: Ask the carters about Balc and Badashan
ev.taican.a.choice.buy_cotton: Buy the full cotton cloth bale for 108 silver
ev.taican.a.choice.walk_market: Spend a day watching Hamza’s grain market
ev.taican.a.title: The Grain Master’s Two Tallies
ev.taican.b.body:
At a yard below the salt hills, miner Farid is checking the head of his iron pick. His sister brings a broken block to the scale and complains that it looks larger than its weight. Farid turns it over: a hollow had been hidden underneath. ‘Tell the buyers the weight,’ she says. ‘They can see the shape for themselves.’

You ask how the salt comes down from the hills. Farid shows you a path used by the pack animals and says the cutters work slowly when the rock is hard. His sister has promised their mother to bring home enough for winter preserving. A neighbour arrives to ask whether a caravan going toward Sapurgan has room for one more load. Farid says the driver will return after supper and can answer.

A full trading block of salt costs 108 silver. Farid also invites you to watch the cutters for two days if you want to see how they prepare the loads. His sister takes the weighed block aside and writes its measure where the buyer can see it.
ev.taican.b.choice.ask_sapurgan: Ask the neighbour about Sapurgan and Balc
ev.taican.b.choice.buy_salt: Buy the full salt trading block for 108 silver
ev.taican.b.choice.watch_miners: Spend two days with Farid’s salt cutters
ev.taican.b.title: At the Salt-Cutting Yard
ev.taican.entry.body:
At the entrance to Taican’s grain market, a porter named Salim is steadying a cart while his daughter ties a cloth over the top sacks. She asks him to lift one corner so she can see the family mark. ‘Your aunt’s grain goes to the mill,’ he says. ‘Ours stays for the road.’ She finds the mark and calls to the miller waiting by the gate.

You ask whether travellers can buy supplies here. Salim points to the scales and says the merchants will post their measures after the morning weighing. His daughter knows which sacks belong to the neighbours who worship at the local mosque; she is taking their small share over before they close the yard. The miller offers to walk with you through the market tomorrow if you want to stay.

The cart wheel catches in a rut. Salim and his daughter put their shoulders to it, while the miller moves the loose stones. Once the wheel rolls free, Salim checks the two family marks again before letting the cart go.
ev.taican.entry.choice.market: Spend a day with the miller at the grain market
ev.taican.entry.choice.pass: Ask Salim about the road and continue
ev.taican.entry.choice.shrine: Walk with the daughter to the mosque yard
ev.taican.entry.title: The Grain Gate at Taican
ev.taican.sackmark.body:
In a yard behind the grain market, a widow named Layla is dividing her harvest between her household and her daughter’s new home. The sacks are the same size. Her daughter marks one with blue thread, but the last piece breaks in her hand. Layla asks her to use a knot in the rope instead. ‘Your grandfather taught me that when thread ran short,’ she says.

You ask how the daughter will recognise her share after the cart is loaded. She shows you the knot, then admits she has never tied it tightly enough on a full sack. Layla calls her younger son to hold the mouth of the bag while she teaches the knot again. The boy counts the turns out loud and gets ahead of her. The daughter laughs and starts over.

The cart driver is ready to leave. He says he can pay a helper 0.8 silver to carry the marked sack to the daughter’s house today. Layla would also welcome someone who stays a day to teach the children how to check the marks after the sacks are weighed. She puts the broken thread in her pocket and watches the daughter finish the knot.
ev.taican.sackmark.choice.stay: Stay a day and help the children check the sacks
ev.taican.sackmark.result.deliver: You carry the marked sack to Layla’s daughter’s house. She unties the knot in front of her husband and shows him how to make it again. The driver pays you 0.8 silver for the delivery.
ev.taican.sackmark.result.stay: You spend the day with Layla and the children, comparing the knots after the sacks leave the scales. By supper the daughter and her brother can each find the right load. Layla thanks you for helping them keep both households’ shares clear.
ev.taican.sackmark.title: The Sack with No Blue Thread
ev.tana-azov.entry.body:
The Don spreads out before it meets the Sea of Azov. Near a landing place, Zoya has set a pot over a small fire. Her grandson Murad is trying to keep a bundle of reeds from rolling into the water. Each time he leans over to catch one, another slides free.

“Sit on the bundle,” Zoya tells him. He does, and the reeds stay put. She says his father had the same trouble when he first brought a load downriver. Murad asks if his father really lost an entire bundle. Zoya says only half, and he had to explain it to the family that ordered it.

Zoya welcomes travellers when they stop beside the river. She points out where the bank is firm enough to approach the water. Murad wants to know the name of the place you came from; he is collecting names his father might recognize when he returns.

Murad asks whether his father will bring more reeds when he returns. Zoya lifts the lid of the little pot and says the order is already filled; today he is carrying the finished bundles to a family farther upriver. "Will they send him back with anything?" the boy asks. "Probably news, and perhaps the basket I lent them." She asks him to stir the pot while she shows you the firm part of the bank. Murad agrees only after she promises he can ask where you came from when she gets back.
ev.tana-azov.entry.choice.pass: Thank Zoya and continue by the river
ev.tana-azov.entry.choice.rest: Spend a day at Zoya's shelter
ev.tana-azov.entry.title: The River Landing at Tana
ev.tana.entry.body: At Tana's market, a cloth merchant is trying to fit a new latch to a cargo chest. His mother holds the lid up while he searches for a missing pin. “You laid it by the leather straps,” she tells him. He finds it exactly there. A younger carrier arriving from the shore asks which chest goes on the next boat. “The one with cotton,” the merchant says. “The leather stays until its owner comes.” You ask why he keeps two lists for them. His mother shows you that one is for things leaving by water and the other for goods due on the road toward Melibar. The carrier points out the street he uses after unloading and offers to show you the market if you stay. His mother lets the lid down carefully, then asks her son to test the latch before he puts anyone's name on the chest. He opens and shuts it twice, pleased that the pin holds. The younger carrier asks whether he may borrow the pin if another chest breaks; the merchant tells him to bring the chest first.
ev.tana.entry.choice.look: Spend a day among the cloth sellers
ev.tana.entry.choice.pass: Ask the road through town and continue
ev.tana.entry.title: The Chest with the New Latch
ev.tana.porridge.body:
Zoya has set out bowls of barley porridge for passing travellers. Murad sits beside her with a cord full of knots. His father tied one knot for every place on a journey toward Kiovia; Murad is trying to put the names back in the right order.

“He remembers the road better than his own birthday,” Zoya says. Karim corrects her from the fire: he remembers both, and it was Zoya who once forgot to send him a birthday letter. She says the letter was written, just left beneath the pot. Murad laughs and points to the last knot, which his father says marks the place where the family received it.

Zoya sells a warm bowl to travellers. If you want to hear the road story, Karim will untie the knots with Murad while you take notes. He has travelled the route himself and can name the stops toward Kiovia.

You ask whether the birthday letter ever reached Karim. He says it did, because his mother tucked it into the food bundle after she found it. Zoya asks Murad to show you the knot that marks the place where he read it. He feels along the cord, stops, then chooses the next knot instead. ‘That one,’ Karim says, ‘where we waited for the rain to ease.’ Zoya ladles another bowl for a boatman and tells Murad to wash his hands before touching the bread. He holds up both palms, dusty from the rope, and goes to the water jar.
ev.tana.porridge.choice.meal: Buy a warm bowl of barley porridge for 0.8 silver
ev.tana.porridge.choice.road: Follow the knots and copy the Kiovia route
ev.tana.porridge.result.meal: You pay Zoya for a bowl. Murad brings you a spoon, then asks if you can remember the name of the first place on his father's route. You eat while he tries the knots again. The porridge warms you and gives you strength for the road. Zoya finds the old birthday letter and shows Murad where she signed it.
ev.tana.porridge.result.road: Karim unties the cord one knot at a time. Murad says each name before his father does; twice he gets it wrong and starts again from the river mouth. You copy the sequence onto your map, marking Tana, Kiovia, and the road between them. At the last knot Zoya admits that she did send the letter in the end. Karim says he still has it.
ev.tana.porridge.title: Zoya's Road Names
ev.tana.receipt.body: A woman bringing cotton to Tana's shore has tucked a receipt inside the wrong roll. Her daughter discovers it while helping a buyer unfold a length of cloth. “This names our neighbour's leather, not this cotton,” the daughter says. The mother remembers setting both papers aside when rain began. She asks the buyer to wait while she checks each bundle. The neighbour arrives carrying a strap and says he has been looking for the paper since morning. “Then help us count before you take it,” the mother replies. He sets down his strap and agrees. You ask whether the buyer will still have time to reach his boat. “If we do it together,” the daughter says, handing you a clean board for the correct marks. The neighbour smiles at her confidence. The mother offers a small payment for help with the count, while the buyer asks someone to carry the corrected receipt to the boat.
ev.tana.receipt.choice.carry: Carry the corrected receipt to the boat
ev.tana.receipt.choice.count: Help count the cloth and leather
ev.tana.receipt.result.carry: The daughter gives you the cotton receipt after the family has checked it. You bring it to the buyer at the boat, and he matches the mark to the roll already aboard. The neighbour later tells the market sellers how you kept the two households' goods from being mixed.
ev.tana.receipt.result.count: You and the daughter count each bundle while her mother writes the correct owner's name. The neighbour gets his leather receipt back, and the buyer takes the cotton with its own mark. The mother pays you for helping the sale finish before the boat leaves.
ev.tana.receipt.title: The Receipt in the Cloth Roll
ev.tana.site_gap.body: Near the shore, a woman tends a broad pan of coconut syrup. Her son is holding a clean mould and wants to pour before the syrup has thickened. “Look at the spoon,” she tells him. He lifts it; the syrup still runs from the back too quickly. A neighbour arrives with a basket and asks whether the next cakes will be ready for her family gathering. The woman says the first batch has cooled and sends her son to fetch it. You ask why she keeps the fire so low. “The juice grows bitter if you hurry it,” she says, moving the wood a little farther from the pan. The boy returns with set cakes and shows you the darker piece from yesterday, when he let the heat rise. The neighbour tastes a corner and asks him to make today's batch like the first one. While they wait, she points out the road she takes south toward Melibar. The boy asks whether the darker cake can still be eaten; his mother keeps it for their own tea.
ev.tana.site_gap.choice.interact: Help judge when the syrup is ready
ev.tana.site_gap.choice.route: Ask about the road to Melibar
ev.tana.site_gap.title: The Coconut Syrup Pan
ev.tanpiju.a.body: When you leave Kinsay and travel a day's journey south-east through a plenteous region, you pass a succession of dwellings and charming gardens before you reach Tanpiju. Peach and mulberry plots line the road, and the air smells of turned earth and canal water.
ev.tanpiju.a.choice.gardens: Walk the garden road from Kinsay
ev.tanpiju.a.choice.mulberry: Ask which gardens feed the silkworms
ev.tanpiju.a.choice.tea: Buy tea from a gardener's stall
ev.tanpiju.a.title: Gardens a Day from Kinsay
ev.tanpiju.b.body: Tanpiju is a great and rich city under Kinsay. The people burn their dead as elsewhere in Manzi, use paper-money, and live by trade and handicrafts, with all necessaries in great plenty and cheapness. Carts from the Heaven City arrive each morning with goods for the local market.
ev.tanpiju.b.choice.funeral: Watch a funeral party pass toward the cremation ground
ev.tanpiju.b.choice.lacquer: Buy lacquerware from a Kinsay trader's stall
ev.tanpiju.b.choice.market: Walk the market where Kinsay goods are sold
ev.tanpiju.b.title: Under Kinsay
ev.tanpiju.entry.body: When you leave Kinsay and travel a day’s journey to the south-east, through a plenteous region, passing a succession of dwellings and charming gardens, you reach the city of TANPIJU, a great, rich, and fine city, under Kinsay. The people are subject to the Kaan, and have paper-money, and are Idolaters, and burn their dead in the way described before. They live by trade and manufactures and handicrafts, and have all necessaries in great plenty and cheapness. But there is no more to be said about it, so we proceed, and I will tell you of another city called VUJU at three days’ distance from Tanpiju. The people are Idolaters, &c., and the city is under Kinsay. They live by trade and manufactures. Travelling through a succession of towns and villages that look like one continuous city, two days further on to the south-east, you find the great and fine city of GHIUJU which is under Kinsay. The people are Idolaters, &c. They have plenty of silk, and live by trade and handicrafts, and have all things necessary in abundance.
ev.tanpiju.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the gate without delay
ev.tanpiju.entry.title: Of the City of Tanpiju and Others
ev.tarsus.entry.body:
A river runs beside the road into Tarsus. Under an awning, Hadiya is tying a roll of cloth to a cart. Her son Yusuf holds the rope while she pulls it tight. He has put the knot on the wrong side, and each time the cart moves the loose end brushes his ear.

“Let me try once more,” he says. Hadiya lets him undo it. She says that when she was young, her mother made her pack the cart for a journey into the hills. She tied everything so tightly that nobody could get the food out at supper. Yusuf asks whether his grandmother still remembers. “She tells that story every time she sees me with a rope.”

Hadiya offers you a place in the shade and points out where the road crosses the water. Yusuf has finally moved the knot to the right side. He asks you to watch the cart while he rolls it a few steps to test his work.

You ask whether the load is meant for the market today. Hadiya says a neighbour is waiting for two rolls, while the rest will leave with a caravan tomorrow. Yusuf pushes the cart a short distance; the knot stays clear of the wheel. ‘Now it works,’ he says. Hadiya checks the lower roll, then asks him to tell the neighbour exactly which cloth is hers. He reads the mark on the wrapping aloud. A ferryman calls from the bank that the crossing is open, and Hadiya points out where you can reach it without bringing the cart through the narrow lane.
ev.tarsus.entry.choice.pass: Thank Hadiya and continue along the river road
ev.tarsus.entry.choice.rest: Spend a day at Hadiya's awning
ev.tarsus.entry.title: The River Road at Tarsus
ev.tarsus.reedbasket.body:
Near the river, Hiba is weaving a basket from reeds. Her grandson Aman has made the handle. It is wide enough for his hand but too short for the basket, and he keeps trying to force it into place.

The basket is for his aunt, who carries bread to relatives outside Tarsus. She lost her old one when a donkey stepped through it. Aman wants to give her a new basket before her next trip. Hiba tells him to soak another reed and make the handle longer. “You can tell her the donkey helped with the design,” she says.

Hiba has several baskets to finish for neighbours and offers a day's pay if you stay to weave with them. You can also sit for a while, share the bread Aman's aunt brought, and hear how the family learned to work by the river.

Aman asks whether the donkey will step on the new basket too. Hiba says his aunt has moved the feeding place since last time, and the animal now stands farther from the door. You ask how they know the handle is long enough. Hiba puts two loaves inside and tells Aman to lift it without squeezing the rim. He tries, then takes out one reed and weaves it back through the handle. ‘Now Aunt can carry it with her arm,’ he says. Hiba checks the knot and asks him to set the basket in the shade until it dries.
ev.tarsus.reedbasket.choice.meal: Sit with Hiba and share the bread
ev.tarsus.reedbasket.choice.work: Stay a day and weave baskets for a wage
ev.tarsus.reedbasket.result.meal: You eat bread beside the river. Hiba says her daughter learned to weave baskets as a child, though she now spends more time carrying bread than making them. Aman listens, then quietly removes his short handle and starts a longer one. His aunt arrives while you are still there and promises to return for it tomorrow. The meal leaves you ready for the road.
ev.tarsus.reedbasket.result.work: You spend the day soaking reeds and holding the basket frames while Hiba and Aman work. Aman makes a new handle. His aunt arrives before dusk, puts six loaves inside, and lifts the basket without straining it. Hiba pays you the promised wage. You leave the next morning as Aman is showing the neighbours how he made the longer handle.
ev.tarsus.reedbasket.title: The Basket for the Journey
ev.tauris.a.body:
Pearl trader Narin has laid a dark cloth over his table so his daughter can see which stones differ in colour. She picks one from a bowl and asks why it is kept apart. ‘Because a customer left it while deciding,’ he says. The daughter puts it back and asks when that customer is coming. Narin admits he does not know, so he writes her name beside the bowl.

You ask about a group of merchants arguing over two roads. One has come from Baldacum with a damaged pack frame; another is waiting for news from Trapezus before sending cloth west. Narin calls them over and asks each to tell you the first reliable stopping place. They disagree about the weather, then discover they travelled in different seasons. His daughter adds the season to both notes.

A full pearl trade parcel costs 135 silver. The hill above the market is open to walk, and the merchants can point out the roads from there. Narin folds the dark cloth over the waiting customer’s pearl before the dust reaches it.
ev.tauris.a.choice.merchants: Ask the merchants about Baldacum and Trapezus
ev.tauris.a.choice.pearls: Buy the full pearl parcel for 135 silver
ev.tauris.a.choice.view: Spend a day walking up the hill above the market
ev.tauris.a.title: The Pearl Table and the Hill Road
ev.tauris.b.body:
On a bench near the covered stalls, interpreter Mariam is helping a cloth seller understand a visitor’s order. The visitor speaks Italian, the seller answers in Persian, and Mariam asks them both to repeat the number of bolts. The seller’s apprentice tries to help by holding up his fingers, but he counts the sample cloth as a full bolt. Mariam takes the sample from him and lets him count again.

You ask how she learned to work between traders. She says her mother kept rooms for travellers and made every child listen at supper. Her own daughter now copies new words into a notebook. A western merchant says he knows the road back toward Constantinopolis; another traveller has just returned from the north and mentions Caffa. Mariam invites the first man to sit, so nobody has to shout across the stall.

She can teach you Persian over twenty days for 20 silver. For now she is making the apprentice read the order back to both customers, one language at a time.
ev.tauris.b.choice.browse: Listen to the northern traveller speak of Caffa
ev.tauris.b.choice.dragoman: Study Persian with Mariam for twenty days and 20 silver
ev.tauris.b.choice.latin: Ask the western merchant about Constantinopolis
ev.tauris.b.title: The Interpreter’s Bench
ev.tauris.c.body:
At a garden outside the market, water keeper Shirin is moving a wooden gate so the next channel can reach a row of young apricot trees. Her nephew has brought dried fruit for the workers and wants to hand it out before everyone washes. She tells him to set the packet on the bench. ‘Then the ants will have it,’ he says. She puts the packet in a clay bowl and asks him to carry the wash water first.

You ask how the garden gets its share. Shirin shows you a list of households with different turns at the qanat outlet. A neighbour arrives to say her pomegranate trees are dry. Shirin checks the list and says their turn follows the apricots. The neighbour watches the gate, then offers to help clear leaves from the channel while she waits. Shirin’s nephew takes the bowl off the bench so no one trips over it.

The garden has space to rest for two weeks, and the nephew sells a small packet of dried fruit for 1.2 silver. Shirin is still checking how far the first trickle has reached.
ev.tauris.c.choice.fruit: Buy a small packet of dried fruit for 1.2 silver
ev.tauris.c.choice.rest: Rest for two weeks with Shirin’s garden household
ev.tauris.c.choice.wander: Walk beside the qanat channels with Shirin
ev.tauris.c.title: The Garden Water Turn
ev.tauris.entry.body:
At a covered market in Tauris, steel seller Farah is arguing gently with her brother over a ledger. He has written the weight of a full trade bale of Damascus steel on the line for a much smaller order. ‘If I send that page to the tax desk, they’ll wonder why the mule is carrying so little,’ she says. Her brother lifts the heavier bale and admits he copied from the wrong tag. Farah puts both tags side by side and asks him to read them aloud.

You ask where new arrivals settle their goods. Farah says the office takes two days to check a large load, while her brother can show you the public well and the road into the market. A porter tells you that the old houses beyond the well have stories from many rulers and many rebuildings; his grandmother remembers where one lane used to bend before a workshop moved there.

Farah’s complete bale of steel is for sale at 145.8 silver. Her brother rewrites the ledger, and she asks you to check the weight once more before she seals it.
ev.tauris.entry.choice.customs: Spend two days registering your goods
ev.tauris.entry.choice.lore: Spend a day hearing the porter’s account of the old lanes
ev.tauris.entry.choice.market: Buy Farah’s full steel bale for 145.8 silver
ev.tauris.entry.title: The Steel Seller’s Ledger
ev.tauris.inkstone.body:
In a potter’s yard behind the market, Samira is setting bowls on a drying shelf while her father grinds a little blue pigment. Her younger brother has written his name beneath every bowl he made, even the ones meant to be sold by their aunt. ‘She needs room for her own mark,’ Samira tells him. He asks why a buyer should not know who shaped the clay. Their father says they can keep both names if the underside is dry enough for another stroke.

You ask how they tell which bowls belong to which order. Samira has a list, but the aunt’s last two bowls look nearly alike. The brother holds them to the light and finds a tiny thumbprint under one rim. He remembers making that one. The aunt arrives and says the other bowl is for a neighbour who has been waiting a week. Samira asks her brother to write the neighbour’s name before the clay dries. He hesitates: his hand is still dusty, and he is afraid of smearing the rim. Their father puts down the pigment and offers him a clean cloth.
ev.tauris.inkstone.choice.day: Stay a day and learn the potter’s drying work
ev.tauris.inkstone.choice.names: Help the family match both names to the orders
ev.tauris.inkstone.result.day: You stay the day shifting the bowls as air and shade change. Samira shows you which rims need more time before anyone writes on them. By dusk her brother can place the aunt’s mark beside his own without smearing the clay.
ev.tauris.inkstone.result.names: You read the orders back while Samira’s brother writes the names with clean hands. The aunt takes the correct bowl to her neighbour, who checks the small mark and thanks the family. Samira folds the corrected list beside the drying shelf.
ev.tauris.inkstone.title: The Potter’s Name on the Bowl
ev.tauris.mentor_astrodice.body: Beside the card table, another reader keeps three dice for the hour of departure.
ev.tauris.mentor_astrodice.choice.ask: Ask what the houses mean on the road
ev.tauris.mentor_astrodice.title: Star-dice in Tauris
ev.tauris.mentor_tarot.body:
Near the caravan lodgings, a widow named Lucia is sorting a set of painted cards while her nephew repairs the box. He asks why two cards show travellers leaving by different roads. ‘Because the painter could not fit both roads on one card,’ she says. He calls that a poor excuse, and she asks him to draw a better one.

You ask what she does with the cards. Lucia says she uses them to teach visitors to tell a choice clearly: what they hope for, what they can afford, and whom the choice will affect. Her nephew says some travellers come back only to tell her what happened next. ‘And you always listen?’ you ask. ‘When they bring supper,’ she says, and the nephew groans because he has been carrying the bowls himself. She puts the repaired box beside her and asks what you want to know.
ev.tauris.mentor_tarot.choice.ask: Ask Lucia to explain how she uses the cards
ev.tauris.mentor_tarot.choice.learn: Study with Lucia for ten days and 60 silver
ev.tauris.mentor_tarot.choice.learn_astr: Pay and learn the star-dice as well
ev.tauris.mentor_tarot.title: The Widow’s Picture Cards
ev.tenduc.a.body:
At a small church, reader Yuhanna is trimming a lamp while his daughter copies a Syriac word from an old page. She has written the final letter twice and asks which form he meant. ‘The one I said slowly,’ he replies. She says he said both slowly. You laugh, and Yuhanna reads the word aloud again, this time pointing to each letter.

You ask what the page records. He says it keeps the names of families who cared for travellers here before his time. A visitor has brought a separate story connecting local Christians with the old tale of Priest John; Yuhanna treats it as the visitor’s account and asks his daughter to mark it as such. She asks why. ‘Then someone who reads it later can still ask who told us,’ he says.

A woman comes to borrow lamp oil for the evening gathering. Yuhanna shows her what remains and asks his daughter to note the amount. There is room to sit and listen through the day, and he can also tell you which post roads lead toward Cambaluc and Cacanfu.
ev.tenduc.a.choice.ask-cambaluc: Ask Yuhanna about the roads to Cambaluc and Cacanfu
ev.tenduc.a.choice.attend: Spend a day at the church gathering and listen to the reader
ev.tenduc.a.choice.offer: Give 1.2 silver for the gathering’s lamp oil
ev.tenduc.a.title: The Reader’s Lamp
ev.tenduc.b.body:
At the cloth market, seller Sira is cutting a fresh label for a full cotton-cloth bale. Her cousin wants to use the old label after the mistake at the posting yard. ‘There is nothing wrong with the string,’ he says. Sira asks him to read the mark aloud. He stops halfway, sees why she wants a clean tag, and starts writing.

Beside them a Muslim grain trader and a Christian weaver are comparing how their families count bundles. You ask whether either method is easier on a busy day. The weaver says the best one is the one the next person can read. A Buddhist neighbour comes to collect a length of cloth for her household and jokes that she can read neither man’s hurried hand. They make the cousin show her his new mark before she leaves.

Sira’s full trade bale costs 108 silver. The grain trader knows the northern way toward Egrigaia; he stays until the cousin has made one last label that everyone can read.

The cousin asks the neighbour to read the tag once more. She points to the last stroke and says it looks like another seller’s mark. Sira hands him a fresh reed pen. ‘This time write slowly enough for her,’ she says. He does, and the neighbour nods.
ev.tenduc.b.choice.ask-north: Ask the grain trader about the northern road to Egrigaia
ev.tenduc.b.choice.buy-cloth: Buy Sira’s full cotton-cloth bale for 108 silver
ev.tenduc.b.choice.walk: Spend a day hearing how the market keeps its accounts
ev.tenduc.b.title: The Cloth Marker’s Stall
ev.tenduc.entry.body:
At the Fengzhou posting yard, clerk Miriam is drying a sheet with yesterday’s rain still on its edges. Her father keeps the water jars there and worries the ink will run again. ‘Put it on the shelf away from the door,’ he tells her. She lifts it, then asks him to move the shelf; he has placed it directly under a leak. They both laugh as they find a dry spot together.

You ask where a traveller should register. Miriam points to the desk and then toward the market, where a cloth seller has just found that one of her bundles is marked for the wrong caravan. The seller’s young cousin insists he copied the mark correctly. Miriam says the posting books can settle it if they spend the day checking. At a stone heap beside the road, another family is replacing a wind-torn ribbon; they invite passersby to help hold it while they tie the knot.

Miriam’s father brings you water. ‘Take a cup before you choose where to go,’ he says. The cousin appears at the yard gate with the disputed bundle under his arm.
ev.tenduc.entry.choice.market: Spend a day checking the cloth bundle at the market
ev.tenduc.entry.choice.pass: Register and continue through the posting yard
ev.tenduc.entry.choice.shrine: Help the family tie a new ribbon at the roadside stones
ev.tenduc.entry.title: At the Fengzhou Posting Yard
ev.tenduc.ribbons.body:
At the roadside stones, the grandmother you met earlier is showing her grandson how to cut a ribbon from a damaged coat. A neighbour says the coat still has a good sleeve and offers to mend it instead. The boy holds up the torn hem. ‘This part is too short to wear,’ he says. His grandmother agrees and asks him to leave the sleeve alone.

You ask why they tie cloth here. She says her family stops to remember people returning by the road, and the strips help children notice when the wind has changed. The neighbour’s daughter arrives with water and asks if her father’s ribbon is still there. The grandmother finds a faded green strip and lets the girl replace it herself. A gust sends the boy’s new strip across the ground. He chases it, then returns with a question: should it go beside the green one or where the wind will catch it first? The two children wait while the grandmother considers.

The boy still has the good sleeve folded over his arm.
ev.tenduc.ribbons.choice.sew: Help the neighbour mend the remaining coat sleeve
ev.tenduc.ribbons.choice.wind: Spend a day teaching the children to read the wind
ev.tenduc.ribbons.result.sew: You help sew the good sleeve back onto the coat. The neighbour’s daughter ties the green ribbon herself, and the boy sets his new strip beside it. The grandmother thanks you and takes the repaired coat home.
ev.tenduc.ribbons.result.wind: You stay the day, returning to the stones whenever the wind shifts. By evening the children can tell which strip faces the road and which has turned toward the market. Their grandmother lets them choose the place for the new ribbon.
ev.tenduc.ribbons.title: The Wind at the Roadside Stones
ev.tiju.entry.body: When you leave Cayu, you ride another day to the south-east through a constant succession of villages and fields and fine farms until you come to TIJU, which is a city of no great size but abounding in everything. The people are Idolaters (and so forth). There is a great amount of trade, and they have many vessels. And you must know that on your left hand, that is towards the east, and three days’ journey distant, is the Ocean Sea. At every place between the sea and the city salt is made in great quantities.
ev.tiju.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.tiju.entry.title: Of the Cities of Tiju, Tinju, and Yanju
ev.trapezus.entry.body:
Trebizond stands where the mountains meet the Black Sea. Tamar has spread two wool cloaks over a low wall above the water. Her daughter Ana takes one down because the wind keeps lifting its corner. The other belongs to her younger brother Davit, who has left it outside since morning.

“He says it needs more air,” Ana tells you. Tamar says he forgot it when he went to watch boats. She has been repairing both cloaks before her children travel inland, and she wants Davit back to try his on before she finishes the hem.

Tamar asks where you are bound and points out the lane down to the boats. Ana can show you the places where travellers wait for a crossing. If you have a day, Tamar will walk with you through the streets and ask the sailors which boats have gone toward Caffa.

You ask Anna whether Davit knows which cloak is his. ‘He knows,’ she says, ‘but he will claim mine is warmer.’ Tamar calls toward the ships, and he appears carrying a small coil of rope for his pack. He tries on the cloak she kept for him; one sleeve sits too high. His mother asks him to stand still while she loosens the seam. Davit says he can wait, then points to a boatman below who has promised news of the Caffa passage. Anna reminds him to ask about the departure day as well as the fare.
ev.trapezus.entry.choice.look: Spend a day with Tamar above the harbour
ev.trapezus.entry.choice.pass: Thank Tamar and continue through the town
ev.trapezus.entry.title: Above the Water at Trebizond
ev.trapezus.tworoads.body:
Tamar has laid two travel bags by her door. Ana is going south toward Aleppo, where an aunt who taught her to weave has asked her to visit. Davit is taking their father's old spindle southeast toward Edessa; a friend there promised to repair its bent shaft.

Ana thinks Davit's bag is too heavy. He says she packed all the food into his, and empties it onto the floor to prove his point. Tamar divides the bread between them. Ana slips an extra piece back into his bag when he is not looking.

They leave by different inland roads in the morning. Tamar can walk with one child as far as the first rest place; she asks whether you will accompany the other. Both know the stopping places from family journeys, so you can choose which road to learn as you go.

You ask why Davit carries the old spindle all that way. ‘Father used it before I was born,’ he says. ‘My friend knows a turner who may straighten it.’ Anna asks whether he has written the friend’s address where he can find it. Davit pats one pocket, then another, and finally takes a folded note from the bread cloth. Tamar tells him to put it in his belt before the food stains the ink. Anna laughs, but checks her own letter to the aunt too. Their mother gives each of them a small packet of salt for the road and asks them to meet the family again when they can.
ev.trapezus.tworoads.choice.ana: Walk one day with Ana toward Aleppo
ev.trapezus.tworoads.choice.davit: Walk one day with Davit toward Edessa
ev.trapezus.tworoads.result.ana: You spend the day on the road with Ana. She points out the turns her aunt taught her and names the places where the family has stayed on earlier journeys. At the first rest place she opens her bag and finds a small packet of dried fruit that Tamar slipped in beside the bread. You mark Trebizond, Aleppo, and the route between them on your map. Ana thanks you and sets off again in the morning.
ev.trapezus.tworoads.result.davit: You spend the day with Davit on the eastern road. He shows you the places where his father once stopped with the spindle in his pack. At the first rest place he finds the extra bread Ana gave him and smiles; he saves it for breakfast. You mark Trebizond, Edessa, and the route between them on your map. Davit takes the spindle out once more to check that its shaft has survived the day.
ev.trapezus.tworoads.title: Two Roads from Tamar’s Door
ev.tripolis.entry.body:
After reaching Tripolis, you follow a cart carrying goods for a ship down to the harbour. It stops beside the quay. The bottom of a wooden crate has split, leaving sugar stuck to a wheel. Hassan and another porter lift it onto an old piece of sailcloth.

"My sister packed this one," Hassan says. "She draws a little moon on the side. When I find it, I'll know whose account it goes on."

His sister is writing on the next batch of crates under a shed. She runs over, sees the crack, and says she will fetch a carpenter. Hassan starts to lift the crate again. "Gather the corners of the cloth first," she tells him. "We can still get the sugar back in."

A ship is waiting for its cargo. The coastal road leads south; people here also travel north to Antioch. For now the brother and sister are trying to get this one crate aboard.
ev.tripolis.entry.choice.pass: Ask them for the southern road and keep travelling
ev.tripolis.entry.choice.rest: Help gather the sugar and rest in town for a day
ev.tripolis.entry.title: The Sugar Crate at the Harbour
ev.tripolis.oven.body:
The communal oven is hot. People wait with dough on wooden boards as the baker loads one batch after another. An old man arrives last with three rounds covered in sesame seeds. "For my grandson's ship," he says.

The baker asks when it sails. The man only knows that his grandson asked him to come before noon. Two women ahead of him move their boards aside to make room.

The man thanks them, scattering sesame seeds from his sleeve. His grandson is sailing to Alexandria for the first time. Before leaving he complained that the bread was too hard; now he has asked for three rounds and seems to be in a hurry for them.

The baker asks whether the grandson can keep the loaves dry. "He grew up in this yard," the old man says. "He knows what a cloth is for." A woman near the oven offers a spare wrapper, and the old man thanks her before remembering he brought one of his own. The baker takes the little boards in order and says the sesame loaves can go into the next batch. The old man peers towards the port through the doorway, hoping there is still time to carry them down.
ev.tripolis.oven.choice.bake: Help carry the bread to the harbour
ev.tripolis.oven.choice.damascus: Wait for this batch and ask the baker about the road to Damascus
ev.tripolis.oven.result.bake:
The bread is hot when it comes out. You and the old man carry the board between you to the quay. His grandson sees him from the ship and runs down the gangplank. "Share them on the way," the old man says. "Don't eat them all at once." The young man takes a bite and says this batch is just right.

Back in town, the baker is making room for the next batch. The old man collects his board and says he will come tomorrow to keep an eye on his neighbour's dough.
ev.tripolis.oven.result.damascus:
As he loads the oven, the baker tells you that caravans for Damascus gather east of town. Before leaving, their drivers often bake thin loaves to carry for several days. He points to the long boards against the wall; they are used to slide the dough into the oven.

The old man hears where you are headed and offers you a piece of fresh sesame bread. You remember where the caravan gathers.
ev.tripolis.oven.title: Bread for the Ship
ev.tripolis.quay.body:
At the quay, a young woman looks from one boat to another. She holds a short length of blue rope tied with three knots. Her father ties its match to the family boat's oar so that she can recognise it when he comes in.

"The boat is here, but the oar isn't," she says. "Father says he lent it to the next boat. They say he didn't. I need to find it before they leave."

A porter overhears her. "Your father went to buy a new oar this morning. Ask him before you search every boat in the harbour." She blushes but still wants to know what happened.

The girl holds up the knotted end for the loader to see. "If it is our oar, the middle knot will be tight. Father always pulls that one twice." He admits he did not look at the rope and tells her to ask the other crew before accusing anyone. A younger boy runs past with a coil of line and says he saw her father at the carpenter's stall. She calls after him to ask whether he was buying wood or fetching a finished oar, but he is already aboard a boat. She turns back to the two crews.
ev.tripolis.quay.choice.help: Help her ask about the oar on both boats
ev.tripolis.quay.choice.road: Ask the porter for the coastal road to Tyre
ev.tripolis.quay.result.help:
The other boat's master takes you to the stern. The old oar is there, with its blue rope still tied to the handle. He says he borrowed it that morning while her father went into town to buy a new one. He had promised to return it by noon. She remembers that her father spoke in a hurry that morning; she caught only the words "the oar is next door."

They carry the old oar back together. The master grins. "Next time, tell your father to write it down. It'll save you a walk round the harbour." She offers you some water and remembers your help.
ev.tripolis.quay.result.road:
The porter takes you to the end of the quay and points south along the coast. "For Tyre, follow those mule carts. They leave through the south gate this afternoon."

The young woman comes over. "Father sails to Tyre in a few days. If you meet him, tell him I found the old oar. Next time he lends something, he can tell me the whole story." The porter laughs, and so does she.
ev.tripolis.quay.title: The Blue Rope on the Boats
ev.tyrus.entry.body:
The road reaches the sea at Tyre. Beside some old stonework, Salma has spread a cloth over a low shelter. She is mending her younger brother's sandal with a thick needle. He holds the other sandal against his foot and announces that this pair will last until he is grown.

“You said that about the last pair,” Salma tells him. “It lasted six weeks.” He says the stones near the shore are unusually sharp. She gives him the needle to hold while she tests the new stitching.

Salma offers you water and asks where you came from. Her brother supplies three guesses before you can answer. She knows which stretch of the coastal road stays clear after rain, and draws it with her finger in the dust. When you take out your map, she asks you to mark the shelter too. “Travellers bring their sandals to me. My brother asks each one where they came from, then draws their roads in the dust.”
ev.tyrus.entry.choice.pass: Thank Salma and continue along the coast
ev.tyrus.entry.choice.rest: Stay by Salma's shelter for a day
ev.tyrus.entry.title: Arriving at Tyre
ev.tyrus.fishrack.body:
Farida is tying a new crosspiece to a drying rack. Her daughter Lina holds it up from below. A strip of salted fish hangs from the old side of the frame, just out of the reach of a cat that has been following the work.

Lina says her uncle taught her the knot before he went inland to work as a carpenter. She has tied it twice, and it still slips. “He used to pull the rope with his teeth,” she says. Farida makes her take it out of her mouth. “He also lost a tooth. Use both hands.”

Farida sells small packets of fish to people on the road. The rack needs another crosspiece before she can hang today's catch. She asks whether you would like food for the journey or have time to stay and work with them. The cat sits beneath the unfinished side, waiting for an answer of its own.
ev.tyrus.fishrack.choice.buy: Buy Farida’s salted fish for 0.8 silver
ev.tyrus.fishrack.choice.stay: Spend the day helping them finish the rack
ev.tyrus.fishrack.result.buy: You pay Farida for a packet. Lina wraps it in a clean scrap of cloth and ties the knot her uncle taught her; this time it holds. On the road, you eat the fish with bread and feel stronger. Farida counts the coins into the small pot she keeps for new rope. The cat receives one tiny piece that fell from the rack.
ev.tyrus.fishrack.result.stay: You hold the frame while Farida fastens the crosspiece. Lina tries the knot again with both hands. It stays tight, and she hangs the first fish on the new side. By evening the rack is full. Farida gives you supper and a place beneath the shelter for the night; you leave the next morning. She tells the nearby families who helped build it, and they greet you when you pass.
ev.tyrus.fishrack.title: The Fish Rack by the Shore
ev.yarcan.entry.body:
At a Yarcan cloth stall, a merchant named Nasir is tying up a bolt his sister has finished weaving. She arrives with a narrower strip and asks him to add it to the parcel. ‘That is for our aunt,’ he says. ‘If I sell it with the rest, she will come looking for her border.’ His sister unrolls the strip to show the little flower their aunt asked for.

You ask whether travellers often buy from this family. Nasir says they trade with caravans and neighbours alike. Across the lane, a cobbler who grew up with them is repairing Nasir’s boots. He asks the sister to bring the aunt’s strip closer so he can compare its blue thread with the cord he has for the boot. She laughs that he has found yet another reason to leave his workbench.

Nasir can point you toward the wells used by departing caravans. His sister invites you to stay a day if you want to see how cloth, leather and river stone pass from one household to the next. The cobbler holds up the repaired boot and asks whose foot it belongs to.
ev.yarcan.entry.choice.look: Stay a day with Nasir’s family and neighbours
ev.yarcan.entry.choice.pass: Ask about the next wells and continue
ev.yarcan.entry.title: The Cloth Stalls at Yarcan
ev.yarcan.loomreed.body:
In a weaving room, Dilara has stopped her loom with half a border unfinished. A narrow reed has split, and the blue thread keeps slipping out of line. Her little sister has gone to fetch a replacement but returns with a reed for a wider loom. ‘It fits the frame,’ the girl says. Dilara shows her why the teeth leave too much space for this pattern.

You ask when the cloth must be ready. Dilara says their aunt wants it for a family gathering tomorrow, after a cousin returns from the caravan road. She could borrow the right reed from a neighbour, though she would rather replace her own first. Her sister says she can walk over with a message and explain the delay; the aunt will understand if she knows what happened. Dilara asks the girl to read the note aloud before taking it.

The proper reed costs 1 silver at the next yard. Dilara has laid out the threads in order so she can resume as soon as it arrives. Her sister holds the note and waits for a decision.
ev.yarcan.loomreed.choice.buy: Pay 1 silver for the proper loom reed
ev.yarcan.loomreed.choice.letter: Walk with the sister and explain the delay
ev.yarcan.loomreed.result.buy: You bring the proper reed to Dilara. She fits it while her sister holds the threads, then weaves the blue border straight. The aunt arrives before dusk and thanks you for helping them finish in time.
ev.yarcan.loomreed.result.letter: You walk with the girl to her aunt’s house. The aunt reads Dilara’s note and offers the right reed from her own storeroom. The sisters finish the border together; you remember how quickly the family found a way through the trouble.
ev.yarcan.loomreed.title: The Broken Reed in the Loom
ev.yarcan.site_gap.body:
In an orchard, keeper Farida has wrapped cuttings in damp cloth. Her son wants to graft them before the afternoon heat rises. She says the tree is ready, but first he must ask whose branch he has brought. It came from their neighbour’s old tree, whose fruit the two families have shared since the children were small. The neighbour arrives with a basket and asks whether one cutting will be enough.

You ask how the new branch will take. Farida shows the sloping cut and where the bark layers should meet. Her son holds the tree steady; the neighbour promises to water it while Farida is away at market. Farida says she will leave the binding loose enough for a new bud to grow. The son asks if the fruit will taste exactly like the old tree’s. ‘We will have to wait and see,’ his mother says.

The neighbour has travelled toward Cascar recently and can name the stopping places. Farida sets another cutting on the damp cloth for you to watch her fit before the sun reaches the row.
ev.yarcan.site_gap.choice.interact: Watch Farida fit the new cutting
ev.yarcan.site_gap.title: The Orchard Keeper’s Grafting Knife
ev.yasdi.battuta_a.body:
In a Yazd lodging house, the keeper, Hamid, is mending a torn mat. His daughter brings bread to two travellers who came from Isfahan and had earlier crossed the Fars hills. They tell her how small lodgings along that mountain road keep food ready for people who arrive late.

‘Do they know who is coming?’ she asks. ‘Usually not,’ one traveller says. ‘That’s why your father keeps an extra loaf, isn’t it?’ Hamid smiles and asks her to set the bread beside the guests. The travellers also pass on a story they heard in Shiraz about a religious elder who welcomed strangers. You can stay overnight, join the evening prayers, or ask them about the road they took from Isfahan to Yazd.
ev.yasdi.battuta_a.choice.cell: Stay overnight at the lodging house
ev.yasdi.battuta_a.choice.shiraz: Ask how they travelled from Isfahan to Yazd
ev.yasdi.battuta_a.title: A Lodging Keeper’s Tale
ev.yasdi.entry.body:
In a Yazd workshop, a weaver named Roya cuts a loose thread from a length of silk. Her younger brother holds the cloth up to the light and points to a place he thinks she has missed.

‘That one belongs to the pattern,’ she says, turning the fabric over for him to see. A merchant waiting by the door will take this piece with him when it is ready. He tells you that Yazd silk travels far; for the road beyond the town, he is filling every water skin he has. Roya’s brother wants to know where you are headed so he can tell you which courtyard still has a well.

You ask the merchant why he is waiting instead of collecting the cloth. He says Roya promised to check the edge in daylight; last time a folded corner hid a loose stitch, and his buyer noticed first. Roya tells him that was another order and asks her brother to bring the whole length outside. The boy balances it across both arms. ‘This one is for your buyer with the blue border, yes?’ she asks. The merchant confirms it, then asks if the courtyard well is open. Her brother says it is, though the keeper has a queue of potters waiting. Roya promises to finish the edge while he fills a skin.
ev.yasdi.entry.choice.look: Spend a day looking around and taking notes
ev.yasdi.entry.title: The Weavers of Yazd
ev.yasdi.threadwell.body:
Roya’s brother has promised to bring water for the workshop, but the shared jar at the well is cracked. Water keeps leaking onto his sandals. Roya needs the silk rinsed before the merchant returns.

The well keeper lends him a sound jar now and asks him to help repair the broken one when the potter arrives. He looks at the workshop, then at you. ‘I need to get water to Roya. Could you help with the old jar later?’ The keeper sets the sound jar between them and tells the boy to carry it to Roya first. The potter will look at the cracked one after she finishes a neighbour’s order.

You ask whether the cracked jar has served the well long. The keeper says her father left it there years ago; everyone knows its blue rim and brings it back after use. Roya’s brother asks if a repair will hold. The potter, passing with another customer’s bowl, says she needs to see the crack dry before promising anything. He reaches for the borrowed jar, then stops because his sandals are wet and his hands are slippery. The keeper wipes the handle with a cloth and asks him to hold it by both sides. He takes two careful steps, glances back at you, and says his sister will worry if the water is late again.
ev.yasdi.threadwell.choice.carry: Carry water back to Roya now
ev.yasdi.threadwell.choice.repair: Spend a day helping mend the jar
ev.yasdi.threadwell.result.carry: You take a smaller jar back to the workshop. Roya rinses the silk and hangs it where the air can reach it. Her brother brings you a cup of cool water before going back for the next load. You feel refreshed.
ev.yasdi.threadwell.result.repair: The potter shows Roya’s brother how to seal the crack, then lets the repair dry. You spend the day helping him and carrying water in another jar. By evening the caretaker knows your name and thanks you for keeping the workshop supplied.
ev.yasdi.threadwell.title: Roya’s Water Jar
